Earth has a magnetic field; compass points to the magnetic north. Electromagnet = coil of wire round an iron core with current; strength changes with number of coils, current (cells) and core. Fair test, variables, results table, graph.
34|9 Magnetism.notYet: Not taught: domains or electron explanations of magnetism, magnetic flux density or tesla, right-hand grip rule, motors, generators, electromagnetic induction, transformers, F=BIL, Earth's core dynamo or magnetic reversals, solar wind, Ohm's law and calculations with V, I, R.
34|9 Magnetism.example: A student makes an electromagnet by winding wire round an iron nail and connecting it to a cell. She wants to make it stronger. Give two changes she could make. Answer: Any two of: add more turns of wire (coils); use more cells (a bigger current); use an iron core (a nail) if there is none. Do not accept 'use a longer wire' alone.

35|1 Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
35|1 Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle.teaches: Photosynthesis as carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts. Leaf structure, stomata, and how water and CO2 enter. Rate factors: light, CO2, temperature. Uses of glucose (respiration, starch, cellulose, proteins). Carbon cycle: photosynthesis, respiration, combustion, decay. Greenhouse gases, global warming, climate change effects, reducing emissions.
35|1 Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle.notYet: ATP, light-dependent and light-independent stages, RuBP, Calvin cycle, photolysis, enzymes in photosynthesis, limiting-factor graph theory, chloroplast internal structure (thylakoids, grana), C3/C4 plants, ocean acidification chemistry, radiative forcing calculations, balanced symbol equations beyond word equations.
35|1 Photosynthesis and the carbon cycle.example: Question: Marcus put a piece of pondweed in water under a lamp and counted the bubbles of oxygen it gave off. (a) Name the gas in the bubbles. (b) He moved the lamp closer to the pondweed. Predict what happened to the number of bubbles and explain why. Answer: (a) Oxygen. (b) The number of bubbles increased, because more light energy was available so the pondweed photosynthesised faster and made more oxygen.

35|2 Properties of materials.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
35|2 Properties of materials.teaches: Atoms have a nucleus of protons and neutrons with electrons in shells. Atomic number gives the number of protons and electrons. Electronic structure of the first 20 elements. Periods and groups. Group 1 (alkali metals) and Group 7 (halogens): reactivity and melting point trends. Full outer shells and noble gases. Ionic and covalent bonding at a simple level. Simple molecules versus giant structures (diamond, sodium chloride) and their properties.
35|2 Properties of materials.notYet: Relative atomic mass calculations, isotopes, mole concept, electronegativity, ionisation energy, orbitals/sub-shells, writing ionic or half equations, dot-and-cross diagrams for double bonds, metallic bonding detail, electrolysis, transition metal chemistry, bond energies, intermolecular force names.
35|2 Properties of materials.example: Sodium has atomic number 11. (a) How many electrons does a sodium atom have? (b) Write its electronic structure. (c) Which group of the Periodic Table is it in, and how do you know? Answer: (a) 11. (b) 2,8,1. (c) Group 1, because it has one electron in its outer shell.

34|Science Skills.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 8 Learners Book
34|Science Skills.teaches: Working scientifically at Stage 8: planning fair tests, naming independent, dependent and control variables, making predictions, choosing equipment, and spotting hazards and risks in a lab picture. Learners record results in tables, take repeat readings, find a mean, plot line graphs and bar charts, spot anomalies, describe patterns, and evaluate and suggest improvements. They use accuracy, precision, reliability and conclusion.
34|Science Skills.notYet: No formal uncertainty or error bars, standard deviation, statistical tests, or formal correlation coefficients. No rearranging equations, standard form, or significant-figure rules. No hypothesis-testing jargon (null hypothesis), no formal risk-assessment documents or COSHH. No IGCSE terms such as systematic or random error, or resolution. Avoid content from other chapters.
34|Science Skills.example:
A student tests how the mass of a trolley affects how far it rolls down a ramp. (a) Name the independent variable. (b) Name the dependent variable. (c) Give one variable that must be kept the same. (d) The student repeats each test three times and gets 52 cm, 50 cm and 54 cm. Calculate the mean distance.

Answer: (a) mass of the trolley. (b) distance rolled. (c) Any one: height or angle of the ramp, the same trolley and surface, or the same release point. (d) (52 + 50 + 54) ÷ 3 = 156 ÷ 3 = 52 cm.

35|3 Forces and energy.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
35|3 Forces and energy.teaches: Density as mass ÷ volume (g/cm³, kg/m³), measuring mass and volume (displacement), floating and sinking. Temperature (°C, thermometer) versus thermal energy; energy flows from hot to cold. Energy stores and transfers, conservation of energy, Sankey-style ideas. Particle model: particles move faster when heated. Conduction, convection, radiation; evaporation cools a liquid because the faster particles escape.
35|3 Forces and energy.notYet: Specific heat capacity (Q=mcΔT), kinetic energy ½mv² and GPE mgh calculations, efficiency percentage formulae, power (P=E/t), pressure, latent heat, Kelvin scale, absolute zero, Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, U-values, infrared wavelengths, rearranging density with unit conversions between kg/m³ and g/cm³.
35|3 Forces and energy.example: A block of metal has a mass of 240 g and a volume of 30 cm³. (a) Calculate its density. (b) Will it float or sink in water, which has a density of 1 g/cm³? Explain. Answer: (a) density = mass ÷ volume = 240 ÷ 30 = 8 g/cm³. (b) It sinks, because its density (8 g/cm³) is greater than the density of water (1 g/cm³).

42|4 3D shapes.teaches: Naming and describing 3D shapes: cube, cuboid, sphere, cylinder, cone, pyramid (square- and triangle-based), prism (triangular). Counting faces, edges and vertices. Describing faces as flat or curved and naming 2D face shapes (square, rectangle, triangle, circle). Sorting 3D shapes by properties. Spotting 3D shapes in everyday objects. Words: face, edge, vertex/vertices, flat, curved.
42|4 3D shapes.notYet: Volume or surface area formulae, nets as formal constructions, Euler's formula, angles in degrees, right angles on 3D shapes, parallel faces, radius/diameter/circumference, hexagonal or pentagonal prisms, cross-sections, symmetry of 3D shapes, capacity in litres tied to shape.
42|4 3D shapes.example: Sam has a square-based pyramid. (a) How many faces does it have? (b) How many vertices does it have? (c) What shape are its sloping faces? Answer: (a) 5 faces (b) 5 vertices (c) triangles.

35|4 Maintaining life.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
35|4 Maintaining life.teaches: Plants: water uptake by osmosis through root hair cells (large surface area, thin wall), xylem transport, transpiration through stomata and guard cells, and factors affecting its rate (temperature, wind, humidity, light). Humans: excretion, kidneys, urea, urine, lungs and skin, and the urinary system. Fetus: placenta, umbilical cord, and effects of smoking, alcohol and drugs.
35|4 Maintaining life.notYet: Do not ask about water potential, active transport, cohesion-tension, the nephron, filtration and selective reabsorption, ADH, osmoregulation, dialysis, deamination, the urea cycle, ATP or ribosomes, hormones in pregnancy, or the placenta's detailed diffusion gradients. Do not require calculations of rate using formulae.
35|4 Maintaining life.example: Question: A plant is moved from a cool, still room to a hot, windy place. (a) Predict what happens to the rate of transpiration. (b) Explain your answer. Answer: (a) It increases. (b) Heat gives water molecules more energy so they evaporate faster from the leaf. Wind blows away water vapour near the stomata, so more water diffuses out of the leaf. More water is then pulled up the xylem.

35|5 Reactivity.book: Cambridge Lower Secondary Science 9 Learners Book
35|5 Reactivity.teaches: Reactivity series (e.g. potassium, sodium, lithium, calcium, magnesium, aluminium, zinc, iron, copper, silver, gold) from reactions with water, acid and oxygen. Displacement of less reactive metals from solutions or oxides (thermite). Making salts from acid with metal, base/alkali or carbonate. Crystallisation, filtering, word equations, conservation of mass, balanced symbol equations, electron diagrams, ions.
35|5 Reactivity.notYet: Ionic half-equations, oxidation and reduction as electron transfer, oxidation numbers, electrode potentials, electrolysis, extraction by blast furnace equations, moles and molar calculations, state symbols, ionic equations, titration calculations, percentage yield, activation energy, Group 1 trends explained by atomic radius.
35|5 Reactivity.example: Question: Zinc is added to blue copper sulfate solution. (a) Predict what you would see. (b) Write the word equation. (c) Explain why the reaction happens. Answer: (a) Reddish-brown solid (copper) forms on the zinc and the blue solution fades to colourless. (b) zinc + copper sulfate → zinc sulfate + copper. (c) Zinc is more reactive than copper, so it displaces (pushes out) copper from the copper sulfate solution.

42|6 Measurement, area and perimeter.teaches: Measuring and comparing length (m, cm), mass (kg, g) and capacity (l, ml) using suitable units and scales; choosing sensible units and estimating. Perimeter of 2D shapes (rectangles, polygons) by adding side lengths. Area as the number of squares covered, counted in whole and half squares on a grid. Words: perimeter, area, square, estimate.
42|6 Measurement, area and perimeter.notYet: No area formula (length × width) and no cm² or m² units. No perimeter formulae or missing-side algebra. No circles, circumference, or compound L-shapes with unlabelled sides. No decimals or mixed-unit conversions beyond simple m–cm, kg–g, l–ml facts. No angles or degrees.
42|6 Measurement, area and perimeter.example: A rectangle on a 1 cm grid is 5 cm long and 3 cm wide. (a) What is its perimeter? (b) Count the squares inside it. How many squares does it cover? Answer: (a) 5 + 3 + 5 + 3 = 16 cm. (b) 15 squares (counted on the grid).

42|7 Fractions of shapes.teaches: Recognising and shading unit fractions and non-unit fractions of shapes (halves, thirds, quarters, sixths, eighths, tenths). Equal parts, numerator and denominator in simple use. Seeing that different-looking equal shares can be the same fraction. Equivalence by folding, shading and fraction walls (1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8, 1/2 = 3/6). Partitioning squares, rectangles and circles.
42|7 Fractions of shapes.notYet: Not yet: fractions of quantities or amounts, adding or subtracting fractions, improper fractions or mixed numbers, decimals and percentages, simplifying by dividing, finding common denominators, ordering unlike fractions by calculation, area formulae, angles in degrees.
42|7 Fractions of shapes.example: A rectangle is split into 8 equal squares. 4 squares are shaded. (a) What fraction is shaded? (b) Write another fraction that is equal to it, using the same rectangle folded into 2 equal parts. Answer: (a) 4/8 (b) 1/2, so 4/8 = 1/2.

42|8 Time.teaches: Reading and telling time on analogue clocks (o'clock, half past, quarter past, quarter to, five-minute intervals) and digital clocks (e.g. 3:45). Using a.m. and p.m. Knowing 60 minutes in 1 hour, 24 hours in a day, and the months and days of the year. Reading calendars. Ordering and comparing simple times and events. Using seconds, minutes and hours as units.
42|8 Time.notYet: 24-hour clock notation (e.g. 15:30). Calculating elapsed time across hours with minutes, or timetables with many steps. Time zones. Converting minutes to seconds in multi-step problems. Speed or rate. Leap-year rules. Reading to the nearest minute on analogue clocks. Angles in degrees on clock hands.
42|8 Time.example: Sam starts reading at quarter past 4 in the afternoon. He stops at half past 4. How many minutes did he read for? Answer: 15 minutes. (Quarter past 4 is 4:15, half past 4 is 4:30.)

42|5 Multiplication and division.teaches: Multiplication as equal groups, arrays and repeated addition; division as sharing and grouping. Learners link × and ÷ as inverses and use fact families. They double 2× to get 4× and double 4× to get 8×. They build 3×, 6× and 9× facts (6× is double 3×; 9× is 10× minus one group). Tables up to 10 × 10, with words such as 'product', 'multiple', 'share', 'group' and 'array'.
42|5 Multiplication and division.notYet: Long multiplication or short/long division, remainders, formal written methods, multiplying by 7 or 11/12 as a focus, fractions of amounts, decimals, negative numbers, area formulae, factors/prime numbers, BIDMAS, algebra with letters, and numbers beyond about 100 in answers.
42|5 Multiplication and division.example: Maya knows 3 × 7 = 21. Use this to work out 6 × 7. Then write a division fact using 42 and 6. Answer: 6 × 7 is double 21, so 42. Division fact: 42 ÷ 6 = 7 (or 42 ÷ 7 = 6).

42|9 More addition and subtraction.teaches: Adding two- and three-digit numbers, regrouping ones into tens (and tens into hundreds), with totals within 1000. Reordering addends to make friendly sums, e.g. 38 + 25 + 12. Subtracting by regrouping a ten as 10 ones, using partitioning, number lines and place-value counters. Complements: pairs to 10, 20, 100, and sometimes 1000. Words: regroup, partition, complement, total, difference.
42|9 More addition and subtraction.notYet: Formal column addition or subtraction with several regroupings, decimals or money with decimals, numbers beyond 1000, negative numbers, estimating by rounding to the nearest 10 or 100 formally, multiplication or division, algebra with unknowns beyond a missing box, and inverse-operation proofs.
42|9 More addition and subtraction.example: Mia has 47 stickers and Sam has 36. (a) How many stickers do they have altogether? (b) Mia gives away 19 stickers. How many does she have left? Answer: (a) 47 + 36 = 83 (regroup 13 ones as 1 ten and 3 ones). (b) 47 − 19 = 28 (regroup 1 ten as 10 ones: 37 − 9 = 28 after taking 10, or partition 47 as 30 + 17).

42|10 Graphs.teaches: Collecting and sorting data, then showing it in pictograms and bar charts. Pictograms use a key where one symbol stands for 1, 2, 5 or 10. Learners read and draw bar charts with equal-width bars and labelled axes. They answer questions on most, least, total and difference. Sorting uses Venn diagrams (two overlapping circles) and Carroll diagrams (yes/no, a property and 'not'). Words: data, tally, key, title, axis, label, frequency, sort.
42|10 Graphs.notYet: Mean, median, mode or range; line graphs; pie charts; scatter graphs; scales that need interpolating (for example reading 35 between marks of 10); intersection and union notation; complement sets; probability or chance as numbers; percentages; negative numbers; large data sets; three-set Venn diagrams.
42|10 Graphs.example: A pictogram shows favourite fruits. Key: 🍎 = 2 children. Apple has 5 symbols, banana has 3 symbols, and grape has 4 symbols. (a) How many children chose apple? (b) How many more children chose apple than banana? Answer: (a) 5 × 2 = 10 children. (b) Banana is 3 × 2 = 6, so 10 − 6 = 4 more children.

42|11 More multiplication and division.teaches: Multiplication and division facts for the 2, 3, 4, 5, 10 tables (and 6, 7, 8, 9 where covered), and their links as inverse operations. Doubling and halving, arrays, and fact families. Multiplying and dividing two-digit numbers by 2, 3, 4, 5 and 10 using partitioning, number lines and jottings. Division as sharing or grouping. Word problems with remainders. Words: multiply, divide, product, share, group, remainder, double, half.
42|11 More multiplication and division.notYet: Formal written long multiplication or short division algorithms; multiplying by two-digit numbers; three-digit by one-digit calculations; division with decimals or fractions; remainders written as fractions; factors, multiples, prime numbers, square numbers; algebra, or missing-number equations using letters.
42|11 More multiplication and division.example: A baker puts 4 buns in each box. She has 38 buns. How many full boxes can she fill, and how many buns are left over? Answer: 9 full boxes, 2 buns left over (9 × 4 = 36, 38 − 36 = 2).

42|12 More fractions.teaches: Finding unit fractions and simple non-unit fractions of whole-number amounts (e.g. 1/4 of 20, 3/4 of 12) using equal sharing and division facts. Comparing and ordering fractions with the same denominator or on number lines and fraction walls (halves, thirds, quarters, fifths, sixths, eighths, tenths). Adding and subtracting fractions with the same denominator, with answers less than or equal to 1. Words: numerator, denominator, equivalent, whole.
42|12 More fractions.notYet: Not taught: adding or subtracting fractions with different denominators, mixed numbers and improper fractions, simplifying or cancelling fractions, finding common denominators, converting to decimals or percentages, multiplying or dividing fractions, fractions of quantities with remainders, ratio.
42|12 More fractions.example: Sam has 20 stickers. He gives 1/4 of them to his sister. How many stickers does he give away? Answer: 5 (20 ÷ 4 = 5).

42|13 Measure.teaches: Measuring and comparing mass in grams (g) and kilograms (kg), capacity in millilitres (ml) and litres (l), and temperature in °C. Reading scales marked in whole units, 10s, 50s, 100s and halves. Estimating, choosing sensible units, and ordering. Simple one-step problems. Knowing 1 kg = 1000 g and 1 l = 1000 ml. Reading thermometers and temperatures such as 20 °C.
42|13 Measure.notYet: No decimals such as 1.5 kg, no converting with multiplication or division beyond simple 1000 facts, no negative temperatures or below-zero calculations, no Fahrenheit, no volume in cm³, no density or weight as force, no area or perimeter, no fractions of scales with awkward divisions.
42|13 Measure.example: A jug holds 1 litre of juice. Sam pours out 400 ml. How many millilitres of juice are left in the jug? Answer: 600 ml (1000 − 400 = 600).

42|15 Angles and movement.teaches: Angles as turns and corners. Right angle as a quarter turn. Learners compare angles with a right angle (smaller than, greater than, equal to), using a paper 'angle tester'. Clockwise and anticlockwise turns; quarter, half and three-quarter turns. Compass points N, S, E, W. Position on grids, and movement described by left/right/up/down.
42|15 Angles and movement.notYet: No degrees or protractors (90°, 180°, 360°). No terms acute, obtuse, reflex. No bearings, NE/SW compass points, or coordinates with negative numbers. No angle sums, no angles in triangles or on a line, no rotational symmetry, no translations or reflections as formal transformations.
42|15 Angles and movement.example: Faisal faces north. He makes a quarter turn clockwise. Which direction is he facing now? (Answer: East.)

42|16 Chance.teaches: Chance language for describing how likely events are: certain, impossible, likely, unlikely, even chance, more/less likely. Learners judge everyday events (e.g. 'it will rain tomorrow') and simple spinners, dice and bags of coloured counters. They place events on a chance line using words, and test ideas with simple trials.
42|16 Chance.notYet: Probability as a number or fraction (1/2, 0.5, 50%, 0 to 1 scale). Calculating probability as favourable over total outcomes. Ratio of outcomes. Sample space tables, tree diagrams, relative frequency, expected outcomes, independent events, 'fair' defined mathematically. Percentages.
42|16 Chance.example: A bag has 5 red counters and 1 blue counter. Aisha takes one counter without looking. Is she more likely to take a red counter or a blue counter? Explain why. Answer: Red, because there are more red counters (5) than blue (1).

42|14 Time (2).teaches: Reading and telling time on analogue clocks (o'clock, half past, quarter past/to, five-minute intervals) and digital clocks (e.g. 7:45). Using a.m. and p.m. Days, months, seasons. Reading simple timetables (bus, train, school, TV) to find start/finish times, and comparing times. Words: hour, minute, second, earlier, later, timetable.
42|14 Time (2).notYet: 24-hour clock, time zones, calculating elapsed time across hours and minutes with borrowing (e.g. 2 h 45 min to 5:10), converting between minutes and seconds with large numbers, speed, Roman numerals, timetables with seconds, decimals of hours, angles in degrees on clock faces, fractions as numbers, leap-year rules.
42|14 Time (2).example: A bus timetable shows: Park 8:00 a.m., School 8:15 a.m., Library 8:30 a.m., Market 8:45 a.m. Mia gets on the bus at the school stop. At which stop does she get off if she rides for 30 minutes? Answer: Market (8:15 + 30 minutes = 8:45 a.m.).

54|Characteristics and classification of.topic: Characteristics and classification of living organisms
54|Characteristics and classification of.teaches: Seven characteristics of living things (MRS GREN: movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition). Binomial naming (genus capitalised, species lower case, italic). Using and making dichotomous keys. Five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, prokaryotes, protoctists. Vertebrate classes, arthropod classes, flowering plants (monocot/dicot), ferns. Viruses: protein coat and genetic material, not cells.
54|Characteristics and classification of.notYet: Three-domain system, Archaea/Bacteria split, phylogenetic trees, DNA-sequence classification, cladistics, the full taxonomic hierarchy beyond kingdom/genus/species as required, virus replication cycles (lytic/lysogenic), organelle detail, Gram staining, and the biological species concept with hybrid or ring-species arguments.
54|Characteristics and classification of.example: A student finds an animal with a backbone, fur and mammary glands. (a) Name the major group it belongs to. (b) The scientific name of the grey wolf is Canis lupus. State what 'Canis' tells you about the wolf. Answer: (a) mammals (vertebrates). (b) Canis is the genus to which the wolf belongs.

54|Biological molecules.teaches: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins are made of C, H, O (proteins also N, sometimes S). Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polymers of glucose. Fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol. Proteins are chains of amino acids. Food tests: iodine (starch), Benedict's (reducing sugar), biuret (protein), ethanol emulsion (fat). DNA is a double helix of two strands with complementary base pairs A–T and C–G, and a sequence of bases codes for proteins.
54|Biological molecules.notYet: Not required: glycosidic, peptide or ester bond chemistry, condensation and hydrolysis mechanisms, α/β glucose, amylose/amylopectin, primary-to-quaternary structure, saturated vs unsaturated chemistry, nucleotide components (deoxyribose, phosphate), DNA replication, transcription, translation, ATP, ribosomes, enzyme kinetics, and A Level terms.
54|Biological molecules.example: A student adds biuret solution to a food sample and it turns purple. (a) Which nutrient is present? (b) Name the test and colour change for starch. Answer: (a) protein; (b) iodine solution, changing from brown/orange to blue-black.

42|17 Pattern and symmetry.teaches: Identifying and drawing lines of symmetry (vertical, horizontal, diagonal) on 2D shapes, using mirrors or folding. Completing symmetrical shapes and patterns about a given line, on squared or dotty paper. Sorting shapes by symmetry. Making and continuing patterns with shapes, using translation and reflection. Words: symmetry, line of symmetry, symmetrical, mirror line, reflect, pattern.
42|17 Pattern and symmetry.notYet: Rotational symmetry and order of rotation, angles in degrees, coordinates, reflecting in oblique lines or off the grid, translation vectors, tessellation terms, symmetry of 3D shapes (planes), named quadrilateral properties (parallel sides), perimeter or area formulae, circles' radius or diameter.
42|17 Pattern and symmetry.example: A square has 4 lines of symmetry? Question: Here is half of a shape on squared paper, with a dashed vertical mirror line on its right side. The left half is an L-shape made of 3 squares in a column plus 1 square to the left of the bottom square. Draw the other half so the whole shape is symmetrical. Then say: how many lines of symmetry does a rectangle that is not a square have? Answer: The reflected half is the mirror image on the right of the line (3 squares in a column, plus 1 square to the right of the bottom square, placed so it is the same distance from the line). A non-square rectangle has 2 lines of symmetry (one vertical, one horizontal).

54|Enzymes.teaches: Enzymes are biological catalysts, which are proteins that speed up reactions and are not used up. Substrate, product and active site. Lock-and-key model: shape is specific. Effects of temperature (rate rises, then the enzyme denatures at high temperature) and pH (optimum). Examples: amylase, protease, catalase. Interpreting graphs and designing investigations with variables and controls.
54|Enzymes.notYet: Not required: induced-fit model, Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Km/Vmax, competitive and non-competitive inhibition, activation energy calculations, allosteric sites, tertiary-structure bonding detail, enzyme immobilisation, Q10 calculations, ATP, ribosomes, or industrial enzyme process detail beyond simple examples.
54|Enzymes.example: Amylase is mixed with starch at 20, 30, 40, 50 and 60 °C. The rate of reaction is highest at 40 °C and is zero at 60 °C. (a) Explain why the rate is zero at 60 °C. (b) Name the substrate and the product of this reaction. Answer: (a) The high temperature changes the shape of the enzyme's active site, so the enzyme is denatured and the substrate no longer fits. (b) The substrate is starch and the product is maltose (a sugar).

54|Plant nutrition.teaches: Photosynthesis as carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts. Word and balanced symbol equations. Starch test with iodine, including destarching and variegated leaves. Leaf structure: cuticle, epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll, stomata, guard cells, xylem, phloem. Limiting factors: light, CO2, temperature (graphs). Uses of glucose; mineral ions nitrate and magnesium.
54|Plant nutrition.notYet: Light-dependent and light-independent stages, ATP, NADPH, photolysis, the Calvin cycle, RuBP, Rubisco, thylakoids and grana, photosystems, C3/C4 plants, compensation point calculations, enzyme kinetics and Q10, and chromatography of pigments (Rf values).
54|Plant nutrition.example: A leaf is partly covered with black paper for 24 hours after being destarched. It is then removed, boiled in water, put in hot ethanol and tested with iodine solution. (a) Predict the result for the covered area and the uncovered area. (b) Explain why the leaf is put in hot ethanol. Answer: (a) The covered area stays orange-brown/yellow (no starch), because there was no light for photosynthesis. The uncovered area turns blue-black (starch present). (b) Ethanol removes chlorophyll, so the colour change with iodine is easy to see.

54|Movement into and out of cells.topic: Movement into and out of cells
54|Movement into and out of cells.teaches: Diffusion: net movement of particles down a concentration gradient due to random motion; factors (gradient, temperature, surface area, distance). Osmosis: net water movement through a partially permeable membrane from dilute to concentrated solution (higher to lower water potential). Plant cells: turgid, plasmolysed, flaccid; animal cells: lysis, crenation. Active transport: movement against the gradient using energy from respiration, carrier proteins. Practicals: potato cylinders, percentage change in mass, and surface area to volume ratio.
54|Movement into and out of cells.notYet: Avoid calculating water potential values or solute potential (pressure potential), the Gibbs free energy, the Na+/K+ pump mechanism or ATP hydrolysis detail, co-transport, facilitated diffusion by channel types, endocytosis/exocytosis, Fick's law formula, and A Level terms such as incipient plasmolysis or the Ψ equation.
54|Movement into and out of cells.example: A student places cylinders of potato in a concentrated sugar solution for 30 minutes. The cylinders' mass decreases from 5.0 g to 4.2 g. (a) Calculate the percentage change in mass. (b) Explain, using the term osmosis, why the mass changed. Answer: (a) change = −0.8 g; (−0.8 ÷ 5.0) × 100 = −16% (a 16% decrease). (b) The sugar solution had a lower water potential (more concentrated) than the potato cells, so water moved out of the cells by osmosis, down its concentration gradient, across the partially permeable cell membrane, so the potato lost mass.

54|Cells.teaches: Structure and function of animal, plant and bacterial cells: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, cell wall, chloroplasts, large permanent vacuole with cell sap, mitochondria, ribosomes, plasmids, and a loop of DNA with no nucleus. Specialised cells (root hair, palisade, red blood cell, neurone, sperm, egg) linked to function. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size. Units mm, µm.
54|Cells.notYet: Details of organelle ultrastructure (cristae, Golgi, rough ER, endosymbiosis), electron microscope resolution calculations, protein synthesis steps, stem cells and differentiation genes, osmosis water potential, cell cycle and mitosis phases, prokaryote/eukaryote classification detail, ATP production steps, and the structure of a virus.
54|Cells.example:
A student draws a palisade cell from a leaf. The drawing is 60 mm wide. The actual cell is 0.03 mm wide. (a) Calculate the magnification. (b) Name two structures in the palisade cell that are not found in a bacterial cell. (c) Explain how the palisade cell is adapted for photosynthesis.

Answer: (a) magnification = 60 ÷ 0.03 = ×2000. (b) Any two: nucleus, chloroplasts, large permanent vacuole, mitochondria (the nucleus and chloroplasts are the safest). (c) It contains many chloroplasts with chlorophyll, which absorb light energy for photosynthesis. It is tall and positioned at the top of the leaf, so it receives plenty of light.

54|Human nutrition.teaches: Balanced diet and the sources and functions of carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins C and D, minerals (calcium, iron), fibre and water. Deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets). Alimentary canal and associated organs. Ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation and egestion. Teeth types and structure, caries. Mechanical and chemical digestion. Amylase, protease and lipase, bile, and villi adaptations.
54|Human nutrition.notYet: Exact enzyme names for every step (maltase, pepsinogen). Hormonal control of secretions. Peristalsis control by nerves. Detailed liver metabolism (deamination, urea) and glucose regulation. Energy calculations from kJ values. Lacteal biochemistry, active transport mechanisms in detail, micelles. Protein sequencing or amino acid structure. Cholera and oral rehydration detail.
54|Human nutrition.example: Question: The small intestine wall is covered with villi. (a) Name the process by which digested food moves from the small intestine into the blood. (b) State two features of a villus that make absorption efficient. (c) Name the enzyme that digests starch in the mouth and the product it forms. Answer: (a) Absorption (by diffusion and active transport). (b) Any two: large surface area; thin wall, one cell thick, short diffusion distance; dense network of capillaries giving a good blood supply that maintains a concentration gradient; lacteal for fats. (c) Amylase; maltose.

54|Transport in animals.teaches: Single vs double circulation; mammalian heart structure (atria, ventricles, valves, septum, coronary arteries); the cardiac cycle, pulse and ECG; arteries, veins and capillaries (structure and function); hepatic portal vein, renal and pulmonary vessels; blood components (red cells, white cells, platelets, plasma); phagocytes and lymphocytes; heart disease risk factors.
54|Transport in animals.notYet: A Level material: Starling's law, the cardiac output formula, haemoglobin dissociation curves, the Bohr effect, the chloride shift, the roles of the SAN and AVN, pressure changes in the cardiac cycle, antibody structure, clonal selection, hydrostatic and oncotic pressure, tissue fluid formation.
54|Transport in animals.example: Name the blood vessel that carries blood from the heart to the lungs, and state two ways its blood differs from the blood in the aorta. Answer: The pulmonary artery. Its blood is deoxygenated (low in oxygen) and has a higher carbon dioxide concentration, whereas the aorta carries oxygenated blood at higher pressure. (Any two valid differences, such as oxygen content, carbon dioxide content or pressure, are accepted.)

54|Transport in plants.teaches: Xylem (dead, hollow, lignified vessels carrying water and mineral ions up) and phloem (living sieve tubes carrying sucrose and amino acids). Positions in root, stem and leaf. Root hair uptake, transpiration, evaporation from mesophyll cells, stomata, and the transpiration stream. Factors affecting transpiration rate (light, temperature, humidity, wind). Wilting. Translocation from sources to sinks. Potometer experiments.
54|Transport in plants.notYet: Do not ask about: cohesion-tension theory in molecular detail, water potential in kPa, mass flow pressure gradients, companion cell mitochondria and active loading, apoplast/symplast pathways, Casparian strip, or calculating water potential. Avoid ATP, aphid stylet experiments, and ringing details beyond the basics. Also avoid osmosis calculations.
54|Transport in plants.example:
Question: A student cuts a leafy shoot and places it in a potometer in a bright, windy room. (a) Describe how water moves from the soil to the leaf of a plant. [3] (b) State two changes to the room that would slow the rate of water uptake. [2]

Answer: (a) Water enters root hair cells by osmosis; it moves across the root into the xylem vessels; it is pulled up the xylem to the leaf, where it evaporates from the surface of mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata (transpiration). (b) Any two: lower the light intensity, lower the temperature, increase the humidity, reduce air movement/wind.

54|Respiration and gas exchange.teaches: Aerobic respiration (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, energy released for muscle contraction, heat, active transport) and anaerobic respiration (lactic acid in muscles; ethanol and CO2 in yeast). Oxygen debt. Human gas exchange: trachea, bronchi, alveoli, diaphragm and intercostal muscles, ventilation. Lime water and hydrogencarbonate indicator tests. Reading breathing-rate graphs and comparing inspired and expired air.
54|Respiration and gas exchange.notYet: Do not ask about the mitochondrial stages (glycolysis, Krebs cycle, electron transport chain), ATP synthesis or NAD. Avoid the detailed biochemistry of lactate conversion in the liver, partial pressure, the Bohr effect and haemoglobin dissociation curves. Avoid calculating respiratory quotient. Keep the word equation only, with no balanced symbol equation beyond C6H12O6 unless it is given.
54|Respiration and gas exchange.example: The graph shows a learner's breathing rate (breaths per minute) at rest, during 5 minutes of exercise, and during recovery. Breathing rate rose from 15 to 40 breaths per minute during exercise and stayed high for several minutes afterwards. Explain why the breathing rate stays high after exercise stops. Answer: During hard exercise, muscles respire anaerobically and produce lactic acid, building up an oxygen debt. After exercise, extra oxygen is needed to break down the lactic acid, so the learner keeps breathing faster and deeper to take in more oxygen until the debt is repaid.

36|Unit 1: Computers are everywhere.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 1: Computers are everywhere.teaches: Computers are found in many places (home, school, shops, hospitals) and can be used for different jobs, such as writing, drawing, playing games, and finding things out. A computer runs different programs for different tasks. Learners name common devices (laptop, tablet, desktop), use simple words like program, data and information, and count objects in pictures to small numbers.
36|Unit 1: Computers are everywhere.notYet: No hardware or software jargon (CPU, RAM, operating system, input/output devices). No binary, bits, bytes, storage sizes or networks and internet protocols. No algorithms, coding, sequences, debugging or variables. No data types, databases, spreadsheets or charts. No e-safety rules beyond basics. No counting above about 10 or any calculation.
36|Unit 1: Computers are everywhere.example: Question: Sam uses a computer program to draw a picture of a cat. Is Sam using the computer to (a) draw or (b) count? Answer: (a) draw.

36|Unit 4: Be a designer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 4: Be a designer.teaches: Learners use simple drawing/design software (e.g. 2Paint-type tools) to make digital pictures and designs. They choose and use tools such as shapes, lines, fill colour, brush, eraser, undo, and select, copy and paste. They save and open files, and talk about what they designed and how they could improve it. Words: design, tool, shape, colour, save, undo.
36|Unit 4: Be a designer.notYet: No vector vs bitmap graphics, pixels, resolution or layers. No file formats (JPEG, PNG), copyright, or image editing software jargon. No algorithms, code, variables or loops. No coordinates, angles in degrees, or formal evaluation criteria. No typing-heavy tasks or keyboard shortcuts.
36|Unit 4: Be a designer.example: Question: You drew a circle by mistake in your picture. Which tool or button can you use to take away your last drawing step? A) Save B) Undo C) Fill D) Print. Answer: B) Undo.

36|Unit 3: Be a data detective.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 3: Be a data detective.teaches: Learners sort objects, people and pictures into groups by one clear property (man/woman, hat/no hat, small/large, colour, shape). They fill in simple tables with words or shading, count items in each group (small numbers, up to about 10), and order things by size. They know 'sort', 'group', 'table', 'data'.
36|Unit 3: Be a data detective.notYet: No charts or graphs (bar charts, pictograms, tally charts), no averages, no databases, spreadsheets or fields. No sorting by two properties at once, no Venn or Carroll diagrams, no searching or filtering with AND/OR, no algorithms or binary. No large numbers or percentages.
36|Unit 3: Be a data detective.example: Look at the picture of 5 shapes: 3 red circles and 2 blue squares. a) Name ONE way to sort the shapes. b) How many shapes are red? Answer: a) Sort by colour (or by shape: circles and squares). b) 3 shapes are red.

36|Unit 2: Be an animator.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 2: Be an animator.teaches: Learners make simple animations on screen. They know that an animation is a series of still pictures (frames) shown one after another to make things appear to move. They plan a short story with a beginning, middle and end. They use simple tools, such as drawing, moving, copying and sequencing, and give instructions in order. They say what they like and what they would change. They test by playing and fixing mistakes.
36|Unit 2: Be an animator.notYet: Not taught: frames per second or frame rate, keyframes, tweening, loops, repeat blocks, variables, events, conditions, coding in Scratch-style languages, file formats, layers, vector versus bitmap, algorithms with formal terms, debugging vocabulary, or the history of animation.
36|Unit 2: Be an animator.example: Mia draws a ball at the top of the page. In the next picture the ball is a little lower. In the next it is lower again. What happens when she shows the pictures one after another quickly? Answer: The ball looks like it is moving or falling down (it is an animation).

54|Diseases and immunity.teaches: Pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists) cause transmissible disease. Spread by direct contact, body fluids, cuts, insect vectors, contaminated food and water, and airborne droplets. Prevention: hygiene, sanitation, vaccination. Immunity: phagocytes engulf pathogens; lymphocytes make antibodies against specific antigens; memory cells give faster secondary responses; vaccination gives active immunity. Interpreting graphs of cases or deaths over time (HIV, measles, MRSA).
54|Diseases and immunity.notYet: Not required: B-cell/T-cell types, clonal selection, plasma cells, MHC, antigen presentation, cytokines, monoclonal antibodies, interferon, and detailed HIV replication or reverse transcriptase. Also avoid immunology calculations, epidemiological statistics, herd immunity formulae, and detailed antibiotic resistance genetics.
54|Diseases and immunity.example:
Question: Vaccination against measles was introduced in the USA in 1963. A vaccine contains a weakened or dead form of the measles virus. Explain how vaccination protects a person from measles. [3]

Answer: The vaccine contains antigens, which stimulate lymphocytes to make specific antibodies (1). Memory cells are produced and stay in the blood (1). If the real virus infects later, memory cells respond faster and make more antibodies quickly, so the person does not become ill (1).

36|Unit 5: We can network.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 5: We can network.teaches: Stage 1 learners find out that computers and devices can be joined (connected) so they can share things like pictures, music and messages. They name familiar devices (tablet, computer, phone, printer), say what a network is in simple words, and see that wires or Wi-Fi can connect devices. They practise staying safe and kind online and asking a trusted adult for help.
36|Unit 5: We can network.notYet: Do not ask about the internet's structure, routers, servers, IP addresses, packets, LAN/WAN, bandwidth, protocols, or how Wi-Fi works. No cloud storage, encryption, passwords rules in detail, or cyber-security terms. No typing, coding, or algorithms. Avoid long reading; keep wording very short and use pictures.
36|Unit 5: We can network.example: Question: Look at the picture of a computer and a printer joined by a wire. Why are they joined together? Choose one: A) So the computer can send a picture to the printer. B) So the printer can eat the computer. C) So the computer can fall asleep. Answer: A) So the computer can send a picture to the printer.

36|Unit 6: Be a problem solver.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 6: Be a problem solver.teaches: Problem solving with simple algorithms. Learners break a familiar task into small steps (e.g. making a sandwich, getting dressed). They put steps in the correct order and spot a missing or wrong step. They follow and give instructions such as forward, backward, left and right, and use arrows or pictures on grids. They find and fix mistakes (debug) in short sequences of 3–6 steps. Words: problem, step, order, instruction, algorithm, sequence, bug.
36|Unit 6: Be a problem solver.notYet: No loops or repeat commands, no if/then selection, no variables, no flowcharts with decision boxes, no pseudocode syntax, no text-based coding. No decomposition or abstraction as formal terms. No turns in degrees, no coordinates, no efficiency or Big-O, no binary.
36|Unit 6: Be a problem solver.example: Here are the steps to brush your teeth, but they are mixed up: (A) Rinse your mouth. (B) Put toothpaste on the brush. (C) Brush your teeth. Write the letters in the correct order. Answer: B, C, A.

36|Unit 8: Be a data collector.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 8: Be a data collector.teaches: Stage 1 learners collect simple data by asking classmates a question (e.g. favourite ice-cream). They sort objects into groups, make tally marks, and show results in a pictogram or block graph. They name the groups, count each group, and say which is most or least popular. Numbers stay small (to about 10 or 20).
36|Unit 8: Be a data collector.notYet: No bar charts with scales, no axes labels, no frequency tables, no mean, median, mode or average. No databases, spreadsheets or software charts. No tally groups of five beyond simple counting. No percentages, fractions of data or large numbers. Avoid terms like 'data set', 'variable' or 'survey bias'.
36|Unit 8: Be a data collector.example: A pictogram shows favourite ice-creams. Vanilla has 5 pictures, strawberry has 3 pictures, chocolate has 7 pictures. Which ice-cream is the most popular? Answer: chocolate (it has the most pictures, 7).

36|Unit 7: Computers control things.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 7: Computers control things.teaches: Computers and devices follow instructions to control things, such as toys, traffic lights, washing machines and robots. Learners name common output devices (screen, speaker, printer). They give simple step-by-step instructions, for example 'forward', 'turn left', 'turn right'. They see that a person gives the instructions and the device does what it is told. Words are short and familiar.
36|Unit 7: Computers control things.notYet: No programming code, algorithms by name, loops, repeat, selection (if/then), variables, debugging terms, sensors, microcontrollers, binary, or input/output theory beyond naming devices. No turn angles in degrees. No flowcharts. Avoid long written answers; Stage 1 learners mostly point, say or tick.
36|Unit 7: Computers control things.example: Look at the picture of a printer. Is it an input device or an output device? Say its name. Answer: It is a printer. It is an output device (it gives us paper with words or pictures).

36|Unit 10: We are connected.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 10: We are connected.teaches: Stage 1 learners find out that devices such as computers, tablets and phones can connect to each other and to the internet. They know that the internet lets us find information, watch videos and talk to people far away. They recognise a 'no connection' picture and say why. They learn to ask a trusted adult for help and to stay safe online.
36|Unit 10: We are connected.notYet: Not taught: how Wi-Fi, routers, servers or IP addresses work, the words 'network' protocols or 'bandwidth', web browsers and search engines in detail, email, passwords and privacy settings, cyberbullying, digital footprints, data packets, or fixing connection faults step by step.
36|Unit 10: We are connected.example: Your tablet shows a picture saying it has no internet. Which is a good thing to do? a) Ask a grown-up for help b) Throw the tablet c) Hide the tablet. Answer: a) Ask a grown-up for help.

36|Unit 9: Be a games developer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 9: Be a games developer.teaches: Learners use a simple program-making tool (such as Scratch Jr or a block-based tool) to make a simple game. They choose a character (sprite) and a background, and use blocks to make it move, make a sound or say something. They run the program, find mistakes and fix them. They say what the game should do. Words: game, program, sprite, command, instruction, run, debug, algorithm (simple), order.
36|Unit 9: Be a games developer.notYet: No text code (Python), no variables or score variables, no loops with conditions (if/else), no events with broadcasts, no coordinates (x, y), no angles in degrees, no sprite-design theory, no testing plans, no game-design documents, no networks or the internet, no binary.
36|Unit 9: Be a games developer.example: Mia makes a game. She wants her cat sprite to move forward and then make a meow sound. She puts the blocks in this order: 'play meow', 'move forward'. What does the cat do first? How can Mia change the program so the cat moves first? Answer: The cat meows first. Mia swaps the blocks so 'move forward' comes before 'play meow'.

36|Unit 11: Be an artist.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 1
36|Unit 11: Be an artist.teaches: Learners use simple drawing/painting software or apps to make digital pictures. They choose and use tools such as brush, pencil, shape, fill colour, eraser, undo, and select colours and line sizes. They open, save and name a picture, and say what they made. Words: tool, colour, shape, line, save, undo, mouse, click, screen.
36|Unit 11: Be an artist.notYet: No coding or algorithms for drawing (e.g. turtle commands, loops, repeat, angles in degrees). No vector versus bitmap, pixels or resolution, layers, file formats, copyright, editing photos, or typing precise coordinates. No area, symmetry maths or formal geometry.
36|Unit 11: Be an artist.example: Question: You drew a red circle by mistake and want to take it away. Which tool can you click to take away your last mistake: undo, save or fill? Answer: undo.

37|Term 1.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 2
37|Term 1.teaches: Unit 1: planning and making simple games in block-based Scratch-style tools; sequences of instructions, repeat loops, events (when clicked), sprites, backdrops, debugging. Unit 2: collecting, sorting and grouping data, tally charts, pictograms, block graphs, answering questions. Unit 3: input, output, storage, devices, computer parts. Unit 4: frame-by-frame animation, storyboards, sequencing images.
37|Term 1.notYet: Not taught: variables, score counters, conditionals (if/else), nested loops, functions, text code (Python), spreadsheets formulas, averages, CPU/RAM/binary, operating system details, networks, keyframes/tweening, frame-rate numbers, algorithms by name beyond simple use.
37|Term 1.example: A tally chart shows favourite fruit: apple IIII, banana IIII II, grape III. Which fruit did the most children choose, and how many chose it? Answer: Banana, 7 children.

37|Term 3.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 2
37|Term 3.teaches: Unit 9: the internet is a network of connected computers; safe sharing (keep passwords and personal details private, tell a trusted adult); sharing work digitally. Unit 10: planning a story with a storyboard, using text, images and sound in software, sequencing. Unit 11: what computers and robots do, giving step-by-step instructions, and simple programs that move a sprite or robot.
37|Term 3.notYet: Not taught: IP addresses, protocols, servers or Wi-Fi mechanisms, search engine ranking, copyright law, variables, loops with conditions, selection (if/else), debugging terminology beyond 'mistake', binary, AI or machine learning, sensors and actuators, and text-based coding such as Python.
37|Term 3.example: Aisha is making a story on the computer. She draws four pictures to show what happens at the start, middle and end before she uses the software. What is this plan called? A) a password B) a storyboard C) a robot D) a network. Answer: B) a storyboard.

38|Unit 1: Making programs clear.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 1: Making programs clear.teaches: Block-based programs (Scratch-style) with sprites. Learners follow, edit and correct algorithms and spot errors. They simplify programs by using repeat blocks for repeated steps and write concise algorithms. They reset a sprite's size and position when the Green flag is clicked (go to x y, set size to %). They run more than one algorithm in one program, for example on a click and on the Green flag.
38|Unit 1: Making programs clear.notYet: Do not ask about variables, conditions (if/else), nested loops, forever-loop logic, functions or custom blocks, broadcast messaging, or text-based code such as Python. Avoid angles in degrees, coordinate calculations, negative-number arithmetic beyond reading 'change size by −20', and Big O or efficiency timing.
38|Unit 1: Making programs clear.example: A sprite program is: When green flag clicked, Move 10 steps, Move 10 steps, Move 10 steps, Move 10 steps, Turn a quarter turn right. (a) Which block of code can replace the four Move 10 steps blocks? (b) Why is the new program better? Answer: (a) Repeat 4 [Move 10 steps]. (b) It is shorter and more concise, so it is easier to read, edit and correct.

37|Term 2.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 2
37|Term 2.teaches: Unit 5: identifying common devices (laptop, tablet, desktop, smartphone), portable vs non-portable, input and output devices, and how devices connect to share things. Unit 6: designing simple things with algorithms/sequences. Unit 7: collecting, sorting and showing data in pictograms and tables, then answering simple questions. Unit 8: making digital art with simple tools such as shapes, colours, brushes, undo and save.
37|Term 2.notYet: Do not ask about the internet vs the web, routers, Wi-Fi protocols, IP addresses, bits and bytes, binary, CPU or RAM, storage sizes, databases, spreadsheets with formulae, bar-chart scales, vector vs bitmap, pixels, resolution, file formats, loops or variables in code, or cyber-security.
37|Term 2.example: Look at these four devices: a desktop computer, a tablet, a laptop and a smartphone. Which one is NOT portable, meaning you cannot easily carry it around? Answer: the desktop computer.

38|Unit 3: Be a data expert.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 3: Be a data expert.teaches: Collecting data with tally charts, surveys and questionnaires. Sorting data into categorical (colours, pets, favourite foods) and discrete (counted whole numbers, e.g. shoe sizes, siblings). Filling in electronic forms with text boxes, drop-down lists, tick boxes and radio buttons. Spreadsheet rows, columns and cells; cell addresses like B3 (column letter, then row number). Formatting cells: bold, colour, borders, number and currency.
38|Unit 3: Be a data expert.notYet: Formulas and functions (=SUM, =A1+B1), cell ranges (A1:B5), absolute references, sorting and filtering, charts and graphs from spreadsheets, continuous data, databases and fields, validation rules, mean/median/mode, and data protection law.
38|Unit 3: Be a data expert.example: A spreadsheet has a cell in column C, row 4, coloured yellow. (a) What is the cell address of the yellow cell? (b) Is 'favourite pet' categorical or discrete data? Answer: (a) C4 (column letter first, then row number). (b) Categorical.

38|Unit 5: Networks are everywhere.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 5: Networks are everywhere.teaches: Networks are groups of connected devices that share information. Learners name network parts (computers, tablets, printers, cables, Wi-Fi), see that devices can be connected by wires or wirelessly, and know that the internet is a very large network. They discuss everyday networks, what is shared (files, printers, internet), and simple safe use.
38|Unit 5: Networks are everywhere.notYet: Do not ask about IP addresses, packets, protocols, routers vs switches, LAN/WAN, bandwidth, servers in detail, network topologies, binary, encryption, or how data is transmitted. No technical speeds or units (Mbps). Avoid jargon such as 'hardware protocol' or 'client-server'.
38|Unit 5: Networks are everywhere.example: Mia's school has computers that all use one printer. Why is this possible? A) The computers are connected in a network. B) The printer is very big. C) The computers are turned off. Answer: A) The computers are connected in a network.

38|Unit 2: Hardware and software work to.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 2: Hardware and software work to.topic: Unit 2: Hardware and software work together
38|Unit 2: Hardware and software work to.teaches: Hardware is the physical parts of a computer that you can touch (keyboard, mouse, monitor, speakers, printer, tablet). Software is the programs or instructions that tell hardware what to do. Hardware and software need each other. Learners name input and output devices in simple terms. Instructions must be in the right order and precise. A bug is a mistake in code. Learners spot and fix simple bugs.
38|Unit 2: Hardware and software work to.notYet: CPU internals, RAM/ROM, fetch-decode-execute, binary, operating system versus application software, compilers, syntax versus logic error classification, variables, selection or loops in text code, networks, storage capacities (GB), debugging with trace tables, algorithms in pseudocode, formal input/process/output/storage categories.
38|Unit 2: Hardware and software work to.example: Question: Sam says, 'A mouse is software because I use it to click on things.' Is Sam right? Explain your answer. Answer: No. A mouse is hardware because it is a physical part of the computer that you can touch. Software is the programs or instructions, such as a drawing app, that tell the computer what to do.

38|Unit 4: Be a designer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 4: Be a designer.teaches: Learners plan and make a simple digital design, such as a poster or slide. They use basic tools: text, images, shapes, colour, font size and layout. They know the words designer, audience, purpose, template, edit, save and improve. They choose good-looking, clear designs, give feedback on their own and others' work, and use a simple plan or sketch.
38|Unit 4: Be a designer.notYet: No coding, algorithms, loops or variables. No pixels, resolution, file formats or compression. No vector or bitmap graphics. No HTML or CSS. No copyright law or licensing. No user-interface or UX theory, no databases or spreadsheet formulas, and no networks.
38|Unit 4: Be a designer.example: Sam is making a poster for the school book fair. He wants people to read the title from far away. What should he do to the title text? Answer: Make the font size bigger (and choose a clear colour that stands out from the background).

38|Unit 6: Be a storyteller.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 6: Be a storyteller.teaches: Using Scratch-style block coding to make an animated story. Learners choose a backdrop and sprites, then add scripts: when green flag clicked, say/think, wait, switch backdrop, move, glide, broadcast and receive messages, play sounds. They plan with a storyboard, run, test and fix (debug) the code, and use sequence, with simple repeat.
38|Unit 6: Be a storyteller.notYet: Not yet: variables, scoring or lives, if/else conditions, sensing, loops inside loops, custom blocks (functions), coordinates and angles in degrees, cloning, text-based languages like Python, algorithms in formal notation, flowcharts, or binary and data representation.
38|Unit 6: Be a storyteller.example: Question: A story has two backdrops, a forest and a castle. Which block, added to the backdrop's code, makes the picture change to the castle after the characters finish talking? A) switch backdrop to castle  B) play sound  C) hide  D) turn right. Answer: A) switch backdrop to castle (placed after the talking blocks, so the order of the sequence is correct).

38|Unit 7: Computers and robots.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 7: Computers and robots.teaches: Computers follow instructions (programs) and robots are machines that follow programs to do tasks. Learners sort tasks done by people, computers and robots. They name robot parts (sensors, motors), give simple step-by-step instructions, and spot where a robot or computer helps. They use words such as input, instruction, program and sensor. They also discuss how robots help people.
38|Unit 7: Computers and robots.notYet: No text-code syntax (Python, Scratch scripts with variables). No binary, algorithms with selection or nested loops, or flowchart symbols. No AI or machine learning. No actuator or microcontroller terms. No coordinates or angles in degrees for turns. No sensor calibration, ethics or programming theory.
38|Unit 7: Computers and robots.example: Question: A robot vacuum cleaner stops when it gets near a wall. Which part of the robot tells it the wall is close? A) wheel B) sensor C) battery. Answer: B) sensor. A sensor detects things around the robot, so it knows when to stop.

38|Unit 11: Be a data designer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 11: Be a data designer.teaches: Data in tables and spreadsheets: rows, columns, cells, and headings in the first row. Cell addresses written column letter then row number (B3), and the Name Box. Collecting data from classmates and entering it in a table. Choosing data formats: text, number, date, currency. Simple spreadsheet layout.
38|Unit 11: Be a data designer.notYet: Formulas, functions (SUM, AVERAGE), cell ranges (A1:A5), cell references in calculations, absolute references, sorting and filtering, charts and graphs analysis, databases, fields and records, data types like Boolean or integer, validation, and CSV files.
38|Unit 11: Be a data designer.example: In a spreadsheet, the column is labelled B and the row is labelled 4. What is the cell address where they cross? Answer: B4 (column letter first, then row number).

38|Unit 9: Sending secret messages.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 9: Sending secret messages.teaches: Secret codes replace letters with symbols, pictures (e.g. fruit) or numbers. Vocabulary: plain text (the original message), ciphertext (the coded message), code, encode, decode, key/chart. Learners use an A=1 to Z=26 chart to encode and decode short words and messages, make their own code charts, and swap messages with a partner to decode.
38|Unit 9: Sending secret messages.notYet: Not taught: named ciphers (Caesar, shift, substitution, Vigenère), encryption algorithms, keys and public/private keys, binary or ASCII, hacking, cryptography maths, modular arithmetic, frequency analysis, internet security or HTTPS, and writing programs to encrypt. Keep numbers within 1–26.
38|Unit 9: Sending secret messages.example: Use the code A=1, B=2, C=3, D=4, E=5 ... Z=26. Question: The ciphertext is 3 1 20. What is the plain text word? Answer: CAT (3=C, 1=A, 20=T).

38|Unit 8: Be a musician.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 8: Be a musician.teaches: Using Scratch-style block code to make music. Learners pick sprites (Drum, Speaker) from a library and add code to them. They follow a given algorithm and match blocks to it. They use event blocks (when sprite clicked, when key pressed), play sound/drum/note blocks, and simple repeat. They run, test and fix programs. Words: sprite, algorithm, code, block, sound, run, debug.
38|Unit 8: Be a musician.notYet: Not taught: variables, functions or custom blocks, conditionals (if/else), broadcast messages, loops nested or with conditions, Python or text code, sound file formats, sampling rates or frequency in hertz, musical theory such as notation and tempo in BPM, binary, and flowchart symbols.
38|Unit 8: Be a musician.example: A Drum sprite has this code: 'when this sprite clicked' then 'play drum' then 'repeat 4' blocks. Which block starts the program when you click the Drum sprite? Answer: the 'when this sprite clicked' block (the event block at the top of the code).

38|Unit 10: Be a game developer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 10: Be a game developer.teaches: Planning and building a simple game in Scratch-style block coding. Learners write algorithms, then add code to sprites (e.g. Block-G). They use event blocks (when green flag clicked, when key pressed), motion, looks, sound, repeat loops and simple sequences. They test, find bugs, debug and improve the game. Words: algorithm, sprite, sequence, repeat, event, debug, input, output.
38|Unit 10: Be a game developer.notYet: Not taught: variables and score-keeping maths, if/else selection with conditions, operators (and/or), functions or custom blocks, broadcasts, clones, coordinates (x/y) calculations, angles in degrees for turning, text-based languages (Python), flowchart symbols, Boolean logic, game physics.
38|Unit 10: Be a game developer.example: A sprite has this algorithm: 1) When the space key is pressed. 2) Move 10 steps. 3) Play a sound. Which block starts the code, and in what order do the other two blocks go under it? Answer: 'When space key pressed' is the first (event) block. Then 'move 10 steps', then 'play sound', in that sequence.

38|Unit 12: Be a problem solver.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 3
38|Unit 12: Be a problem solver.teaches: Solving problems by decomposing them into smaller parts, spotting patterns, and writing clear step-by-step algorithms. Learners use sequence, simple repeats (loops) and simple 'if' decisions in block-based programs such as Scratch. They test programs, find bugs (errors) and debug them. They use flowcharts and plain-language instructions for everyday tasks.
38|Unit 12: Be a problem solver.notYet: Avoid text-based code (Python, JavaScript), variables, functions, arrays, nested loops, Boolean logic (AND/OR/NOT), binary, sorting or searching algorithm names, Big O or efficiency, pseudocode syntax, formal flowchart symbol rules, and 'abstraction' as a technical term. Avoid terms like iteration, selection, or syntax errors.
38|Unit 12: Be a problem solver.example: A robot must draw a square. A learner writes: move 50 steps, turn right, move 50 steps, turn right, move 50 steps, turn right, move 50 steps, turn right. How could they make this algorithm shorter using a repeat block? Answer: Use 'repeat 4' around 'move 50 steps, turn right'.

39|Unit 2: Be a data controller.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 2: Be a data controller.teaches: Data handling with simple databases and spreadsheets. Learners know data, record, field, table and sort. They collect data with tally charts and tables, enter it in a spreadsheet (rows, columns, cells), sort and search it (e.g. alphabetical, smallest to largest), and make simple charts. They answer questions from the data and check it for mistakes.
39|Unit 2: Be a data controller.notYet: No SQL, queries or Boolean AND/OR searches. No formulae or functions such as SUM, AVERAGE or IF. No cell references like A1:B5, relational databases, primary keys or data types. No mean, median or mode. No binary, encryption, GDPR or big data. No Python or algorithms.
39|Unit 2: Be a data controller.example: A class table has the columns Name, Age and Favourite pet. Each row is one child's information. (a) What is one row in a database called? (b) You want the oldest child first. Which column do you sort, and in which order? Answer: (a) a record. (b) Sort the Age column from largest to smallest (descending).

39|Unit 3: Be a network designer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 3: Be a network designer.teaches: Learners design simple networks. They name devices (computer, tablet, printer, router, switch, server) and say what each does. They know a network connects devices to share files, printers and internet. They compare wired (cables) and wireless (Wi-Fi) links, and draw simple network diagrams. They know a small network such as a classroom or home network, and that the internet is a large network. They use plain words and spot what a network needs.
39|Unit 3: Be a network designer.notYet: Not taught: IP addresses, MAC addresses, packets, protocols (TCP/IP, HTTP), LAN/WAN definitions, network topologies (star, bus, ring), bandwidth or speed calculations, DNS, encryption, firewalls, binary, client-server detail, OSI layers.
39|Unit 3: Be a network designer.example: Mia's school wants all the classroom computers to use one printer. Which device could join the computers and the printer together in a network: a switch, a keyboard or a microphone? Answer: A switch. It connects devices so they can share the printer.

39|Unit 7: Be a data boss.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 7: Be a data boss.teaches: Learners use a simple database or data table. They know the words record (a row), field (a column), and data table. They count records and fields. They search a table to find information and say which fields they looked at. They match data types (text, number, currency, date/time, yes/no) to fields. They may sort data and answer questions from it.
39|Unit 7: Be a data boss.notYet: Not taught: SQL or query languages, multiple linked tables, primary/foreign keys, validation rules, Boolean operators (AND/OR) in complex searches, spreadsheet formulas, databases design, data protection laws, big data, normalisation, and data types such as integer, string or float.
39|Unit 7: Be a data boss.example: A library data table has the fields Title of Book, Classification, Date Borrowed and Outstanding Fine. Which data type is best for the field 'Date Borrowed'? a) Text b) Currency c) Date/Time. Answer: c) Date/Time.

39|Unit 1: Be an animator.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 1: Be an animator.teaches: Stage 4 learners follow, predict and debug simple algorithms that use repetition (loops). They use count-controlled 'repeat' blocks in a block-based language (Scratch). They animate sprites with motion, looks and sound blocks, add comments to explain blocks of code, and build programs that use repetition. Words: algorithm, repeat, loop, sprite, costume, comment, debug, sequence.
39|Unit 1: Be an animator.notYet: Not taught: variables, scores or counters; selection (if/else); conditions in loops; nested loops; infinite or 'repeat until' loops as theory; functions or custom blocks; events and broadcasts; text languages like Python; Boolean logic; binary; efficiency or Big-O; formal flowchart symbols; coordinates beyond simple movement.
39|Unit 1: Be an animator.example: A sprite runs this algorithm: repeat 4 times { move 10 steps; change costume to next costume; wait 1 second }. (a) How many times does the sprite move? (b) The programmer wants the sprite to move 40 steps in total using the same loop. What should be changed? (c) Write a comment for the loop. Answer: (a) 4 times (b) nothing; the loop already moves 4 × 10 = 40 steps. A wrong-answer fix like 'repeat 10' would give 100 steps. (c) Any clear comment, e.g. 'Make the sprite walk by moving and changing costume four times.'

39|Unit 5: Be a computer scientist.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 5: Be a computer scientist.teaches: Thinking like a computer scientist: decomposing problems into smaller parts, spotting patterns, and writing clear step-by-step algorithms. Learners identify repeated instructions (iterations) and count how many times they repeat. They use simple loops (repeat n times) in block-based programs such as Scratch, predict outputs, and find and fix errors (debug). Words: algorithm, sequence, repeat, loop, iteration, instruction, debug.
39|Unit 5: Be a computer scientist.notYet: No 'while' or 'for' loop syntax, no text-based code (Python), no variables or arithmetic in loops, no nested loops, no conditions or 'if' selection inside loops, no infinite-loop theory, no Boolean logic, no efficiency or Big-O, no formal flowchart symbols, no functions or procedures.
39|Unit 5: Be a computer scientist.example: A robot fills a jug using these instructions: 'Pour one cup of water into the jug.' Repeat this 4 times. The jug is then full. (a) Which instruction is repeated? (b) How many iterations are there? (c) What would happen if the robot did only 3 iterations? Answer: (a) Pour one cup of water into the jug. (b) 4. (c) The jug would not be full because there would not be enough water in it. (If it did 5, the water would overflow.)

39|Unit 4: Be a storyteller.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 4: Be a storyteller.teaches: Planning and making an animated story in block-based programming (Scratch-style). Learners use storyboards, characters (sprites), backdrops, and sequences of commands. They use simple repeat loops, events (when flag clicked, key pressed), speech/say and wait blocks, and broadcast messages. They test, find and fix errors (debug) and improve their work.
39|Unit 4: Be a storyteller.notYet: No text-based coding (Python, JavaScript, HTML). No variables, scores, lists or functions/custom procedures. No nested loops, conditions with if/else logic, Boolean operators, or algorithms in formal flowchart notation. No coordinates or angles in degrees. No cloning, parallel threads, or sensors. No film or video editing software.
39|Unit 4: Be a storyteller.example: A learner's story has a cat sprite that must say 'Hello!' and then wait 2 seconds before moving. Put these blocks in the correct order: (A) wait 2 seconds (B) when green flag clicked (C) say 'Hello!' (D) move 10 steps. Answer: B, C, A, D.

39|Unit 6: Be a musician.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 6: Be a musician.teaches: Learners use Scratch-style block programming to make music. They pick sound blocks, play notes and drums, and set the tempo. They use sequences, and repeat loops to build tunes. They make and test programs, debug them, and change values (note, beats) to alter the music. Words used: sequence, repeat/loop, tempo, note, beat, input, output, bug, debug, algorithm.
39|Unit 6: Be a musician.notYet: Not taught: variables with calculations, functions or procedures with parameters, nested loops, conditionals (if/else) with sensors, events and broadcast messages used in complex ways, Boolean logic, text-based code (Python), sound-wave ideas (frequency, amplitude, Hz), MIDI or file formats, and digital audio editing.
39|Unit 6: Be a musician.example: A program plays note C for 1 beat, then note E for 1 beat, then note G for 1 beat. Ali wants the three notes played 4 times. Which block should he use, and what number goes in it? Answer: a repeat (loop) block, with 4 put in it, around the three note blocks. (Accept 'repeat 4'.)

39|Unit 8: Be an innovator.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 8: Be an innovator.teaches: Learners act as innovators: they think of ideas to solve a simple problem or improve something, then plan, make and test a simple digital product (e.g. a program in block-based Scratch, a poster or a simple animation). They use words such as idea, design, plan, test, improve, feedback, user, debug and algorithm. They give and use feedback to make improvements.
39|Unit 8: Be an innovator.notYet: Do not ask about text-based code (Python, HTML), variables in formal terms, data types, binary, networks and protocols, databases, flowchart symbol names, formal testing methods (test tables, iterative development models), intellectual property or patent law, or business and marketing ideas. Do not ask about AI or machine learning.
39|Unit 8: Be an innovator.example: Mia makes a game in Scratch. When she tests it, the sprite walks through a wall. What should Mia do next? A) Delete the game B) Find the mistake in her blocks and fix it (debug) C) Ask someone to play it without fixing it D) Change the colour of the sprite. Answer: B. She should debug by finding and fixing the mistake in her blocks, then test again.

39|Unit 9: Be a code cracker.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 9: Be a code cracker.teaches: Codes are used to hide or share messages. Learners use simple substitution/Caesar-style ciphers with a key (e.g. shift letters by 1-3), encode and decode short words, spot patterns such as common letters, and follow step-by-step instructions (algorithms). Words: code, encrypt, decrypt, key, cipher, message, pattern, decode.
39|Unit 9: Be a code cracker.notYet: Not taught: binary or ASCII conversion, hexadecimal, public/private keys, hashing, modular arithmetic, frequency analysis as a formal method, brute-force attack, RSA, symmetric vs asymmetric encryption, cybersecurity laws, Python code for ciphers, Boolean logic.
39|Unit 9: Be a code cracker.example: A code shifts every letter 1 place forward in the alphabet (A becomes B, B becomes C). Using this code, what does the word CAT become? Answer: DBU.

39|Unit 10: Be a game developer.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 10: Be a game developer.teaches: Algorithms as step-by-step instructions to solve a problem or design a game. Decomposing a game into parts. Repetition (loops): repeat a number of times, repeat until, forever. Sub-routines (custom blocks) reused in a program. Testing parts separately, finding and fixing bugs. Building games in Scratch with sprites, events, variables such as score.
39|Unit 10: Be a game developer.notYet: Not taught: Python or text code, functions with parameters or return values, nested loops, formal flowcharts or pseudocode syntax, Boolean logic and operators, lists/arrays, cloning, broadcast messages, coordinates and angle maths, binary, Big O or efficiency, formal testing terms like test data or trace tables.
39|Unit 10: Be a game developer.example: A Scratch sprite must draw a square. Which algorithm uses repetition correctly? A) move 50, turn, move 50, turn, move 50, turn, move 50, turn. B) repeat 4 times: move 50 steps, turn right. Which is better and why? Answer: B. It uses a repeat loop, so the same instructions are written once, which is shorter and easier to fix.

39|Unit 11: Be a robot controller.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 11: Be a robot controller.teaches: Learners give a robot or on-screen sprite precise step-by-step instructions. They use sequences, then repeat (count-controlled loops) to shorten programs. They use simple commands such as forward, backward, turn left, turn right, with small step counts. They predict where a program ends up on a grid, find and fix bugs (debugging), and plan with algorithms and flowcharts.
39|Unit 11: Be a robot controller.notYet: No turning in degrees or angles, no variables, no selection (if/else) or conditions, no nested loops, no functions or procedures, no sensors or input, no text-based languages (Python), no binary, no efficiency or Big O, no formal pseudocode syntax.
39|Unit 11: Be a robot controller.example: A robot starts facing north on a grid. Its program is: forward 2, turn right, forward 3. Which way is it facing at the end, and how many squares did it move altogether? Answer: It faces east. It moved 5 squares (2 + 3). Bonus: the same moves repeated 4 times could use a loop: 'repeat 4 times: forward 1' instead of writing forward 1 four times.

39|Unit 12: Be an artist.book: Cambridge Primary Computing Learners Book Stage 4
39|Unit 12: Be an artist.teaches: Using a drawing program to make digital art: shapes, lines, fill colours, copy/paste, resize, rotate, flip, group and layer objects, undo, save. Planning a picture, then improving it from feedback. Simple on-screen turtle-style commands (forward, turn, repeat) may appear. Words: pixel, vector, object, tool, effect, canvas.
39|Unit 12: Be an artist.notYet: Not taught: vector versus bitmap file mathematics, resolution and file-size calculations, RGB or hex colour codes, turning angles in exact degrees, coordinates and variables in code, loops with nested repeats, functions, Python or text-based coding, image compression, and copyright law.
