Using tree diagrams to sort objects by yes/no properties (e.g. 'Is it a square?'). Sorting numbers and shapes into Carroll diagrams (2 criteria, e.g. odd/not odd, multiple of 5/not). Sorting into Venn diagrams with 2 overlapping sets, using words like 'both' and 'neither'.
46|Unit 3C: Handling data.notYet: No probability as a number or fraction, no 'likely/unlikely' calculations or chance of events. No pie charts, line graphs, mean/median/mode, or frequency tables with grouped data. No set notation, union/intersection symbols, or three-set Venn diagrams. No percentages, no decimals on scales, and no scales with large numbers.
46|Unit 3C: Handling data.example: Question: Some children were asked about pets. In a Venn diagram, circle A is 'has a dog' and circle B is 'has a cat'. 5 children are only in the dog circle, 3 are in both circles, 4 are only in the cat circle, and 2 are outside both circles. (a) How many children have a dog? (b) How many children were asked altogether? Answer: (a) 5 + 3 = 8 children have a dog. (b) 5 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 14 children.

47|Unit 1B: Geometry.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 1B: Geometry.teaches: Identifying parallel and perpendicular lines and edges in shapes and the environment. Classifying triangles as equilateral, isosceles, right-angled or scalene by sides and right angles. Nets, faces, edges and vertices of cubes and cuboids. Reading and plotting coordinates in the first quadrant (positive whole numbers). Translating and reflecting 2D shapes on grids, with horizontal or vertical mirror lines.
47|Unit 1B: Geometry.notYet: Measuring or calculating angles in degrees (the 180° triangle sum), protractors, acute/obtuse/reflex angle names. Negative coordinates or four quadrants. Rotation, diagonal mirror lines, translation vectors. Volume and surface area formulae. Pythagoras. Area of a triangle. Equations of lines.
47|Unit 1B: Geometry.example: Point A is at (2, 3), B at (6, 3) and C at (6, 7). (a) Which side, AB or BC, is perpendicular to AB? (b) Triangle ABC is translated 3 squares right and 2 squares up. What are the new coordinates of A? Answer: (a) BC is perpendicular to AB (AB is horizontal, BC is vertical). (b) A moves to (5, 5).

47|Unit 1C: Measure.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 1C: Measure.teaches: Mass: read scales, convert kg and g (1 kg = 1000 g), estimate and compare. Time: read analogue and digital clocks in 12-hour and 24-hour form, convert between them, find intervals in hours and minutes. Timetables: read 24-hour tables and work out durations. Area (1): count whole and half squares on a grid, estimate and compare areas in cm². Perimeter (1): add side lengths of rectilinear shapes, in cm and m.
47|Unit 1C: Measure.notYet: Do not use area formulae (length × width) or the area of triangles, circles or circumference. Avoid perimeter formulae, unknown-side algebra, compound shapes with missing lengths, tonnes and pounds, seconds-based time calculations, time zones, speed, angles in degrees, and decimals beyond simple halves.
47|Unit 1C: Measure.example: A train leaves the station at 14:45 and arrives at 16:20. How long is the journey? Answer: 1 hour 35 minutes (14:45 to 15:00 is 15 min, 15:00 to 16:00 is 1 h, 16:00 to 16:20 is 20 min; 15 + 20 = 35 min).

47|Unit 1A: Number.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 1A: Number.teaches: Place value of digits in numbers up to 1 000 000 (and decimals to thousandths). Order, compare and round to the nearest 10, 100, 1000. Number sequences with term-to-term rules. Mental and written addition and subtraction. Multiplication and division facts. Long multiplication (up to 4-digit × 1-digit, 2-digit × 2-digit). Short division with remainders. Multiples, square numbers, divisibility tests (2, 3, 5, 9, 10, 100), factors, and factor pairs.
47|Unit 1A: Number.notYet: Prime factorisation, HCF/LCM, prime numbers beyond a simple intro, negative-number arithmetic, indices beyond squares (cubes, powers), nth-term formulae, long division with 2-digit divisors, standard form, rounding to decimal places or significant figures, algebra.
47|Unit 1A: Number.example: Is 3 456 divisible by 9? Use a test of divisibility to explain. Answer: Yes. The digits add up to 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18, and 18 is in the 9 times table, so 3 456 is divisible by 9.

47|Number.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Number.teaches: Stage 5 place value and rounding: reading, writing and ordering whole numbers up to 1 000 000; digit values (e.g. 4 in 345 210 is 40 000); multiplying and dividing by 10, 100 and 1000; decimals to 2 places (tenths, hundredths); ordering decimals; rounding to the nearest 10, 100, 1000 and rounding decimals to the nearest whole number; negative numbers on a number line; vocabulary: digit, round, approximate, ascending, descending, greater than/less than.
47|Number.notYet: Numbers beyond 1 000 000 or decimals beyond hundredths (thousandths come in Stage 6). No rounding to decimal places or significant figures, standard form, powers of ten notation, or rounding to 10 000/100 000. No negative-number arithmetic, estimating with rounded calculations, or fractions-to-decimal conversion as the focus.
47|Number.example: Question: Round 463 782 to the nearest 1000. Then write the value of the digit 6 in 463 782. Answer: 464 000; the digit 6 has a value of 60 000.

47|Unit 2C: Measure.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 2C: Measure.teaches: Measuring and drawing lines to the nearest millimetre using cm and mm; converting between m, cm, mm; reading 12-hour and 24-hour times and finding intervals in hours and minutes; using calendars (days, weeks, months, years); finding area by counting squares, including part squares (half-squares); finding perimeter of rectilinear shapes; comparing area and perimeter; words: estimate, perimeter, area, square centimetres.
47|Unit 2C: Measure.notYet: Area formula for triangles, parallelograms or circles; circumference or pi; area of compound shapes by subtraction; square metres or km² conversions; time zones; timetables across midnight; seconds-based calculations; angles in degrees; decimals beyond one or two places; algebraic formulae for perimeter.
47|Unit 2C: Measure.example: A rectangle is 7 cm long and 4 cm wide. (a) What is its perimeter? (b) A different rectangle has the same perimeter but is 6 cm long. How wide is it? Answer: (a) 7 + 4 + 7 + 4 = 22 cm. (b) 6 + 6 = 12, 22 − 12 = 10, 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm wide.

47|Unit 2A: Number.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 2A: Number.teaches: Stage 5 number work: extending sequences (including negative numbers, term-to-term rules); general statements such as 'the sum of two odd numbers is even'; ordering positive and negative numbers on number lines and in temperature contexts; decimals to 2 places (tenths, hundredths); decimal complements to 1; doubling and halving; multiplying by 10 and 100; partitioning; written addition and subtraction, including money; short multiplication and division of 3-digit numbers.
47|Unit 2A: Number.notYet: Algebraic letters or nth-term formulae, negative number arithmetic (adding or subtracting negatives), decimals beyond hundredths, multiplying or dividing by decimals, long division, formal long multiplication of 2-digit by 2-digit numbers, percentages, ratio, BODMAS, and standard form.
47|Unit 2A: Number.example: The temperature at 6 am was −4°C. By noon it had risen by 9 degrees. What was the temperature at noon? (Answer: 5°C)

47|Unit 2B: Handling data.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 2B: Handling data.teaches: Planning questions and surveys; collecting data in tally charts and frequency tables; recording results in two-way or Venn/Carroll diagrams; reading and drawing bar charts and line graphs (time on x-axis, e.g. temperature over a day); finding the mode; describing chance with words (impossible, unlikely, equally likely, likely, certain) and comparing events. Whole numbers, simple scales.
47|Unit 2B: Handling data.notYet: No probability as fractions, decimals or percentages, and no 0-1 scale numbers. No mean, median or range (the mode only, or maybe the range as an extension). No pie charts, scatter graphs, or sampling and bias terms. No relative frequency or frequency polygons. No negative-number axes.
47|Unit 2B: Handling data.example: A class recorded how many pets each child has: 0, 2, 1, 1, 3, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2. (a) Complete a tally chart. (b) What is the mode? (c) Is it certain, likely or unlikely that a child chosen at random has 1 pet? Answer: (a) 0: 2, 1: 4, 2: 3, 3: 1. (b) The mode is 1 pet. (c) Likely, but not certain, because 4 of the 10 children have 1 pet. Accept 'unlikely' only with a sensible reason, since 4 out of 10 is fewer than half. A better version is to ask which number of pets is the most likely.

47|Unit 3A: Number.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 3A: Number.teaches: Mental strategies (doubling, halving, near doubles, compensating, partitioning). Decimals to 2 d.p.: place value, ordering, rounding to nearest whole number, adding and subtracting. Percentages as parts of 100 (1%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75%). Equivalent fractions, decimals and percentages. Mixed numbers and improper fractions. Fractions as division. Inverse operations, brackets. Ratio and proportion 'for every', 'in every'.
47|Unit 3A: Number.notYet: Percentages of awkward amounts (e.g. 17%), percentage increase or decrease, recurring decimals, adding fractions with unlike denominators, multiplying or dividing fractions, negative numbers, algebra, ratio notation 3:2 or simplifying ratios, BODMAS with indices, rounding to decimal places, 3 or more decimal places.
47|Unit 3A: Number.example: Question: Amira has 40 stickers. She gives 25% of them to her friend. (a) How many stickers does she give away? (b) Write 25% as a fraction and as a decimal. Answer: (a) 10 stickers (40 ÷ 4). (b) 25% = 25/100 = 1/4, and 0.25.

48|Growing plants.teaches: Learners name and find the main parts of a plant: leaf, flower, stem, roots. They know seeds grow into plants. Seeds and plants need water; plants also need light and warmth. They observe, compare and talk about simple growing tests (e.g. a plant in light or dark). Vocabulary: seed, plant, leaf, flower, stem, root, water, light, grow.
48|Growing plants.notYet: Photosynthesis, chlorophyll, making food or sugar, carbon dioxide or oxygen, germination stages, functions of root hairs, xylem or phloem, pollination, fertilisation, seed dispersal, life cycles, fair-test variables, nutrients or minerals, and a seed's inner parts (embryo, cotyledon). Also avoid soil-nutrient and measurement-based questions.
48|Growing plants.example: Question: Look at the picture of a plant. Which part of the plant takes in water from the soil? A) leaf B) flower C) roots. Answer: C) roots. (Alternative: What two things does a plant need to grow well? Answer: water and light.)

47|Unit 3C: Measure.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 3C: Measure.teaches: Stage 5 measure: estimating, measuring and comparing volume and capacity (ml, l, cm³ cubes) and mass (g, kg), with conversions such as 1 l = 1000 ml and 1 kg = 1000 g. Time: 12-hour and 24-hour clocks, converting between them, reading timetables, calculating intervals, and units such as seconds, minutes, hours, days, weeks, months and years. Area and perimeter of rectangles and rectilinear shapes: counting squares, using cm², m² and cm, m, and finding missing sides. Uses simple whole-number or one-decimal-place values.
47|Unit 3C: Measure.notYet: No formula for the area of triangles, parallelograms or circles. No volume formula (length × width × height) and no cm³ calculations from dimensions. No circumference or π. No time zones or speed. No algebraic formulae. No unit conversions between cm² and m². No compound shapes needing subtraction methods. No angles in degrees.
47|Unit 3C: Measure.example: A rectangle is 8 cm long and 5 cm wide. (a) What is its perimeter? (b) What is its area? Answer: (a) 8 + 5 + 8 + 5 = 26 cm. (b) 8 × 5 = 40 cm².

48|Pushes and pulls.teaches: Forces are pushes and pulls. Learners sort everyday actions and toys (swings, slides, roundabouts, pushing a pram, pulling a wagon) as push or pull. A push or pull can make things start moving, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction. They use words: push, pull, move, turn, swing, stop, fast, slow. They observe and sort.
48|Pushes and pulls.notYet: Not taught: the word 'force' as a measured quantity, newtons, forcemeter, friction, gravity, air resistance, balanced or unbalanced forces, Newton's laws, mass, speed calculations, energy, magnets as forces, fair-test variables, and explaining why. Avoid long written answers and multi-step reasoning. Keep to observing and sorting.
48|Pushes and pulls.example: Question: A child opens a door by taking the handle and moving the door towards herself. Is she pushing or pulling? Circle one: push / pull. Answer: pull.

48|Ourselves.teaches: Children notice how people are similar (head, two eyes, hands, ten fingers) and different (hair colour, eye colour, height, boy or girl). They name body parts: head, arms, legs, hands, feet, eyes, ears, nose, mouth, tongue, skin. They know the five senses: see, hear, smell, taste, touch. They sort, count and compare in simple tallies or pictures, with small numbers.
48|Ourselves.notYet: Not taught: internal organs and their jobs (heart, lungs, brain, stomach), skeleton and bones, how the eye or ear works, nerves, DNA, genes or inheritance, growth stages, healthy diet, hygiene and germs, variation as a term, graphs with scales, fair tests, formal measuring units (cm, kg).
48|Ourselves.example: Question: Look at the picture of four children. Two have brown eyes, one has blue eyes and one has green eyes. Which eye colour is most common? Answer: Brown eyes (2 children, more than any other colour).

48|Materials in my world.teaches: Learners name everyday materials (wood, plastic, metal, glass, fabric, paper, rock) and say what objects are made of. They link a material's property to its use (strong, flexible, soft, waterproof, see-through, warm or cold to touch). They sort objects by one simple property and explain how they sorted.
48|Materials in my world.notYet: Not taught: natural vs man-made or manufactured materials, rigid/opaque/translucent, hardness scales, absorbency tests, fair testing with variables, solids/liquids/gases, states of matter, particles, melting, conductivity, magnetism, recycling processes, chemical names (e.g. polyester, steel alloys), measurements or data tables.
48|Materials in my world.example: A window is made of glass. Give one reason why glass is a good material for a window. (Answer: You can see through it / it is transparent, so light comes in and we can see outside. Accept 'it is hard' or 'it keeps rain out'.)

48|Being alive.teaches: Telling living things (animals, plants, which move, grow, need food and water, have babies) from non-living things (rocks, toys). Naming local places such as garden, pond, playground and the plants and animals found there. Matching adults with young (hen–chick, cow–calf, frog–tadpole). Sorting healthy foods (fruit, vegetables) and drinks (water, milk) from less healthy ones.
48|Being alive.notYet: The seven life processes or MRS GREN, respiration, photosynthesis, food chains, habitats and adaptation, life cycle stages and metamorphosis, nutrients (protein, vitamins, carbohydrates), balanced diet proportions, digestion, classification groups (vertebrates, mammals), 'dead' versus 'never alive', and cells.
48|Being alive.example: Look at the picture of a cat, a flower, a stone and a toy car. Which two are alive? Answer: the cat and the flower.

47|Unit 3B: Geometry.book: Cambridge Primary Mathematics Stage 5 Learners Book
47|Unit 3B: Geometry.teaches: Estimate, measure and draw acute and obtuse angles in degrees with a protractor; know angles on a straight line total 180° and angles at a point total 360°. Classify triangles (equilateral, isosceles, right-angled, scalene). Find lines of symmetry in 2D shapes and patterns. Identify 3D shapes (prisms, pyramids) and their nets. Use coordinates in the first quadrant; translate shapes; reflect in horizontal or vertical mirror lines.
47|Unit 3B: Geometry.notYet: Angle sum of a triangle (180°) or of a quadrilateral, and algebraic angle problems. Negative coordinates and all four quadrants. Rotational symmetry and order of rotation. Rotation of shapes. Reflection in diagonal mirror lines. Parallel-line angle rules. Volume or surface area formulae. Circles, radius and circumference. Pythagoras.
47|Unit 3B: Geometry.example:
Question: A straight line has two angles on it. One angle is 125°. What is the size of the other angle? Show how you know.
Answer: 55°, because angles on a straight line add up to 180° and 180° − 125° = 55°.

48|Hearing sounds.teaches: Sounds come from things around us (voices, instruments, animals, machines). Sounds can be loud or quiet, and made in different ways, such as hitting, plucking or blowing. We hear with our ears. Sounds travel to our ears from a source. Sounds get quieter as we move away. Words: sound, hear, ear, loud, quiet, near, far.
48|Hearing sounds.notYet: Vibrations as the cause of sound, sound waves, particles, pitch (high/low) as a measured idea, volume or decibels, the parts of the ear (eardrum, cochlea), speed of sound, echoes, how sound travels through solids, liquids and gases, soundproofing materials, frequency.
48|Hearing sounds.example: Mia stands close to a drum and hits it. Then she walks far away from the drum while a friend hits it in the same way. How does the sound seem to Mia when she is far away? Answer: Quieter (it is harder to hear).

49|Looking at rocks.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|Looking at rocks.teaches: Rocks are natural, found outdoors, and can be hard or soft, rough or smooth, or waterproof. Learners sort and describe rocks by simple properties. Uses: building, roads, statues, tiles, jewellery. Soil is made of tiny pieces of rock and bits of dead plants and animals. Other natural materials include wood, cotton, wool and clay, and they are used to make things.
49|Looking at rocks.notYet: No rock types (igneous, sedimentary, metamorphic), no rock cycle, no weathering or erosion as processes, no fossil formation, no humus or soil layers, no particle sizes by name, no minerals or Mohs hardness, no chemical or formal test terms, no permeability, no atoms or particles.
49|Looking at rocks.example: Mia has a hard, grey rock. Give one thing people use hard rock for. Answer: Any one of: building houses or walls, making roads, or making statues. (Also accept paving or tiles.)

49|Changing materials.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|Changing materials.teaches: Pushing, pulling, squashing, bending, twisting and stretching change the shape of some materials (clay, sponge, rubber band, foam, wire, paper). Elastic materials return to their shape. Heating and cooling change materials: ice melts, chocolate melts, water freezes. Sea water is salty, and salt is left when the water evaporates. Words: twist, bend, stretch, squash, melt, freeze, elastic.
49|Changing materials.notYet: Particle model, solids/liquids/gases as states with particle arrangement, melting and boiling points in °C, condensation cycle, dissolving and solubility theory, reversible vs irreversible terms, forces measured in newtons, Hooke's law, extension measurements, elasticity as a property with energy ideas, thermal conductivity.
49|Changing materials.example: Mia has a rubber band, a piece of clay and a metal spoon. Which one can she stretch and then watch go back to its first shape? Answer: the rubber band, because it is elastic.

49|Electricity.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|Electricity.teaches: Everyday items that use electricity (mains and battery); electricity safety (never touch sockets, plugs or pylons; keep water away from electricity); building a simple circuit with a cell, wires and a bulb; a circuit must be a complete loop for the bulb to light; buzzers and motors; switches open or close (break) a circuit.
49|Electricity.notYet: Current, voltage, volts, amps, resistance; circuit symbols and diagrams; series versus parallel circuits; conductors and insulators as formal terms; electrons; how a battery works; brightness changing with the number of cells; fuses; calculations.
49|Electricity.example: Mia makes a circuit with a cell, a bulb and wires. The bulb does not light. She sees one wire is not joined to the cell. Why is the bulb off? Answer: The circuit has a gap, so it is not a complete loop. Electricity cannot flow round to the bulb. Joining the wire to the cell makes the bulb light.

49|Going outside.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|Going outside.teaches: Habitats near home (e.g. woodland, pond, garden, desert, sea) and what minibeasts and plants need there (food, water, shelter). Caring for the environment: litter, recycling, looking after wildlife. Weather words (sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, snowy, foggy). Reading simple block graphs, tables and weather symbols. Extreme weather (storms, floods, drought, heatwave) and staying safe.
49|Going outside.notYet: Food chains, producers/consumers, adaptation, the water cycle (evaporation, condensation), climate vs weather, climate change, greenhouse effect, ecosystems, biodiversity, measuring wind speed or temperature in degrees, reading scales, isotherms, and pollution science. Also no fair-test variables, averages or percentages.
49|Going outside.example: A learner counts the minibeasts found in four places: under a log 8, on a path 2, on a flowerbed 5, on a dry sunny wall 1. (a) Which place had the most minibeasts? (b) Why might minibeasts like living under a log? Answer: (a) Under the log. (b) It is dark, damp and gives shelter/hiding from animals that eat them.

49|The Earth and the Sun.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|The Earth and the Sun.teaches: Day is the part of the Earth facing the Sun; night is the part facing away. The Sun seems to move across the sky: low in the morning, high at midday, low in the evening. Shadows change length and direction through the day, and are longest when the Sun is low. Words: Sun, Earth, day, night, shadow, morning, midday, evening, high, low.
49|The Earth and the Sun.notYet: Earth's rotation on its axis (24 hours), the 23.5° tilt, orbit and a year, seasons, time zones, the Moon's phases, compass directions (east/west), light travelling in straight lines, opaque/transparent/translucent, measuring shadow lengths in cm, and sundials as calculations.
49|The Earth and the Sun.example: Look at the picture of a child and a tree with a long shadow. The Sun is low in the sky. Is it more likely to be midday or evening? Why? Answer: Evening (or morning is also accepted if the picture does not show which). The Sun is low, so shadows are long. At midday the Sun is high and shadows are short.

49|Light and dark.book: Cambridge Primary Science 2 Learners Book PDF
49|Light and dark.teaches: Light sources (Sun, lamps, torches, candles, fire, screens) make their own light; the Moon, mirrors and shiny things only reflect light, so they are not sources. Darkness is the absence of light. Learners test what happens in a dark place. A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light. Shadow shape matches the object. Shadows change size when the object moves nearer to or further from the light source. Simple observation, sorting and recording.
49|Light and dark.notYet: Light travelling in straight lines as a rule, rays and ray diagrams, reflection angles, how we see (light entering the eye), transparent/translucent/opaque terms in depth, umbra/penumbra, eclipses, Earth's rotation causing shadow changes, speed of light, wavelength, and measuring in degrees or with formulae.
49|Light and dark.example: Which of these is a light source: the Moon, a candle, a mirror or a book? Answer: a candle, because it makes its own light. (The Moon and mirror only reflect light.)

50|Looking after plants.teaches: Main plant parts (roots, stem, leaves, flower) and their jobs. Plants need light, water and suitable warmth to grow and stay healthy. Roots take in water; it moves up the stem to the leaves (celery in coloured water). Learners predict, observe, compare, and run simple fair tests with a few plants.
50|Looking after plants.notYet: Photosynthesis, chlorophyll, glucose or carbon dioxide; xylem and phloem; transpiration, osmosis or root hairs; mineral nutrients in detail; stomata; pollination, seed dispersal and life cycles; measuring growth with formal units or graphs; variables named as 'independent/dependent'; cell structure.
50|Looking after plants.example: Question: Mia puts a white flower in water with red dye for one day. The petals turn pink. What does this show about how water moves in a plant? Answer: Water moves up the stem from the roots to the flower (the petals), carrying the dye with it.

50|Looking after ourselves.teaches: Food groups: carbohydrates (energy), proteins (growth and repair), fats, fruit and vegetables (vitamins, minerals), fibre, water. Sorting foods into groups. A healthy diet is balanced, with the right amounts. Too much sugar, fat or salt is unhealthy. Exercise keeps the heart, muscles and bones healthy. Sleep helps the body rest. Reading simple tables and comparing sugar per 100ml. Fair tests and predicting.
50|Looking after ourselves.notYet: Do not ask about calories or kilojoules, BMI, or the nutrient tests (iodine, Benedict's, biuret). Avoid enzymes and digestion chemistry, named vitamin deficiency diseases, cholesterol, metabolism, heart rate calculations, hormones, percentages, or the detailed workings of the circulatory system.
50|Looking after ourselves.example: Question: Amira eats a lunch of chicken, rice and carrots, and drinks water. (a) Name one food in her lunch that is a good source of protein. (b) Why does her body need protein? (c) Amira says, 'A drink with lots of sugar is a healthy choice.' Is she right? Explain. Answer: (a) Chicken. (b) Protein helps the body grow and repair itself. (c) No. Too much sugar is unhealthy. It can damage teeth and give energy the body may not need. Water is a better choice.

50|Living things.teaches: Telling living from non-living things (move, grow, feed, reproduce, sensitive to surroundings). Plants and animals need food/nutrition and grow. Animals move and have young or lay eggs, with shelters such as nests. Sorting humans by features (height, hair colour, eye colour). Sorting living things into plant/animal groups by simple observable features. Simple words only.
50|Living things.notYet: The seven life processes named formally (MRS GREN), cells, organs, photosynthesis, respiration, vertebrate/invertebrate classes (mammal, reptile, amphibian), classification keys, branching diagrams, species, genes or DNA, inheritance, life cycle stages with metamorphosis, food chains, balanced diet details, and nutrient names.
50|Living things.example:
Question: A rock, a cat and a tree are in a picture. Which one is non-living, and give one reason why you know it is not alive.
Answer: The rock. It does not grow, eat or feed, or have young (any one reason is acceptable).

50|Our five senses.teaches: The five senses (sight, hearing, touch, taste, smell) and the body part for each: eyes, ears, skin, tongue, nose. Sounds can be loud or quiet, high or low. Touch finds rough, smooth, hot, cold. Tongue tastes sweet, sour, salty, bitter. Smell helps animals find food. Learners make simple fair tests, fill in tables and compare results.
50|Our five senses.notYet: Nerves, brain signals, taste buds, receptors, the retina, pupil reflex, eardrum and vibrations in the ear, frequency, decibels, how light enters the eye, and the parts of the ear. Also no wave diagrams, no formulae, and no named nerve pathways. Avoid the word 'stimulus'.
50|Our five senses.example: Question: Sam closes his eyes. His friend puts a lemon slice on his tongue. Sam says it tastes sour. (a) Which sense does Sam use to taste the lemon? (b) Name the body part he uses. (c) Name one other sense he could use to find out what the food is, and the body part for it. Answer: (a) taste; (b) tongue; (c) smell with the nose (or touch with the fingers/skin, or sight with the eyes).

50|Forces and movement.teaches: Forces are pushes and pulls. Forces can start, stop, speed up, slow down or change the direction of movement, and can change an object's shape (stretch, squash, bend, twist). Bigger forces have bigger effects. Forcemeters measure force in newtons (N), using whole-number readings. Friction is a force between touching surfaces that slows movement. Rough surfaces give more friction than smooth ones. Learners predict, make fair tests, record results and compare surfaces.
50|Forces and movement.notYet: Gravity as a force with weight vs mass, air resistance and water resistance calculations, balanced and unbalanced forces, resultant force, Newton's laws, F = ma, speed calculations, pressure, moments, elastic limit, Hooke's law, force arrows with magnitude, and mass in kilograms versus weight.
50|Forces and movement.example: Ravi pulls a toy car across three surfaces with a forcemeter. Carpet: 6 N. Wood: 3 N. Plastic sheet: 1 N. (a) Which surface was hardest to pull the car on? (b) Which force makes it hard to pull? Answer: (a) Carpet, because it needed the biggest pull (6 N). (b) Friction.

50|Investigating materials.teaches: Learners describe materials by properties: hard/soft, flexible/rigid, strong/weak, waterproof/absorbent, transparent/translucent/opaque, rough/smooth, shiny/dull, magnetic/non-magnetic. They sort materials using tables, Venn diagrams and branching keys. They link properties to uses, run simple fair tests (change one thing, keep others the same), measure in cm or by counting, and find that magnets attract only some metals such as iron.
50|Investigating materials.notYet: Avoid atoms, particles, solids/liquids/gases explained by particle arrangement, conductivity of heat or electricity as theory, density, elasticity or Hooke's law, magnetic poles and field lines, alloys, steel composition, forces in newtons, mean averages, and variables named as independent/dependent. Avoid chemical reactions and states of matter changes.
50|Investigating materials.example: A class tests which of four materials (plastic, wood, steel, cotton) is best for making a window. Q: Which property must a window material have, and which material from the list is best? Answer: It must be transparent (see-through); none of these four is transparent as listed, so a better answer is to name clear plastic, which is transparent, waterproof and light. Simpler version: Which property is needed for a window? Transparent.

51|Humans and animals.teaches: Animals with and without backbones; skeletons (endoskeleton, exoskeleton, hydrostatic idea only simply). Main human bones: skull, ribs, backbone/spine, pelvis, femur, humerus, jaw. Skeleton functions: support, protection, movement. Muscles pull on bones; joints; pairs of muscles. Medicines vs other drugs, safe use, how medicines help. Measuring bone lengths in cm and comparing results.
51|Humans and animals.notYet: Muscle names like biceps/triceps in detail, antagonistic pairs and contract/relax mechanisms at cellular level, joint types (ball-and-socket, hinge) technical detail, bone marrow making blood cells, calcium, cartilage, tendons/ligaments, receptors, antibiotics vs viruses, addiction mechanisms, bone density calculations.
51|Humans and animals.example: Question: Mia says, 'My ribs protect my heart and lungs.' (a) Is Mia right? (b) Name one other part of the skeleton that protects an organ and say which organ it protects. Answer: (a) Yes, the ribs form a cage around the heart and lungs. (b) The skull protects the brain (or the backbone protects the spinal cord).

51|Solids, liquids and gases.teaches: Matter is anything that has mass and takes up space. Solids, liquids and gases are the three states. Particle model: particles are tiny; in solids they are close, in a regular pattern, and vibrate; in liquids they are close but can slide past each other; in gases they are far apart and move quickly. Melting, freezing and boiling. Different solids melt at different temperatures. Melting and boiling points of water and other materials (°C). Reading simple tables and thermometers.
51|Solids, liquids and gases.notYet: Not taught: condensation and evaporation as a full water cycle explanation, sublimation, plasma, forces between particles, kinetic energy, particle diagrams for changes of state in detail, density, pressure, atoms, molecules, elements, compounds, Kelvin, latent heat, heating curves, particle numbers or calculations.
51|Solids, liquids and gases.example: Question: Ice is heated and turns into water. (a) What is the name of this change of state? (b) Water boils at 100 °C. What happens to the particles of water as it changes into a gas? Answer: (a) Melting. (b) The particles move faster and spread far apart from each other, so they are no longer close together (they become a gas, water vapour).

51|Living things and environments.teaches: Birds' features (beaks, feet, feathers) suited to food and habitat. Snail needs and choosing a habitat. Local habitats (pond, woodland, desert, seashore) and the animals living there. Making and using branching/yes-no keys. Invertebrates (insects, spiders, snails, worms, centipedes). Human effects: pollution, manure, litter, clearing land. Water pollution and cleaning. Reduce, reuse, recycle. Reading simple bar charts.
51|Living things and environments.notYet: Food chains and webs, predator-prey energy ideas, adaptation and natural selection, classification into kingdoms, Latin names, vertebrate group details, ecosystems and biodiversity terms, eutrophication and chemical causes, carbon cycle, climate change and greenhouse gas, quantitative sampling (quadrats), mean calculations.
51|Living things and environments.example:
Question: Look at this key for three minibeasts.
1a Has legs: go to 2
1b Has no legs: it is an earthworm
2a Has six legs: it is an ant
2b Has eight legs: it is a spider
Use the key to name a minibeast that has eight legs. Then write one yes/no question you could add to the key to tell a snail from an ant.
Answer: Spider. Sample question: 'Does it have a shell?' (snail yes, ant no).

51|Sound.teaches: Sound is made by vibrations and travels through solids, liquids and gases (air, water, wood, metal). Sound gets quieter as it moves away from the source. Loud and soft sounds (volume) depend on how big the vibration is. Muffling materials block sound. High and low pitch come from fast and slow vibrations. Pitch changes with the length of strings, tubes or bars. Learners use the words vibration, volume, pitch, muffle and source.
51|Sound.notYet: Not taught: frequency and hertz, amplitude, decibels, wavelength, speed of sound figures, longitudinal waves and compressions, echoes and reflection, how the ear works in detail, sound in a vacuum explained by particles, the oscilloscope, and the formula for wave speed.
51|Sound.example: Mia plucks a rubber band stretched over a box. She then plucks a shorter, tighter rubber band. (a) What moves backwards and forwards to make the sound? (b) Is the sound from the shorter, tighter band higher or lower? Answer: (a) The rubber band vibrates. (b) Higher, because it vibrates faster.

51|Electricity and magnetism.teaches: Electricity flows around a complete circuit from a cell or battery. Learners know the components: cell, battery, bulb, wire, switch, buzzer. They draw and build simple circuits and predict whether bulbs or buzzers work. Open switch = break, closed = complete. Mains is dangerous. Magnets have N and S poles, like poles repel, unlike attract. Magnets differ in strength. Iron and steel are magnetic.
51|Electricity and magnetism.notYet: Not taught: current, voltage, amps, volts, resistance, Ohm's law; series versus parallel names; circuit symbols calculations; electrons or charge; conductors and insulators as formal terms; electromagnets; magnetic fields and field lines; domains; Earth's core; calculating strength. Avoid 'current' as a measured quantity.
51|Electricity and magnetism.example: Aisha builds a circuit with a cell, a bulb, a switch and wires. The switch is open. (a) Will the bulb light? (b) What must Aisha do to make it light, and why? Answer: (a) No, because the circuit has a gap, so the electricity cannot flow all the way round. (b) Close the switch, which completes the circuit so electricity can flow around it and light the bulb.

52|States of matter.teaches: Evaporation is a liquid changing to a gas below boiling point, faster when warmer, windier, or with a larger surface area. Uses: drying washing, salt from seawater. Condensation: water vapour cools to liquid. The water cycle (evaporation, condensation, precipitation, collection). Boiling and melting points, thermometer readings in °C, fair tests, predictions and line graphs.
52|States of matter.notYet: No particle model (kinetic theory), no molecules, bonds, or energy explanations. No latent heat, vapour pressure, or humidity. No sublimation, deposition or freezing-point depression. No Kelvin, no Fahrenheit conversion. No transpiration or water-cycle detail beyond basics. No calculations of rates or density.
52|States of matter.example: Two identical wet T-shirts are hung outside. One is hung on a sunny, windy day and the other on a cold, still day. Which T-shirt dries faster, and why? Answer: The T-shirt on the sunny, windy day dries faster. Warmth and moving air make water evaporate (change from liquid to water vapour) more quickly.

52|The life cycle of flowering plants.topic: The life cycle of flowering plants
52|The life cycle of flowering plants.teaches: Flowers make seeds for reproduction. Parts of a flower: petals, sepals, stamen (anther, filament), carpel (stigma, style, ovary). Pollination by insects or wind, and self- vs cross-pollination in simple terms. Seed dispersal by wind, water, animals and explosion. Seed parts and germination. Life cycle stages: seed, germination, growth, flowering, pollination, seed formation. Fair-test pollination investigations.
52|The life cycle of flowering plants.notYet: Fertilisation in detail (pollen tube, nucleus fusion, ovule), gametes, mitosis/meiosis, dicots vs monocots, cotyledon function in depth, photosynthesis equations, genetics or variation, alternation of generations, hormones, and asexual reproduction details beyond simple examples.
52|The life cycle of flowering plants.example:
A dandelion seed has a ring of light, feathery hairs. (a) How is the dandelion seed dispersed? (b) Give a reason for your answer. (c) Name the part of a flower where the seeds form.

Answer: (a) By wind. (b) The light, feathery hairs help it float and be carried far through the air. (c) The ovary.

52|Shadows.teaches: Light travels in straight lines from a source. Materials are transparent, translucent or opaque. A shadow forms when an opaque object blocks light. Silhouettes and shadow puppets. A shadow's size changes with the distance between source, object and screen. Fair test: change one variable, measure shadow length in cm, record in tables, draw line graphs. Light intensity is measured with a light sensor or meter. Scientists such as Ibn al-Haytham.
52|Shadows.notYet: Ray diagrams with angles in degrees, the law of reflection, refraction, the speed of light calculations, wavelength or the electromagnetic spectrum, how the eye forms images, umbra and penumbra terminology, similar triangles or ratios, lux units, eclipses explained with geometry, photons or waves.
52|Shadows.example: Mia holds a toy figure between a torch and a wall. She moves the toy closer to the torch. (a) What happens to the size of the shadow on the wall? (b) Explain why the shadow has the same shape as the toy. Answer: (a) The shadow gets bigger. (b) Light travels in straight lines and cannot pass through the opaque toy, so the light is blocked in the shape of the toy.

52|Investigating plant growth.teaches: Seed structure (testa, embryo, food store); seed dispersal ideas; germination as a seed starting to grow into a seedling. Germination needs water, warmth and air, not light. Plants need light, water, warmth and space to grow. Fair tests: change one variable, keep others the same. Learners record results in tables, draw bar charts, predict, and spot patterns.
52|Investigating plant growth.notYet: Photosynthesis, chlorophyll, glucose, or word and symbol equations. Respiration in seeds. Enzymes, hormones, auxins or gibberellins. Monocot/dicot, cotyledon detail, plumule/radicle. Mineral ions by name (nitrate, magnesium). Phototropism mechanisms. Stomata, xylem and phloem, transpiration. Statistics such as mean or line of best fit.
52|Investigating plant growth.example: Dembe plants 10 cress seeds on damp cotton wool in each of 3 places: a warm window, a warm dark cupboard and a cold fridge. After 5 days, 9 seeds germinated in the window, 9 in the cupboard and 1 in the fridge. (a) What was the one thing Dembe changed? (b) Name two things she should keep the same to make it a fair test. (c) What do the results tell you about what seeds need to germinate? Answer: (a) the temperature/place (warmth). (b) Any two: number of seeds, type of seed, amount of water, type of cotton wool, time left. (c) Seeds germinate well without light, but need warmth, because the cold fridge seeds mostly did not germinate.

52|The way we see things.teaches: Light travels in straight lines from a source (Sun, lamp, torch, candle, screen) in all directions. We see when light enters the eye, from a source or reflected off objects. Mirrors reflect light. Periscopes use two mirrors to see over or around things. Shiny, smooth surfaces reflect best. Light changes direction when reflected. Fair tests, predictions, tables, bar charts.
52|The way we see things.notYet: Angles of incidence and reflection, the law of reflection, measuring angles with a protractor. Refraction, lenses, the spectrum or colour mixing, wavelength, the speed of light (numbers), ray diagrams with normals, parts of the eye (retina), concave/convex mirrors, opaque/transparent definitions beyond basic ideas, and the term 'photon'.
52|The way we see things.example: A periscope has two mirrors. Explain how a periscope lets a child see over a high wall. Answer: Light from the object over the wall travels in a straight line to the top mirror. The mirror reflects it down to the bottom mirror. That mirror reflects it into the child's eye, so the child sees the object.

53|The human body.teaches: Human body systems at Stage 6. The heart is a pump with blood vessels (arteries, veins, capillaries) carrying blood around the body. Blood carries oxygen and nutrients. Pulse and heart rate change with exercise. Lungs, skeleton, muscles and digestion link to the life processes. Effects of exercise, diet, smoking and drugs on health. Circulatory systems of other vertebrates are compared with the human one.
53|The human body.notYet: Not taught: heart chambers and valves in detail, double circulation pathways, red and white cell structure, haemoglobin, alveoli gas exchange, diffusion, aerobic and anaerobic respiration, glucose equations, ATP, mitochondria, enzymes, hormones, nervous system, blood pressure values.
53|The human body.example: Question: Sam measures his pulse at rest and straight after running. Explain why his pulse is faster after running. Answer: His muscles need more oxygen and nutrients when he runs, so the heart beats faster to pump blood around the body more quickly and carry them to the muscles.

52|Earth's movements.teaches: The Sun is a star; Earth and Moon are spheres. The Sun only appears to move across the sky because Earth rotates on its axis once every 24 hours, giving day and night. Shadows change length and direction through the day. Sunrise and sunset times are read from tables and graphs. Earth orbits the Sun once a year (about 365 days). Planets of the solar system and their order. Stars are far away.
52|Earth's movements.notYet: Do not ask about: axial tilt (23.5°) explaining seasons, leap years, lunar phases or eclipses explained by geometry, gravity calculations, orbital speed, distances in light-years, star life cycles, galaxies, planet temperatures or moon counts, equinoxes and solstices, time zones calculated, latitude and longitude.
52|Earth's movements.example: Question: The table shows sunrise and sunset times in Kingston, Jamaica. On 1 January the Sun rose at 06:34 and set at 17:43. (a) Explain why the Sun seems to move across the sky during the day. (b) Which part of Earth's movement gives us day and night? Answer: (a) The Sun does not really move. The Earth spins (rotates) on its axis, so the Sun appears to move from east to west. (b) The Earth rotating (spinning) on its axis once every 24 hours; the side facing the Sun has day and the side facing away has night.

53|Materials: properties and changes.teaches: Properties of materials: electrical and thermal conductors/insulators, hardness, strength, flexibility, solubility, magnetism, transparency. Reversible changes (melting, freezing, dissolving, evaporating, condensing) versus irreversible chemical changes (burning, rusting, baking, vinegar with bicarbonate). Evidence of a reaction: gas bubbles, colour change, temperature change, new substance. Separating mixtures by filtering, evaporating and sieving. Fair tests.
53|Materials: properties and changes.notYet: Atoms, molecules, particle models of bonding, chemical formulae and symbol equations, word equations with named products, the pH scale, acids and bases in detail, exothermic/endothermic terms, the conservation of mass calculation, metal reactivity series, ionic or covalent bonding, and balancing equations.
53|Materials: properties and changes.example:
Sam stirs a spoonful of salt into water and it seems to disappear. Then he stirs sand into water and it does not. (a) What word describes the salt in the water? (b) How could Sam get the salt back from the salt solution? (c) Is this change reversible or irreversible?
Answer: (a) It dissolves (salt is soluble; a solution forms). (b) Heat the solution so the water evaporates, leaving the salt behind. (c) Reversible.

53|Rocks, the rock cycle and soil.topic: Rocks, the rock cycle and soil
53|Rocks, the rock cycle and soil.teaches: Three rock types: igneous (cooled magma/lava; fast cooling gives small crystals, slow cooling gives large crystals), sedimentary (sediment compacted and cemented in layers; fossils form in it) and metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure). The rock cycle as a continuous process. Soil: particles, humus, air, water. Comparing rocks and soils by testing and observing fairly. Words: weathering, erosion, sediment, fossil, permeable.
53|Rocks, the rock cycle and soil.notYet: Mineral names and chemical composition, Mohs hardness scale, named metamorphic grades, plate tectonics, magma chambers and volcano types, radiometric dating, geological time periods, soil horizons or profiles, pH and nutrient chemistry, cation exchange, biogeochemical cycles, and calculations of percentages or densities.
53|Rocks, the rock cycle and soil.example: Question: Granite and basalt are both igneous rocks. Granite has large crystals and basalt has very small crystals. What does this tell you about how each rock cooled? Answer: Granite cooled slowly, probably underground, which gave the crystals time to grow large. Basalt cooled quickly, probably at the surface after a volcano erupted lava, so its crystals stayed small.

53|Food chains and food webs.teaches: An ecosystem is a habitat with its living things interacting with the non-living environment. Learners use producer, consumer, predator, prey, herbivore, carnivore and omnivore. They draw food chains with arrows meaning 'energy goes to', and read simple food webs. Plants make food using light. They predict what happens if one population in a web changes.
53|Food chains and food webs.notYet: Trophic levels, primary or secondary consumer ranks, energy pyramids, percentage energy transfer (10% rule), biomass, decomposers' nutrient cycling detail, photosynthesis equations, chlorophyll, carbon or nitrogen cycles, bioaccumulation, population-growth curves, and named respiration or ATP processes.
53|Food chains and food webs.example: A pond food web: pondweed → snail → fish → heron, and pondweed → tadpole → fish. (a) Name the producer. (b) What does the arrow between snail and fish mean? (c) Disease kills most of the snails. Suggest one effect on the tadpoles and explain why. Answer: (a) pondweed. (b) The energy (food) goes from the snail to the fish, because the fish eats the snail. (c) The number of tadpoles may go down, because the fish have less snail to eat so they eat more tadpoles. Accept any sensible prediction with a reason.

53|Light and the Solar System.teaches: Light travels in straight lines. Reflection from shiny surfaces and mirrors (periscopes, reflected rays shown with arrows). Refraction: light bends when passing between air, water and glass, so a straw looks bent. The Sun is a star. The eight planets in order, scale models of distances, Earth's rotation and orbit, Moon phases (waxing, waning).
53|Light and the Solar System.notYet: Angle of incidence/reflection measured in degrees, law of reflection with calculations, refractive index, Snell's law, total internal reflection, lenses and ray diagrams, wavelength, speed of light figures, light years, gravity equations, tides, eclipses in detail, planet moons data, stellar life cycles.
53|Light and the Solar System.example: A straw in a glass of water looks bent where it meets the water's surface. (a) Name this effect. (b) Explain what happens to the light to make the straw look bent. Answer: (a) Refraction. (b) The light changes direction (bends) as it passes from water into air, so it seems to come from a different place than the straw really is.

53|Forces and electricity.teaches: Mass (kg, g) is the amount of matter; weight is a gravity force measured in newtons with a forcemeter. Learners know balanced and unbalanced forces, friction, air and water resistance, upthrust, and how forces change shape, speed or direction. They compare floating and sinking by density ideas. They use circuit symbols (cell, battery, lamp, switch, buzzer, motor, wire) and draw series and parallel circuits.
53|Forces and electricity.notYet: Not taught: the formula weight = mass × gravitational field strength (W=mg, 10 N/kg), density calculations (mass/volume), Archimedes' principle, pressure, Newton's laws, resultant force sums, moments, current in amps, voltage, resistance, Ohm's law, and current values in series versus parallel circuits.
53|Forces and electricity.example: Question: An astronaut takes a rock from Earth to the Moon. Does the rock's mass change, and does its weight change? Explain. Answer: The mass stays the same because the amount of matter in the rock is unchanged. The weight is less on the Moon because the Moon's gravity pulls with a smaller force than Earth's.

53|Working like a scientist.teaches: Working scientifically at Stage 6: using books, websites and experts for research; planning fair tests by changing one variable, measuring another and controlling the rest; making repeated observations over time; sorting living things and materials with keys, Venn and Carroll diagrams; finding patterns in tables, bar and line graphs; making predictions; using words like variable, evidence, conclusion.
53|Working like a scientist.notYet: Not taught: independent, dependent and control variable terminology as formal terms; hypothesis writing; mean, range or anomaly calculations; line of best fit; correlation; statistical tests; percentage error; Linnaean binomial naming; taxonomy ranks; formal evaluation of reliability and validity; scientific notation; SI unit conversions.
53|Working like a scientist.example: Amy wants to find out whether the temperature of water changes how fast sugar dissolves. She changes the water temperature. Name two things she must keep the same to make it a fair test. Answer: any two of: the amount (volume) of water, the amount of sugar, the type of sugar, the stirring, the size of the container (and how she measures the time).

1|Characteristics and classification of.topic: Characteristics and classification of living organisms
1|Characteristics and classification of.teaches: Seven characteristics of living things (movement, respiration, sensitivity, growth, reproduction, excretion, nutrition). Binomial naming (genus and species, italic/capitalised). Using and making dichotomous keys. Five kingdoms: animals, plants, fungi, prokaryotes, protoctists. Vertebrate classes, arthropod classes, and flowering plants (monocots and dicots), ferns. Virus structure (protein coat, genetic material) and viruses as non-cellular.
1|Characteristics and classification of.notYet: Domains (Archaea/Bacteria/Eukarya), taxonomic ranks beyond genus/species in detail, DNA-sequence or phylogenetic classification, species definitions with fertile offspring, virus replication cycles (lytic/lysogenic), bacterial cell wall chemistry, ribosomes, ATP, detailed meiosis or evolution.
1|Characteristics and classification of.example: Figure 1.14 shows a spider, a housefly, a centipede and a crab. (a) Name the major group these animals all belong to. (b) State one feature that all of them share. Answer: (a) Arthropods. (b) Any one of: jointed legs, exoskeleton, segmented body.

1|Cells.teaches: Cell structures and functions in animal, plant and bacterial cells: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane, cell wall, chloroplasts, vacuole, plasmid, circular DNA. Specialised cells (root hair, palisade, red blood cell, neurone, sperm, egg, ciliated cell) with structure linked to function. Magnification = image size ÷ actual size, unit conversions (mm, µm), and scale drawings.
1|Cells.notYet: Do not ask about ribosome function, mitochondrial respiration details, ATP, the endomembrane system (Golgi, rough ER), the electron microscope's ultrastructure, prokaryote/eukaryote classification, cell cycle or mitosis, stem cells, resolution calculations, or A Level cell biology. Also avoid osmosis calculations and the details of bacterial reproduction.
1|Cells.example: A palisade cell in a photograph is 60 mm long. Its actual length is 0.12 mm. (a) Calculate the magnification. (b) Give one feature that palisade cells have that a bacterial cell does not, and state its function. Answer: (a) 60 ÷ 0.12 = ×500. (b) Chloroplasts (or a nucleus, or a large vacuole): chloroplasts contain chlorophyll to absorb light for photosynthesis.

1|Biological molecules.teaches: Carbohydrates, fats and proteins as made of C, H, O (protein also N). Starch, glycogen and cellulose are polymers of glucose. Fats are made of fatty acids and glycerol. Proteins are chains of amino acids. Food tests: iodine (starch), Benedict's (reducing sugars), biuret (protein), ethanol emulsion (fat). DNA: double helix, two strands, bases A–T and C–G pairing, a sequence of bases.
1|Biological molecules.notYet: Not yet taught (A Level content): glycosidic or peptide bond formation, condensation and hydrolysis mechanisms, alpha and beta glucose, amylose and amylopectin, saturated vs unsaturated chemistry, primary to quaternary protein structure, nucleotide structure (deoxyribose, phosphate), hydrogen bond detail, DNA replication, transcription, translation, ATP, ribosomes. Also avoid non-reducing sugar tests (sucrose) unless the syllabus extension applies.
1|Biological molecules.example: A student adds Benedict's solution to a food sample and heats it in a water bath. The solution turns from blue to brick-red. (a) Name the type of nutrient present. (b) Name the chemical test used to show that a different sample contains protein, and give the positive colour. Answer: (a) a reducing sugar (e.g. glucose); (b) biuret test, the solution turns from blue to purple (violet).

1|Plant nutrition.teaches: Photosynthesis as carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, using light energy absorbed by chlorophyll in chloroplasts. Word and balanced symbol equations. Starch test with iodine, destarching, and variegated or covered leaves. Leaf structure: cuticle, epidermis, palisade, spongy mesophyll, stomata, guard cells, xylem, phloem. Limiting factors (light, CO2, temperature) with graphs. Uses of glucose.
1|Plant nutrition.notYet: Light-dependent and light-independent stages, photolysis, NADP, ATP, RuBP, Calvin cycle, rubisco, C3/C4 plants, chloroplast grana/stroma detail, absorption spectra, compensation point calculations, water potential in guard cell mechanism, mineral ion deficiency details (covered separately).
1|Plant nutrition.example: A destarched geranium leaf has part of it covered with black paper. The plant is left in sunlight for 24 hours. The leaf is then tested for starch with iodine solution. (a) What colour shows starch is present? (b) Predict the result for the covered part and the uncovered part. (c) Explain these results. Answer: (a) blue-black. (b) Covered part stays orange-brown/yellow-brown (no starch); uncovered part turns blue-black (starch present). (c) Covered part got no light, so no photosynthesis and no glucose to store as starch; light is needed for photosynthesis.

1|Movement into and out of cells.topic: Movement into and out of cells
1|Movement into and out of cells.teaches: Diffusion: net movement of particles down a concentration gradient, from random motion, with no energy needed. Factors: gradient, temperature, surface area, distance. Osmosis: net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane, from high to low water potential. Effects on plant tissue (turgid, plasmolysed, flaccid) and animal cells. Active transport: movement against a gradient using energy from respiration, with carrier proteins. Examples: gas exchange, root hair uptake. Core practicals: potato cylinders, mass and length changes, percentage change.
1|Movement into and out of cells.notYet: Not taught: water potential calculations in kPa, Ψs/Ψp, or the Fick's law equation. Also not taught: the molecular detail of ATP hydrolysis, carrier protein conformational change, co-transport, endocytosis, facilitated diffusion by channel proteins, the Nernst equation, or the surface area to volume ratio of cell models beyond simple cubes. Use 'water potential' only qualitatively.
1|Movement into and out of cells.example: Potato cylinders of equal mass were placed in sucrose solutions. In 0.8 mol/dm³ sucrose the cylinder lost mass; in distilled water it gained mass. (a) Explain, using the term osmosis, why the cylinder in distilled water gained mass. (b) Suggest why the cylinder in 0.8 mol/dm³ sucrose became soft and flaccid. Answer: (a) Water moved into the potato cells by osmosis, from a high water potential (dilute solution) to a lower water potential (cell cytoplasm), through the partially permeable cell membrane, so mass increased. (b) The sucrose solution had a lower water potential than the cells, so water left the cells by osmosis. The cells lost water, and the vacuole and cytoplasm shrank. The cells lost turgor, so they became flaccid.

1|Human nutrition.teaches: Balanced diet: carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins (C, D), minerals (calcium, iron), fibre, water; their sources and functions; deficiency diseases (scurvy, rickets, anaemia, kwashiorkor). Alimentary canal parts and functions; ingestion, digestion, absorption, assimilation, egestion; teeth structure, types, decay; mechanical and chemical digestion; amylase, protease, lipase, bile; villi; food tests.
1|Human nutrition.notYet: Not required at IGCSE Core: enzyme kinetics or Michaelis-Menten, active-transport carrier details, hormones such as secretin and CCK, micelle formation, lacteal chemistry, ATP, ribosome and protein synthesis, liver deamination and urea (later chapter), glycogen regulation by insulin, and the detailed structure of amino acids.
1|Human nutrition.example: Name the part of the digestive system where most absorption of digested food takes place, and state two features of its structure that make it efficient at absorption. Answer: The small intestine (ileum). Features: very long; lining folded into villi giving a large surface area; villi have thin walls (one cell thick) giving a short diffusion distance; rich blood supply (capillaries) to carry absorbed food away, maintaining the concentration gradient. (Any two.)

1|Transport in plants.teaches: Xylem (dead, hollow, lignified vessels carrying water and mineral ions up) and phloem (living sieve tubes carrying sucrose and amino acids). Their positions in roots, stems and leaves. Root hairs and water uptake by osmosis. Transpiration, the transpiration stream, and the effects of light, temperature, humidity and wind. Wilting. Translocation from sources to sinks. Potometer and stain experiments.
1|Transport in plants.notYet: Cohesion-tension theory, water potential in kPa, apoplast/symplast pathways, Casparian strip, companion-cell mechanisms, mass flow with proton pumps or ATP, active loading, Münch hypothesis, stomatal guard-cell ion mechanisms, abscisic acid, xerophyte adaptations in detail, calculating water potential.
1|Transport in plants.example: A leafy shoot is placed in a potometer and the bubble moves 24 mm in 6 minutes in still air. Fan wind is then added and the bubble moves faster. (a) State what the potometer measures. (b) Explain why the bubble moves faster in wind. Answer: (a) the rate of water uptake by the shoot, which approximates the rate of transpiration. (b) Wind blows away water vapour from around the leaf, so the water vapour concentration gradient between the air spaces inside the leaf and the outside air is steeper. Diffusion of water vapour out through the stomata is faster, so more water evaporates from the mesophyll cells and more water is pulled up the xylem.

1|Enzymes.teaches: Enzymes are biological catalysts, which are proteins that speed up reactions and are not used up. Learners know the terms substrate, product and active site, and the lock-and-key model. They know specificity. Temperature and pH affect rate: there is an optimum, and denaturation happens at high temperature or extreme pH. They interpret graphs, and plan investigations with amylase, catalase and protease.
1|Enzymes.notYet: Not required: Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Km or Vmax, competitive and non-competitive inhibition, induced-fit detail, allosteric sites, activation energy calculations, coenzymes and cofactors, tertiary structure bonding (hydrogen or disulfide bonds), ATP, ribosomes, and enzyme immobilisation. Avoid quantitative Q10 calculations.
1|Enzymes.example: A student mixed amylase with starch solution at different temperatures and timed how long it took for the starch to disappear. The time was shortest at 40 °C, and at 80 °C the starch was not broken down at all. (a) Explain why no starch was broken down at 80 °C. (b) Name the substance the iodine test shows is still present. Answer: (a) The enzyme was denatured by the high temperature. Its active site changed shape, so the starch (substrate) no longer fitted and could not bind. (b) Starch, which turns blue-black with iodine solution.

1|Transport in animals.teaches: Single vs double circulation; heart structure (atria, ventricles, valves, septum, coronary arteries); the pulmonary and aortic vessels, vena cava, renal and hepatic vessels; arteries, veins and capillaries (structure and function); blood components (plasma, red cells, white cells, platelets); heart rate, exercise, coronary heart disease; reading ECG and ventricular volume graphs.
1|Transport in animals.notYet: A Level content: cardiac cycle pressure changes in detail, myogenic control and Purkinje fibres, oxygen dissociation curves and haemoglobin affinity, Bohr effect, tissue fluid formation by hydrostatic and oncotic pressure, clotting cascade (thrombin, fibrinogen), lymphatic detail, ATP and cell respiration biochemistry.
1|Transport in animals.example: The diagram shows a section through the heart. (a) Name the chamber that pumps blood to the lungs. (b) Explain why the wall of the left ventricle is thicker than the wall of the right ventricle. Answer: (a) right ventricle. (b) The left ventricle pumps blood around the whole body, so it needs to generate higher pressure. Its thicker muscle wall contracts with more force. The right ventricle only pumps blood to the nearby lungs, which needs lower pressure.

1|Diseases and immunity.teaches: Pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists) cause transmissible disease. Spread by direct contact, body fluids, cuts and bites, contaminated food and water, droplets and vectors (e.g. malaria, cholera, HIV). Control by hygiene, sanitation and vector control. Defences: skin, mucus, stomach acid, phagocytes, lymphocytes making antibodies, memory cells, vaccination, active/passive immunity. Reading graphs on disease trends.
1|Diseases and immunity.notYet: A Level detail: MHC and antigen-presenting cells, T-helper/cytotoxic/B-cell clonal selection, plasma cells, cytokines, primary/secondary response mechanics, complement, monoclonal antibodies, ELISA, herd immunity calculations, R0, antibiotic resistance genetics, viral replication steps (reverse transcriptase).
1|Diseases and immunity.example: Question: Measles is caused by a virus, and a vaccine was introduced in 1963. (a) Explain how vaccination protects a person from measles. (b) Suggest why antibiotics would not be used to treat measles. Answer: (a) The vaccine contains a weakened/dead form of the pathogen or its antigens; this stimulates lymphocytes to make specific antibodies and memory cells; if the real virus infects later, antibodies are made quickly, so the person does not become ill. (b) Antibiotics kill bacteria but do not affect viruses.

1|Respiration and gas exchange.teaches: Aerobic respiration (glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water, energy released for muscle contraction, heat, growth, active transport); anaerobic respiration (lactic acid in muscles, ethanol and CO2 in yeast); oxygen debt; human gas exchange: airway structures, alveoli adaptations, ventilation, intercostal muscles and diaphragm, limewater and hydrogencarbonate indicator tests; reading breathing-rate graphs.
1|Respiration and gas exchange.notYet: Do not ask about ATP structure, NAD, glycolysis, Krebs cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, or mitochondrial membranes. Avoid Fick's law, partial pressures, oxygen dissociation curves, haemoglobin affinity, the Bohr effect, lactate conversion pathways, respiratory quotient calculations, or spirometer maths.
1|Respiration and gas exchange.example: A learner's breathing rate was 16 breaths per minute at rest and rose to 40 during hard exercise. (a) Give the increase in breathing rate. (b) Explain why muscles need more oxygen during exercise. Answer: (a) 24 breaths per minute (40 − 16). (b) Muscles respire faster to release more energy for contraction; aerobic respiration uses oxygen to break down glucose, so more oxygen is needed.

10|Unit 2: Equations, factors and formul.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 2: Equations, factors and formul.teaches: Solving linear equations (unknown on both sides, brackets, fractions), forming equations from rectangle/perimeter contexts, simple fractional and x² = k equations. Factorising by common factor, grouping, difference of two squares, and quadratic trinomials (Extended). Changing the subject of a formula, including powers, roots, and the subject appearing twice (Extended).
10|Unit 2: Equations, factors and formul.notYet: Quadratic formula, completing the square, simultaneous equations, algebraic fractions with quadratic denominators, functions and inverse notation f⁻¹(x), logarithms, differentiation, proof by induction, surds rationalisation, and A Level methods such as the factor theorem or partial fractions. Avoid circle theorems and trigonometry-based formulae.
10|Unit 2: Equations, factors and formul.example:
Make r the subject of the formula A = πr² + 4, where r > 0.

Answer: A − 4 = πr², so r² = (A − 4)/π, so r = √((A − 4)/π).

10|Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and st.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and st.topic: Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and standard form
10|Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and st.teaches: Equivalent fractions, simplifying, ordering fractions, and converting between fractions, decimals and percentages (including recurring decimals). Adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing fractions and mixed numbers, with BIDMAS. Percentage of an amount, increase/decrease, reverse percentages, simple and compound interest, percentage change and profit/loss. Standard form a×10^n (1≤a<10) with positive and negative n, and calculations in it.
10|Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and st.notYet: Not yet taught: surds and rationalising, fractional or negative indices (Unit 9 onwards), exponential growth and decay equations, logarithms, algebraic fractions, converting recurring decimals to fractions by algebra (Extended only), upper and lower bounds, percentage problems with compound-interest formula rearrangement for n, and sequences or limits.
10|Unit 2: Fractions, percentages and st.example:
A phone costs $240. In a sale its price is reduced by 15%. (a) Find the sale price. (b) Write the original price, $240 000 000 in cents... Simplified: Write 0.00036 in standard form.

Better single question: A laptop's price is reduced by 15% to $510. Find the original price.
Answer: 510 is 85% of the original. Original = 510 ÷ 0.85 = $600.

10|Unit 1: Collecting, organising and di.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 1: Collecting, organising and di.topic: Unit 1: Collecting, organising and displaying data
10|Unit 1: Collecting, organising and di.teaches: Types of data: categorical, numerical, discrete, continuous. Collecting data with tally tables and frequency tables, two-way tables, and grouped data with class intervals. Primary and secondary data and simple questionnaires. Drawing and reading pictograms, bar charts, pie charts (angles from frequencies), line graphs and simple temperature graphs. Comparing charts and spotting misleading graphs (truncated axes, uneven scales).
10|Unit 1: Collecting, organising and di.notYet: Not yet taught in this chapter: histograms with unequal class widths and frequency density, cumulative frequency, box plots, mean/median/mode from tables, scatter diagrams and correlation, sampling methods, standard deviation, stratified samples. Avoid probability, and avoid statistical tests or A Level ideas.
10|Unit 1: Collecting, organising and di.example: A class of 30 students recorded their favourite sport: football 12, tennis 6, swimming 9, other 3. (a) Draw up a frequency table from the tally. (b) Calculate the angle for football in a pie chart. (c) State whether 'favourite sport' is categorical or numerical data. Answer: (b) 12/30 × 360 = 144°. (c) Categorical (the pie chart angles sum to 360°: 144°, 72°, 108°, 36°).

10|Unit 1: Review of number concepts.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 1: Review of number concepts.teaches: Types of numbers (natural, integer, prime, square, cube, rational, irrational, reciprocal). Multiples, factors, HCF, LCM, prime factor decomposition. Directed number arithmetic. Powers, roots, index laws with integer indices (Extended: zero, negative, fractional). Order of operations (BODMAS), calculator use. Rounding to decimal places and significant figures, estimating by rounding to 1 s.f.
10|Unit 1: Review of number concepts.notYet: Standard form calculations, surds, simplifying algebraic indices or solving exponential equations, upper and lower bounds, percentage error, recurring decimal to fraction proofs, logarithms, sequences, compound interest, and A Level ideas (rationalising, proof by contradiction, modulus, complex numbers).
10|Unit 1: Review of number concepts.example: Write 180 as a product of its prime factors, giving your answer in index form. Then find the highest common factor of 180 and 84. Answer: 180 = 2² × 3² × 5. 84 = 2² × 3 × 7. HCF = 2² × 3 = 12.

10|Unit 1: Making sense of algebra.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 1: Making sense of algebra.teaches: Writing expressions with letters for unknowns (e.g. perimeters with x). Substituting numbers, including negatives, into expressions and formulae. Simplifying by collecting like terms. Expanding single brackets and factorising simply. Index laws for positive integer powers: multiplying, dividing, power of a power. Spotting common errors such as 3a + 2b = 5ab.
10|Unit 1: Making sense of algebra.notYet: Not yet: expanding double brackets (x+3)(x+2), quadratic factorising, algebraic fractions, changing the subject, solving equations or inequalities, simultaneous equations, fractional or negative indices, surds, functions, differentiation, sequences' nth term, and proofs. Avoid area formulae with x unless stated.
10|Unit 1: Making sense of algebra.example:
Question: (a) Write an expression for the perimeter of a rectangle with length (2x + 3) cm and width x cm. Give your answer in its simplest form. (b) Work out the perimeter when x = 4 cm. (c) Expand and simplify 3(x + 2) + 2(x − 1).

Answer: (a) 2(2x + 3) + 2x = 4x + 6 + 2x = 6x + 6 cm. (b) 6(4) + 6 = 30 cm. (c) 3x + 6 + 2x − 2 = 5x + 4.

10|Unit 1: Lines, angles and shapes.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 1: Lines, angles and shapes.teaches: Types of lines (parallel, perpendicular) and angles (acute, right, obtuse, reflex); measuring and drawing with a protractor; angles on a line, at a point, vertically opposite, and in parallel lines (corresponding, alternate, co-interior). Angle sums of triangles and quadrilaterals; polygon angle sums and regular polygons; circle parts and tangent/chord facts; ruler-and-compass constructions.
10|Unit 1: Lines, angles and shapes.notYet: No circle theorems (angle at centre, angles in the same segment, cyclic quadrilaterals, alternate segment). No trigonometry, Pythagoras, congruence or similarity proofs, coordinate geometry, vectors, transformations, or area/arc/sector formulae. No radians. No formal proof wording beyond simple reasons.
10|Unit 1: Lines, angles and shapes.example: ABC is a triangle with angle A = 52° and angle B = 67°. (a) Work out angle C, giving a reason. (b) What type of triangle is it if angle C is the largest angle? Answer: (a) C = 180 − 52 − 67 = 61° (angles in a triangle add up to 180°). (b) Largest angle is 67° (B), so all angles are acute and the triangle is acute-angled (scalene since all angles differ).

10|Unit 2: Perimeter, area and volume.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 2: Perimeter, area and volume.teaches: Perimeter and area of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, trapezia, compound shapes. Circle circumference and area (πd, 2πr, πr²), arc length, sector area. Names of solids (prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone, sphere), nets, faces/edges/vertices. Surface area and volume of prisms, cylinders, pyramids, cones, spheres. Unit conversions (cm², m³), answers to 3 significant figures.
10|Unit 2: Perimeter, area and volume.notYet: No calculus or optimisation, no radians, no similar-shape area/volume ratios (a later unit), no trigonometry in finding heights (Unit on Pythagoras and trigonometry comes later), no frustum problems, no circle theorems (chord and tangent proofs), no surds or exact π algebra beyond leaving answers in terms of π.
10|Unit 2: Perimeter, area and volume.example:
A cylinder has radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Calculate its total surface area. Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
Answer: Total surface area = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2π(25) + 2π(5)(12) = 50π + 120π = 170π = 534 cm² (3 s.f.).

10|Unit 2: Introduction to probability.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 2: Introduction to probability.teaches: Probability as a number from 0 to 1, written as a fraction, decimal or percentage. P(event) = favourable ÷ total for equally likely outcomes. P(not A) = 1 − P(A). Experimental probability and relative frequency, and expected frequency. Sample space diagrams: lists and 2D grids, e.g. two dice or spinners. Independent events: P(A and B) = P(A)×P(B). Mutually exclusive events: P(A or B) = P(A)+P(B).
10|Unit 2: Introduction to probability.notYet: Tree diagrams, conditional probability without replacement, Venn diagram probability with set notation (P(A∩B), P(A|B)), the general addition rule P(A∪B), dependent events, probability distributions, expectation formulae, permutations and combinations, binomial ideas, or any calculus-based or A Level content.
10|Unit 2: Introduction to probability.example:
A fair spinner has eight equal sectors numbered 1 to 8. It is spun once. (a) Find the probability of getting a number greater than 6. (b) The spinner is spun twice. Find the probability that both spins give a 3. (c) The spinner is spun 200 times. How many times would you expect an even number?

Answer: (a) Numbers 7 and 8 give 2/8 = 1/4. (b) 1/8 × 1/8 = 1/64. (c) P(even) = 4/8 = 1/2, so expected frequency = 1/2 × 200 = 100.

10|Unit 4: Further solving of equations.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 4: Further solving of equations.topic: Unit 4: Further solving of equations and inequalities
10|Unit 4: Further solving of equations.teaches: Solving simultaneous linear equations by elimination, substitution and graphs; solving linear inequalities and showing them on number lines; shading regions for inequalities such as y ≥ 0, x + y < 4 and listing integer points; completing the square; the quadratic formula; factorising ax² + bx + c; simplifying algebraic fractions and solving equations with them.
10|Unit 4: Further solving of equations.notYet: No linear programming with an objective function or optimising. No quadratic inequalities, no discriminant for number of roots, no complex numbers. No simultaneous equations with three unknowns or with a quadratic (linear-quadratic pairs). No partial fractions, no calculus, no polynomial division or factor theorem, no matrices.
10|Unit 4: Further solving of equations.example: Solve 2x² + 5x − 3 = 0 by factorising. Answer: (2x − 1)(x + 3) = 0, so x = 1/2 or x = −3.

10|Unit 3: Straight lines and quadratic.book: Cambridge IGCSE 3rd (Third Edition) Edition Mathematics 0580 Core and Extended
10|Unit 3: Straight lines and quadratic.topic: Unit 3: Straight lines and quadratic equations
10|Unit 3: Straight lines and quadratic.teaches: Interpreting and sketching real-life graphs. Straight lines: gradient as rise over run (including negative), y-intercept, y = mx + c, equations from graphs or two points, parallel lines, midpoint and length of a segment, plotting lines. Quadratics: expanding brackets, factorising (including x² + bx + c and ax² + bx + c), solving by factorising, difference of two squares, and the quadratic formula in Extended.
