No half/full adders, flip-flops, latches, multiplexers or transistor-level design. No gate delays. No NAND-only or NOR-only equivalents. No more than three inputs. No hardware or A Level circuit design.
200|Chapter 10: The role of logic gates.example: A safety alarm X sounds when the machine is on (A = 1) AND the guard is open (B = 1), OR when the temperature is too high (C = 1). (a) Write a logic expression for X. (b) Give X when A = 1, B = 0, C = 0. Answer: (a) X = (A AND B) OR C. (b) A AND B = 0, C = 0, so X = 0.

200|Chapter 8: Programming concepts.book: Cambridge IGCSE™ and O Level Computer Science Coursebook (Cambridge International IGCSE)
200|Chapter 8: Programming concepts.teaches: Variables, constants and the basic data types (integer, real, char, string, Boolean). Input and output, arithmetic operators (+ - * / ^, DIV, MOD), sequence, selection (IF, CASE), iteration (FOR, WHILE, REPEAT-UNTIL), totalling, counting, string handling (LENGTH, SUBSTRING, UPPER, LOWER), nested statements, procedures and functions, library routines (ROUND, RANDOM), maintainable code (comments, meaningful names), 1D and 2D arrays, and reading and writing text files. Cambridge pseudocode is used.
200|Chapter 8: Programming concepts.notYet: Object-oriented programming (classes, inheritance), recursion, records, linked lists, stacks and queues, and Big-O complexity. Also not taught: sorting and searching algorithm code beyond basics, exception handling, database/SQL code, floating-point binary representation, and language-specific syntax such as Python-only features. Do not ask for 3D arrays or file formats like CSV/JSON parsing.
200|Chapter 8: Programming concepts.example:
A program totals marks. Complete the pseudocode so it inputs 5 marks and outputs the total.

Total ← 0
FOR Count ← 1 TO 5
   INPUT Mark
   Total ← ______
NEXT Count
OUTPUT Total

Answer: Total + Mark (the running total is updated by adding each mark in turn; Total must be set to 0 before the loop).

205|Chapter 1: Hardware and software\b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 1: Hardware and software\b.teaches: Hardware (internal: CPU, motherboard, RAM, ROM, graphics/sound cards, internal storage; external: monitor, keyboard, mouse, printers, scanners, speakers, external storage) versus software (system and application). Input/output/storage devices. Operating systems and user interfaces (GUI, CLI). Desktop, laptop, tablet, smartphone. Emerging tech: AI, VR, AR, 3D printing, wearables.
205|Chapter 1: Hardware and software\b.notYet: No fetch-decode-execute cycle, registers, buses, cache, clock speed calculations, or CPU architecture (A Level). No binary/hexadecimal, logic gates, assembly language, compilers vs interpreters, virtual memory, paging, TCP/IP, or machine learning algorithms. No programming.
205|Chapter 1: Hardware and software\b.example:
Question: Give two differences between RAM and ROM.
Answer: RAM is temporary (volatile), so its contents are lost when power is off, and it can be read and written. ROM is permanent (non-volatile), is usually read-only, and holds start-up instructions such as the BIOS/bootstrap.

200|Chapter 9: Database structure.book: Cambridge IGCSE™ and O Level Computer Science Coursebook (Cambridge International IGCSE)
200|Chapter 9: Database structure.teaches: Single-table databases: table, record, field, primary key. Choosing data types (text/alphanumeric, character, Boolean, integer, real, date/time). Reading and completing SQL: SELECT, FROM, WHERE (=, <>, <, >, <=, >=, AND, OR, LIKE with %), ORDER BY (ASC/DESC), SUM, COUNT. Writing queries or predicting the output of a given table.
200|Chapter 9: Database structure.notYet: Multiple tables, JOIN, foreign keys, normalisation, relational design, entity-relationship diagrams. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, CREATE TABLE, GROUP BY, HAVING, subqueries, AVG/MAX/MIN, aliases, SQL injection, DBMS internals, data validation theory beyond field types, A Level database ideas.
200|Chapter 9: Database structure.example:
A table STUDENTS has fields StudentID, Name, Age, Class, Score.

StudentID | Name | Age | Class | Score
1 | Amir | 15 | 10A | 72
2 | Bella | 14 | 10B | 85
3 | Chen | 15 | 10A | 90
4 | Dina | 16 | 10B | 64

(a) Write an SQL query to show the Name and Score of all students in class 10A, with the highest score first.
(b) State the output of: SELECT SUM(Score) FROM STUDENTS WHERE Age = 15;

Answer:
(a) SELECT Name, Score FROM STUDENTS WHERE Class = '10A' ORDER BY Score DESC;
(b) 162 (72 + 90).

200|Chapter 11: Programming scenario.book: Cambridge IGCSE™ and O Level Computer Science Coursebook (Cambridge International IGCSE)
200|Chapter 11: Programming scenario.teaches: Working through a programming scenario (a computer-science problem solved as a program). Identify inputs, processes and outputs. Plan with a structure diagram or flowchart and write pseudocode. Code in Python, VB or Java using variables, selection, iteration, arrays, validation, totals and averages. Test with normal, extreme and erroneous data and a trace table. Method 1: analyse the problem on paper. Method 2: practise by coding and running.
200|Chapter 11: Programming scenario.notYet: A Level content: recursion, object-oriented classes and inheritance, stacks and queues, linked lists, Big-O complexity, sorting algorithm code (e.g. quicksort), formal SQL joins, exception-handling syntax, and advanced library or framework use. Also avoid language-specific tricks outside the chosen language and questions on hardware or networking.
200|Chapter 11: Programming scenario.example: A program asks the user to enter 5 test marks (each must be 0 to 100) and outputs the average. (a) State one input and one output. (b) Give one example of extreme test data for the validation. Answer: (a) Input: a test mark, e.g. 72; output: the average mark. (b) Extreme data: 0 or 100 (the boundary values that are still accepted).

205|Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnet.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnet.topic: Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnetic storage devices
205|Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnet.teaches: Backing storage versus internal memory. Magnetic media: fixed hard disk drives, portable hard drives, magnetic tape and tape drives. Optical media: CD, DVD, Blu-ray, with -ROM, -R and -RW. Solid-state: SSDs, memory sticks/flash drives, memory cards. Uses, advantages and disadvantages: capacity, speed, portability, durability, cost. Units: KB, MB, GB, TB. Future trends such as cloud storage.
205|Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnet.notYet: Binary or hex conversion of storage sizes, file-size calculations, and RAID. Also not taught: the physics of flash memory (NAND/NOR gates, floating gates), the maths of disk sectors/tracks and seek time, virtual memory, cache levels, and A Level topics such as file organisation, SSD wear-levelling or data compression algorithms.
205|Chapter 3: Magnetic media and magnet.example: Give two reasons why a magnetic tape is used to back up a company's large database overnight, rather than a memory stick. Answer: any two of: tape has a very large capacity; it is cheap per GB; it is reliable and durable for long-term storage; backups are written in sequential order, so slow access time does not matter. (2 marks)

205|Chapter 2: Input devices and their u.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 2: Input devices and their u.topic: Chapter 2: Input devices and their uses
205|Chapter 2: Input devices and their u.teaches: Input devices and their uses: keyboards, numeric keypads, mouse, touchpad, trackerball, joystick, graphics tablet, scanners, digital cameras, microphones, webcams, sensors. DDE devices: MICR, OCR, OMR, barcode readers, magnetic stripe, chip and PIN, RFID, card readers. Output devices: monitors (CRT/TFT/LCD), projectors, printers (inkjet, laser, dot matrix), speakers, plotters, 3D printers, actuators. Advantages, disadvantages, and suitable uses.
205|Chapter 2: Input devices and their u.notYet: Not taught: binary or ASCII encoding of input, ADC/DAC circuits, device drivers or buffers, resolution calculations, laser printer drum mechanics, capacitive vs resistive touchscreen physics, RFID frequency, QR code error correction, and A Level processor or memory ideas. Also excluded: file size formulae.
205|Chapter 2: Input devices and their u.example:
A supermarket checkout uses a barcode reader. State TWO advantages of using barcode readers instead of typing product codes on a keyboard.

Answer (any two): faster entry of data; fewer errors or typing mistakes; stock levels can be updated automatically; itemised receipts can be produced; prices can be looked up quickly and accurately. (2 marks)

205|Chapter 4: Networks \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 4: Networks \b.teaches: Network types and devices: LAN, WLAN, WAN; routers, switches, hubs, bridges, NIC, modems, proxy servers. Wi-Fi vs Bluetooth, and wired vs wireless. Internet, intranet and extranet. Common network issues: security (passwords, firewalls, encryption, authentication) and the pros and cons of networking. Also covers the use of email, fax, video/web conferencing, and VoIP, and the roles of the client and the server.
205|Chapter 4: Networks \b.notYet: Avoid OSI/TCP-IP layers, subnet masks, IPv4 and IPv6 address calculations, packet switching and routing algorithms, protocols such as HTTP, FTP and DNS in detail, symmetric and asymmetric encryption keys, network topologies (bus, star, mesh) as detailed A Level content, and binary or hex conversions. Also avoid handling bandwidth calculations.
205|Chapter 4: Networks \b.example:
Question: State two advantages of using a wired network instead of a wireless (Wi-Fi) network in an office. [2]
Answer: Any two of: wired connections are generally faster and more stable; they are less prone to interference; they are more secure because someone cannot easily connect from outside the building; the signal does not weaken with distance or walls.

205|Chapter 5: Microprocessor-controlled.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 5: Microprocessor-controlled.teaches: Everyday microprocessor-controlled devices: household items (washing machine, microwave, oven, security system, central heating, cooker) and their advantages and disadvantages for people (saves time, energy, labour; less active lifestyle; dependency; loss of skills). Health problems from prolonged ICT use: RSI, back and neck problems, eye strain, headaches. Causes, prevention (ergonomics, breaks, posture, screen filters, wrist rests, adjustable chairs). Safety: electrocution, trip hazards, fire.
205|Chapter 5: Microprocessor-controlled.notYet: No CPU internals (fetch-decode-execute, registers, buses, clock speed). No sensor ADC/DAC circuits, control algorithms or programming of feedback loops. No assembly code, embedded system design, medical diagnoses, or legal detail such as the Health and Safety at Work Act. Nothing from A Level.
205|Chapter 5: Microprocessor-controlled.example:
Question: Give two health problems that could be caused by using a computer for long periods, and for each give one way to reduce the risk. [4 marks]
Answer: Any two pairs, e.g. Repetitive strain injury (RSI) in wrists and fingers: use a wrist rest, take regular breaks, or use an ergonomic keyboard. Eye strain/headaches: use an anti-glare screen filter, take regular breaks to look away, or adjust screen brightness. Back and neck problems: use an adjustable chair with back support, or set the screen at eye level.

205|Chapter 6: Communication \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 6: Communication \b.teaches: Chapter 6 covers ICT applications: communication (email, video/web conferencing, fax, VoIP), modelling and spreadsheet simulations, computer-controlled systems (sensors, ADC, actuators, microprocessor, feedback), school management, booking, banking (ATM, chip and PIN, EFT, clearing), medical systems, expert systems (knowledge base, rule base, inference engine), retail (POS, EFTPOS, barcodes), recognition systems (OCR, OMR, RFID, MICR), GPS/GIS/satellite navigation. Learners give advantages, disadvantages and describe how systems work.
205|Chapter 6: Communication \b.notYet: Not expected: programming or pseudocode for control, PID or control-theory maths, Boolean logic gates, binary or ADC conversion calculations, network protocols and packet switching, encryption algorithms (RSA), machine-learning or neural-network detail, satellite orbit physics, database SQL, and A Level systems analysis methods.
205|Chapter 6: Communication \b.example: A supermarket uses a computer-controlled greenhouse. (a) Name one sensor it might use and one thing it measures. (b) Explain why an analogue-to-digital converter is needed. Answer: (a) Temperature sensor measures temperature (or a moisture or light sensor). (b) Sensors send analogue signals, but the computer or microprocessor can only process digital data, so the ADC converts the signal into digital form.

205|Chapter 7: Analysis \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 7: Analysis \b.teaches: The systems life cycle for IGCSE ICT: analysis (observation, interviews, questionnaires, examining documents; identifying problems, requirements, inputs, outputs, processes; user and system requirements), design (data capture forms, screen layouts, report layouts, validation rules, file structures), development and testing (normal, abnormal and extreme data; test plans), implementation (direct, parallel, pilot and phased changeover), documentation (technical and user), evaluation.
205|Chapter 7: Analysis \b.notYet: Not taught: programming code, pseudocode, flowchart or trace-table tasks, Big-O, SDLC models such as waterfall, agile or spiral, UML or data flow diagrams, normalisation, formal test types (alpha/beta, white/black box), project management tools such as Gantt charts, and A Level analysis methods.
205|Chapter 7: Analysis \b.example: A school wants to replace its paper-based library records with a computer system. Name two methods of researching the current system during analysis and give one advantage of one of them. Answer: Any two of observation, interviews, questionnaires, or examining documents. For example, observation gives first-hand, reliable information about how the system actually works. Alternatively, interviews allow detailed questions and follow-up, or questionnaires reach many people quickly and cheaply.

205|Chapter 10: Communication with other.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 10: Communication with other.topic: Chapter 10: Communication with other ICT users using email
205|Chapter 10: Communication with other.teaches: Email use: To, Cc, Bcc, subject, attachments, address book, forwarding, replying, signatures. Netiquette, email laws and spam, phishing, malware risks. Email vs fax or post. Internet use: search engines, keywords, URLs, browsers, evaluating reliability of websites, bias, advantages and disadvantages of the internet, safe use, copyright.
205|Chapter 10: Communication with other.notYet: Not taught: SMTP, POP3 or IMAP protocols, mail server routing, packet switching, DNS lookup, IP addressing, encryption algorithms (SSL/TLS handshakes), SQL or programming, GDPR clause detail, network topologies. Also no A Level ideas like Boolean search algorithms or web crawler design.
205|Chapter 10: Communication with other.example: Question: A school secretary sends the same email to 30 parents and does not want parents to see each other's email addresses. Which field should she put the addresses in: To, Cc or Bcc? Give one other reason for using Cc. Answer: Bcc (blind carbon copy), which hides recipients' addresses from one another. Cc is used to send a copy to someone who needs to know but is not the main recipient, and all recipients can see the address.

205|Chapter 9: Audience appreciation \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 9: Audience appreciation \b.teaches: Audience appreciation in ICT: identifying an audience and its needs. Learners judge whether content suits age group, prior knowledge and interests. They consider style, language level, font size, colour, layout, images and sound. They also cover content that is inappropriate and legal issues such as copyright, and they compare audiences such as children and business people.
205|Chapter 9: Audience appreciation \b.notYet: Not taught: A Level topics such as UX research methods, accessibility standards (WCAG), formal usability testing metrics, or market segmentation theory. Also not assessed here: programming, networks, databases, spreadsheet formulae, or detailed copyright law and legal case names. Avoid SEO and analytics too.
205|Chapter 9: Audience appreciation \b.example: A school is making a presentation to teach 7-year-old children about healthy eating. Give two features of the presentation that make it suitable for this audience. Answer: Any two, e.g. large, clear font; simple short words/sentences; bright colours and cartoon images; little text per slide; animation or sound; no complex technical terms.

205|Chapter 8: Physical security \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 8: Physical security \b.teaches: Physical security of computers and data: locks, biometric access, security guards, backups, fireproof storage, UPS. E-safety: protecting personal data online, safe use of email, social media, chat rooms, and the internet, strong passwords, and avoiding cyberbullying. Security of data: malware, viruses, hacking, phishing, pharming, spam, firewalls, antivirus, encryption, and SSL/https. Learners give simple practical advice and describe causes and effects.
205|Chapter 8: Physical security \b.notYet: Not required: how encryption algorithms work (symmetric/asymmetric keys, public/private key maths), digital certificates and the TLS handshake, hashing, network protocols, DDoS mechanics, penetration testing, legislation details (GDPR clauses), risk-assessment matrices, and A Level cryptography or cybersecurity theory.
205|Chapter 8: Physical security \b.example: Give two ways a school can protect the computers in its ICT room from being stolen or accessed by unauthorised people. Answer: Any two, e.g. lock the room door (with key, keypad or ID card); fit biometric entry such as a fingerprint reader; install CCTV or alarms; have a security guard; physically fix computers to desks with security cables. (1 mark each.)

205|Chapter 11: Manage files effectively.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 11: Manage files effectively.teaches: Good file management: sensible folder structures, meaningful file names, file extensions/formats (e.g. .docx, .csv, .txt, .jpg, .png, .gif, .mp3, .pdf), saving, opening, copying, moving, deleting, backups. File compression: lossless (zip, rar, PNG) and lossy (JPEG, MP3), reducing image size by cropping, resolution and colour depth, and why smaller files help storage and email transmission.
205|Chapter 11: Manage files effectively.notYet: Not required: Huffman or run-length encoding worked through, compression algorithms, calculating file sizes in bits or bytes by formula, binary or hexadecimal conversion, bit rate and sampling calculations, encryption, and the operating-system file-system internals (FAT, inodes). Keep to practical, descriptive answers.
205|Chapter 11: Manage files effectively.example: A student wants to email 20 photos saved as JPEG files. Name one method of reducing the total file size so they can send the photos as a single attachment, and state whether the method is lossless or lossy. Answer: Put all the files in one zipped (compressed) folder; zip is lossless, so no data is lost. (Also accept: reduce image resolution or crop the photos, which loses some data.)

205|Chapter 12: Software tools \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 12: Software tools \b.teaches: Chapter 12 (Software tools) covers editing images in graphics software: resizing, cropping, rotating, reflecting/flipping, adjusting brightness and contrast, changing colour, layers, and placing and aligning images in documents. Learners know the words bitmap, resolution, aspect ratio, file format (JPEG, PNG, GIF), and know how to save and export images. Skills are practical and application-based.
205|Chapter 12: Software tools \b.notYet: Do not ask about: how bitmaps are stored as binary or colour depth calculations, file size formulae, compression algorithms (lossy and lossless detail), vector mathematics, pixel-level coding, image-processing algorithms, or programming and A Level graphics concepts such as rasterisation. Avoid exam-style Paper 2 spreadsheet or database tasks, which belong to other chapters.
205|Chapter 12: Software tools \b.example: Question: A student inserts a photograph into a poster. It looks stretched and distorted. Name the setting the student should have kept turned on when resizing the image to prevent this. Answer: Lock aspect ratio (maintain proportions), so that width and height change by the same proportion.

205|Chapter 13: Create or edit a documen.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 13: Create or edit a documen.topic: Chapter 13: Create or edit a document
205|Chapter 13: Create or edit a documen.teaches: Creating and editing word-processed documents in IGCSE ICT: setting page size, orientation and margins; entering and editing text; styles, fonts and alignment; bullets and numbering; inserting and formatting tables (rows, columns, merging cells, borders, shading); headers and footers with automatic page numbers, date, time, filename; placing and aligning them; proofreading.
205|Chapter 13: Create or edit a documen.notYet: Not taught: mail merge or macros, programming or code, databases and SQL, HTML/CSS, spreadsheet formulas inside tables, document version control, accessibility standards, file compression formats, networks or security. Avoid A Level content and software-specific shortcuts or menu paths as the focus.
205|Chapter 13: Create or edit a documen.example: Question: A school secretary wants the school name and the page number to appear at the top and bottom of every page of a 10-page newsletter. State where she should place each item and why using automatic page numbering is better than typing the numbers. Answer: The school name goes in the header and the page number in the footer. Automatic numbering updates itself when pages are added or removed, so it stays correct and consistent on every page.

205|Chapter 14: Corporate house styles \.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 14: Corporate house styles \.teaches: A corporate house style is a consistent look for all of an organisation's documents: logo, colour scheme, fonts, font sizes, alignment, spacing, header/footer content. Learners create, modify and apply styles in word processors, presentations and websites. They use paragraph and character styles, templates, master slides, stylesheets, and check consistency. Benefits: recognition, professionalism, saved time.
205|Chapter 14: Corporate house styles \.notYet: Not taught: CSS syntax and selectors, HTML coding, programming, brand law and trademarks, marketing theory, UX/accessibility standards (WCAG), colour models (RGB/CMYK values), typography terms like kerning, and software-specific scripting or macros.
205|Chapter 14: Corporate house styles \.example:
A company wants all its reports to look the same. Give two items that could be part of its corporate house style, and explain one benefit of using a house style.

Answer: Any two of: logo, colour scheme, font type, font size, header/footer text, alignment. Benefit, e.g. customers instantly recognise the company's documents, or documents look professional and consistent, or time is saved because styles are already set.

205|Chapter 15: Software tools \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 15: Software tools \b.teaches: Chapter 15 (Software tools) covers proofing techniques for ICT work. Learners know the difference between verification (double entry, visual check/proofreading) and validation (range, type, length, presence, format and check digit checks). They also know spell checkers, grammar checkers and proofreading, and that a spell checker cannot catch real-word errors such as 'there' for 'their'. They can also describe the purpose of each check.
205|Chapter 15: Software tools \b.notYet: Not taught: parity checks, checksums, ARQ or error-correcting protocols, binary or hexadecimal, the algorithm for calculating check digits (modulus-11), writing validation code or pseudocode, trace tables, testing with test data (normal, abnormal, extreme), SQL, regular expressions, and A Level data integrity or database normalisation.
205|Chapter 15: Software tools \b.example:
A form asks for a student's age, which must be a whole number from 11 to18. Name the validation check that rejects an age of 25, and explain why validation cannot prove that an age of 15 is the correct age.

Answer: A range check. Validation only checks that the data is reasonable and allowed, not that it is correct. A student who is 14 could be entered as 15 and it would still be accepted. Verification, such as double entry or visual checking, is needed to confirm the data was entered as intended.

205|Chapter 16: Chart types \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 16: Chart types \b.teaches: Choosing a chart for the data: column/bar, line, pie, scatter graph. Creating a chart in spreadsheet software by selecting data ranges and categories. Labelling: chart title, axis titles, data labels, legend/key, category labels, axis scale (min, max, interval), colours, secondary axis, and fitting the chart to the page. Reading simple charts.
205|Chapter 16: Chart types \b.notYet: No statistics beyond reading charts: no correlation coefficients, regression equations, standard deviation, histograms with frequency density, or calculating pie angles by hand. No coding or database/SQL charts. No Excel formulae beyond the basics. No A Level data-visualisation theory or big data.
205|Chapter 16: Chart types \b.example: A teacher has a spreadsheet showing the number of students in each of five year groups. She wants to show each year group's share of the school total. (a) Name the most suitable chart type. (b) Give two labels that must be added so a reader can understand the chart. Answer: (a) Pie chart. (b) Any two of: chart title; legend/key (or category labels on the slices); data labels showing the values or percentages.

205|Chapter 18: Create a database struct.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 18: Create a database struct.teaches: Creating a database structure in database software (e.g. Access): fields, records, tables; choosing data types (text, alphanumeric, numeric, integer, decimal, date/time, Boolean/yes-no, currency); field lengths, primary key, validation rules; importing data; searching with criteria (AND, OR, NOT, <, >, =, wildcards), sorting, calculated fields, grouping, totals; building reports and labels with headings and formatting.
205|Chapter 18: Create a database struct.notYet: Not taught: SQL code (SELECT, JOIN), normalisation, entity-relationship diagrams, foreign keys and relational joins beyond simple use, DBMS theory, transactions, indexing, big-data ideas, and Computer Science database topics from A Level. Avoid algorithms, Boolean algebra and pseudocode.
205|Chapter 18: Create a database struct.example: A school database table has the fields StudentID, Name, DateOfBirth and Member (yes/no). (a) Which field is best as the primary key? (b) Give the best data type for DateOfBirth. (c) Write a search criterion to list students who are members and were born after 1 January 2010. Answer: (a) StudentID, as it is unique for each record. (b) Date/time. (c) Member = Yes AND DateOfBirth > 01/01/2010.

205|Chapter 17: Organise page layout \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 17: Organise page layout \b.teaches: Chapter 17 covers page layout and text formatting in word processing/DTP: setting margins, orientation (portrait/landscape), paper size, columns, headers and footers, page numbers, and page/section breaks. It also covers font type and size, bold/italic/underline, alignment, line spacing, bullets and numbering, tabs, indents and styles. Terms: serif/sans-serif, justified, widow/orphan.
205|Chapter 17: Organise page layout \b.notYet: Not taught: programming, algorithms, binary or hardware questions. Also not taught: mail merge, macros, master pages, advanced typography (kerning, leading in points), CSS/HTML styling, colour models (CMYK/RGB), DTP professional workflow, or software-specific menu paths beyond the book's general steps.
205|Chapter 17: Organise page layout \b.example: A teacher is producing a two-page newsletter. She wants the page number and the school name to appear at the bottom of every page without typing them each time. Which feature should she use? Answer: A footer (with an automatic page number field) placed in the footer area.

205|Chapter 19: Create a presentation \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 19: Create a presentation \b.teaches: Practical presentation software skills (e.g. PowerPoint): creating slides from a master slide with placeholders, consistent fonts, colours and footers; inserting text, images, charts, tables; bullet points; animations and transitions; editing and formatting; speaker notes; saving formats; printing handouts, slide shows. Words: slide, master slide, placeholder, transition, animation, handout, bullets, template.
205|Chapter 19: Create a presentation \b.notYet: Not taught: programming or scripting macros, embedded video codecs/compression maths, web-authoring or HTML, database or spreadsheet formulae, networking/cloud collaboration theory, A Level topics (UX design models, system life cycle analysis), and detailed audience-psychology or copyright law beyond basics.
205|Chapter 19: Create a presentation \b.example:
Question: A teacher wants the school logo and slide number to appear in the same position on every slide of a presentation. Describe how she can do this efficiently. [2 marks]
Answer: Edit the master slide (slide master) and place the logo and the slide number placeholder/footer there, so they automatically appear on all slides based on it, instead of adding them to each slide separately.

205|Chapter 20: Create a data model \b.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 20: Create a data model \b.teaches: Spreadsheet modelling: building a model with labelled cells, text/numbers/dates, formatting (currency, decimals, percentages), formulas with cell references (+ - * /), SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAX, COUNT, IF, ROUND, absolute vs relative references, VLOOKUP/HLOOKUP, named cells, replication. Sorting, filtering, searching, testing a model, what-if changing inputs. Presenting: charts (bar, line, pie) with titles, axis labels, legends; printing formulae view.
205|Chapter 20: Create a data model \b.notYet: Not taught: macros/VBA, pivot tables, INDEX-MATCH/XLOOKUP, nested IF beyond simple use, array formulae, statistical functions (standard deviation, regression), SQL or database normalisation, Python or pseudocode programming, Monte Carlo simulation, A Level modelling theory.
205|Chapter 20: Create a data model \b.example: A school shop's spreadsheet has prices in column B (B2:B10) and quantities sold in column C (C2:C10). (a) Write a formula for cell D2 to calculate the income from the first item, which can be replicated down column D. (b) Write a formula to find the total of all the incomes in D2:D10. Answer: (a) =B2*C2 (b) =SUM(D2:D10)

205|Chapter 21: Web development layers \.book: Cambridge IGCSE information and communication technology. (Graham Brown David Watson) (z-lib.org) (1)
205|Chapter 21: Web development layers \.teaches: Three web layers: content (HTML structure), presentation (CSS styles) and behaviour (scripts, e.g. JavaScript). Learners create a page in a web authoring tool or HTML editor. They use tags such as , , , <body>, <h1>, <p>, <img>, <a>, and tables. They attach a CSS stylesheet, name styles, and set fonts, colours and sizes. They test the page in a browser.
205|Chapter 21: Web development layers \.notYet: Not taught: JavaScript syntax or writing code, DOM, AJAX, PHP or SQL, server-side scripting, responsive design and media queries, CSS box model or flexbox, HTTP methods, frameworks, accessibility standards (WCAG), SEO, and version control.
205|Chapter 21: Web development layers \.example: Question: A web page uses HTML for the text and headings and a CSS stylesheet for the font colour and size. (a) State which web development layer HTML belongs to. (b) State one advantage of using a CSS stylesheet for all pages of a website. Answer: (a) Content (structure) layer. (b) One change to the stylesheet updates the style on every page, so the pages look consistent and it saves time.

209|Chapter 1: Kinematics – describing m.teaches: Distance, displacement, speed, velocity, acceleration as scalars/vectors. Calculate speed = distance/time, acceleration = change in velocity/time (SI units: m, s, m/s, m/s²). Plot and read distance–time and speed–time graphs: gradient gives speed or acceleration, area under speed–time graph gives distance. Free fall, g ≈ 10 m/s², and terminal velocity (qualitative). Use a stopwatch and ruler to measure time and distance.
209|Chapter 1: Kinematics – describing m.notYet: No calculus or differentiation. No equations of motion (v = u + at, s = ut + ½at²) unless marked Extended. No vector resolution or projectile motion with angles. No air-resistance equations, relativity, or instantaneous values from tangent calculations beyond simple graph tangents.
209|Chapter 1: Kinematics – describing m.example: A car travels at a steady 8 m/s for 5 s, then accelerates uniformly to 20 m/s over the next 4 s. (a) How far does it travel in the first 5 s? (b) Calculate its acceleration during the 4 s. Answer: (a) distance = 8 × 5 = 40 m. (b) a = (20 − 8) / 4 = 3 m/s².

209|Chapter 2: Newton’s laws of motion.teaches: Chapter 2 covers force as a push or pull, and balanced and unbalanced forces. It covers Newton's first law (inertia), F = ma with N, kg and m/s², and weight W = mg (g = 10 N/kg). It also covers mass versus weight, friction and drag, terminal velocity, and the link between resultant force and acceleration. Learners use resultant force along one line and read speed–time graphs. Newton's third law is introduced only as paired forces.
209|Chapter 2: Newton’s laws of motion.notYet: Momentum, impulse, F = Δp/Δt, conservation of momentum, and collisions. Also not yet taught: resolving forces into components, vectors at angles, friction coefficients, circular motion, calculus-based motion, relativity, and drag formulae. Avoid kinetic energy and work-done calculations. Avoid F = ma problems with inclined planes or pulleys.
209|Chapter 2: Newton’s laws of motion.example: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3000 N forwards. Air resistance and friction total 1200 N backwards. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Calculate the car's acceleration. Answer: (a) 3000 − 1200 = 1800 N forwards. (b) a = F/m = 1800 / 1200 = 1.5 m/s².

209|Chapter 3: Forces and their effects.teaches: Forces change shape, size, speed or direction. Force is a vector, measured in newtons (N) with a newton meter. Resultant of forces along a line; Newton's first law (balanced forces). F = ma, W = mg (g = 10 N/kg). Friction, drag, terminal velocity. Hooke's law, F = kx, limit of proportionality, extension. Force–extension graphs. Circular motion qualitatively.
209|Chapter 3: Forces and their effects.notYet: Momentum and impulse (Chapter 4 content). Moments and centre of mass (later chapter). Vector resolution into components, trigonometry, and F = mv²/r calculations. Newton's third law as a formal law and pressure are not tested here. Also avoid elastic potential energy ½kx², Young modulus, and stress and strain.
209|Chapter 3: Forces and their effects.example: A trolley of mass 4.0 kg is pulled by a horizontal force of 18 N. A friction force of 6.0 N opposes its motion. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Calculate the trolley's acceleration. Answer: (a) 18 − 6.0 = 12 N. (b) a = F/m = 12 / 4.0 = 3.0 m/s².

209|Chapter 5: Work, power and energy.teaches: Energy stores and transfers (kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic, thermal, nuclear); conservation of energy; work done = force × distance moved (W = Fd); KE = ½mv²; GPE = mgh with g = 10 N/kg; power = work/time or energy/time; efficiency; energy resources (fossil fuels, nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, solar, geothermal); units J, kJ, W, kW, MW.
209|Chapter 5: Work, power and energy.notYet: No work done at an angle (Fcosθ), no derivation of KE or GPE from equations of motion, no variable forces or area under force–distance graphs, no P = Fv, no power in electrical circuits (P = IV) unless covered later, no momentum, no gravitational potential in fields, no A Level energy ideas such as E=mc², no calculus.
209|Chapter 5: Work, power and energy.example: A crane lifts a 200 kg load through a height of 15 m in 30 s. Take g = 10 N/kg. (a) Calculate the gain in gravitational potential energy of the load. (b) Calculate the useful power output of the crane. Answer: (a) E = mgh = 200 × 10 × 15 = 30 000 J (30 kJ). (b) P = E/t = 30 000 / 30 = 1000 W (1 kW).

209|Chapter 6: Pressure.teaches: Pressure = force ÷ area (p = F/A) in N/m² or Pa, with N, m², cm². Why sharp or wide objects press differently. Liquid pressure p = ρgh, increasing with depth and density. Pressure acts equally in all directions in a liquid. Hydraulic systems multiply force, using the same pressure in the fluid. Gases: pressure and the particle model.
209|Chapter 6: Pressure.notYet: Not yet taught: Boyle's law calculations (pV = constant) beyond simple use, if not in the core; atmospheric pressure changing with altitude as a formula; Pascal's principle by name with derivations; manometer calculations with two liquids; Bernoulli, buoyancy and upthrust derivations; pressure from kinetic theory (A Level); the gas law pV = nRT; fluid dynamics.
209|Chapter 6: Pressure.example: A rectangular box weighing 600 N rests on the floor. The face touching the floor measures 0.50 m by 0.30 m. (a) Calculate the area in contact with the floor. (b) Calculate the pressure the box exerts on the floor. (c) The box is turned onto a smaller face of area 0.10 m². State what happens to the pressure. Answer: (a) 0.50 × 0.30 = 0.15 m². (b) p = F/A = 600 ÷ 0.15 = 4000 Pa (4000 N/m²). (c) The pressure increases (to 6000 Pa), because the same force acts on a smaller area.

209|Chapter 4: Energy transfer.teaches: Energy stores and transfers (kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic, thermal, nuclear). Conservation of energy; Sankey-style energy flow. Work done W = Fd; KE = ½mv²; GPE = mgh (g = 10 N/kg); efficiency; power P = E/t and P = W/t. Units J, kW, W. Energy resources: fossil fuels, nuclear, hydroelectric, wind, solar, geothermal, tidal, waves, biofuels; renewable vs non-renewable. Heat transfer by conduction, convection, radiation is covered in Chapter 11 of the book.
209|Chapter 4: Energy transfer.notYet: A Level ideas: work done by a variable or angled force (Fd cosθ), derivation of KE or GPE, momentum and impulse, power as Fv, elastic energy ½kx² derivations, specific heat capacity calculations, entropy, calculus. Also avoid Carnot or thermodynamic efficiency, and electrical energy calculations such as E = IVt.
209|Chapter 4: Energy transfer.example: A crane lifts a 200 kg load through a height of 15 m in 30 s. Take g = 10 N/kg. Calculate (a) the gravitational potential energy gained by the load and (b) the useful power output of the crane. Answer: (a) GPE = mgh = 200 × 10 × 15 = 30 000 J (30 kJ). (b) P = E/t = 30 000 ÷ 30 = 1000 W (1 kW).

209|Chapter 7: Density and floating.teaches: Density = mass ÷ volume (ρ = m/V), units kg/m³ and g/cm³. Measuring mass with a balance and volume by ruler (regular solids), measuring cylinder or displacement (irregular solids, liquids). Rearranging the formula. Floating and sinking: an object floats if its density is less than the liquid's. Comparing densities and converting units (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³).
209|Chapter 7: Density and floating.notYet: Not yet taught: upthrust as a pressure difference, Archimedes' principle calculations, the formula F = ρgV, and pressure in liquids (p = ρgh, which comes in a later chapter). Also avoid hydrometers in detail, the density of gases from the gas laws, specific gravity, and Core-extension 'apparent weight' problems. Avoid A Level fluid dynamics and unfamiliar algebra.
209|Chapter 7: Density and floating.example:
A metal block measures 4.0 cm × 5.0 cm × 2.0 cm and has a mass of 316 g. (a) Calculate its volume. (b) Calculate its density in g/cm³. (c) The density of water is 1.0 g/cm³. Will the block float or sink in water? Explain.

Answer: (a) V = 4.0 × 5.0 × 2.0 = 40 cm³. (b) ρ = m/V = 316 ÷ 40 = 7.9 g/cm³. (c) It sinks, because its density (7.9 g/cm³) is greater than the density of water (1.0 g/cm³).

209|Chapter 8: Temperature and heat.teaches: Thermometers (liquid-in-glass, thermocouple), scale, range, sensitivity, linearity, fixed points 0 °C and 100 °C. Thermal capacity and specific heat capacity, using Q = mcΔT with J, kg, °C. Calculating c by electrical heating (Q = Pt, or VIt). Melting, boiling, evaporation and condensation, with latent heat as energy at constant temperature. Cooling curves and heating curves. Particle explanations.
209|Chapter 8: Temperature and heat.notYet: Kelvin scale and absolute zero, gas laws, kinetic theory equations, internal energy defined as the sum of kinetic and potential energy, Q = mL calculations (specific latent heat is extension or later), heat-loss corrections, entropy, Boltzmann constant, thermodynamic or Celsius definitions beyond fixed points, Stefan's law.
209|Chapter 8: Temperature and heat.example: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium is heated from 20 °C to 60 °C. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is 900 J/(kg °C). Calculate the energy transferred to the block. Answer: Q = mcΔT = 0.50 × 900 × (60 − 20) = 0.50 × 900 × 40 = 18 000 J (18 kJ).

209|Chapter 9: Heat transfer.teaches: Thermal energy moves by conduction (particles vibrating and passing energy on; free electrons in metals), convection (fluids: warmer, less dense fluid rises, cooler denser fluid sinks) and radiation (infrared, needs no medium). Learners know good and bad conductors and insulators, how colour and surface affect emission and absorption, and applications such as vacuum flasks, shiny suits and cooling fins. They do simple experiments and observations.
209|Chapter 9: Heat transfer.notYet: No Stefan-Boltzmann law or T^4, no black-body spectra or wavelength peaks, no U-values or thermal conductivity formulae, no rate calculations (Q = mcΔT is a separate topic), no kinetic theory of gases pressure, no Newton's law of cooling, no quantum or photon explanations of radiation.
209|Chapter 9: Heat transfer.example: A cook uses a saucepan with a shiny metal base and a plastic handle. (a) Explain why the base is made of metal and the handle of plastic. (b) Name the main process by which thermal energy travels through the water in the pan, and describe how it happens. Answer: (a) Metal is a good conductor, so thermal energy passes quickly from the hob to the food. Plastic is a poor conductor (insulator), so the handle stays cool enough to hold. (b) Convection: water at the bottom is heated, expands and becomes less dense, so it rises. Cooler, denser water sinks to take its place, setting up a convection current.

209|Chapter 11: Molecular kinetic theory.teaches: States of matter (solid, liquid, gas) and particle arrangement, spacing and motion; Brownian motion as evidence for moving molecules; gas pressure from molecules colliding with walls; temperature and kinetic energy; absolute zero and Kelvin (T = θ + 273); Boyle's law (pV = constant, p₁V₁ = p₂V₂); effects of heating, volume and temperature on pressure; evaporation.
209|Chapter 11: Molecular kinetic theory.notYet: Ideal gas equation pV = nRT, the mole, Avogadro's number, Maxwell-Boltzmann distributions, root-mean-square speed, ½mv² derivations, pV = ⅓Nmc², Charles's law as a named law, entropy, internal energy formulae, and specific latent heat calculations beyond basics.
209|Chapter 11: Molecular kinetic theory.example: A fixed mass of gas at constant temperature has a volume of 120 cm³ at a pressure of 100 kPa. The gas is compressed to a volume of 40 cm³. (a) Calculate the new pressure. (b) Using ideas about molecules, explain why the pressure increases. Answer: (a) p₁V₁ = p₂V₂, so 100 × 120 = p₂ × 40, giving p₂ = 300 kPa. (b) The same number of molecules are in a smaller volume, so they hit the walls more often (more collisions per second), giving a larger force per unit area and higher pressure.

209|Chapter 10: Changes of state.teaches: Melting, freezing, boiling, evaporation, condensation and solidification. Heating and cooling curves with flat sections at melting and boiling points. Particle model: arrangement, spacing and movement in solids, liquids and gases. Evaporation versus boiling, and what speeds evaporation (temperature, surface area, airflow). Energy is absorbed or released during changes of state. Reading graphs.
209|Chapter 10: Changes of state.notYet: Calculations with specific latent heat (Q = ml) and specific heat capacity (Q = mcΔT). Kinetic energy of particles in joules. Internal energy as the sum of kinetic and potential energy. Intermolecular bonds and Maxwell-Boltzmann ideas. Clausius-Clapeyron, saturated vapour pressure, phase diagrams, triple point. Gas laws. A Level terms.
209|Chapter 10: Changes of state.example: A solid wax is heated steadily and its temperature is recorded. The temperature rises from 20 °C to 60 °C, stays at 60 °C for 5 minutes, then rises again. (a) What is happening to the wax during the 5 minutes at 60 °C? (b) Describe how the arrangement of particles changes during this time. Answer: (a) It is melting (changing from solid to liquid); the temperature stays constant because the energy supplied is used to change state. (b) The particles change from a regular, fixed pattern, vibrating in position, to a disordered arrangement, still close together but able to move past each other.

209|Chapter 12: Thermal properties of ma.teaches: Thermal expansion of solids, liquids and gases (particle explanation, uses and problems such as bridges, rails and bimetallic strips). Thermometers (liquid-in-glass, thermocouple, fixed points). Specific heat capacity, c = ΔE/(mΔT), unit J/(kg °C). Experiments to measure c with a heater, joulemeter or thermometer. Mass in kg, temperature in °C.
209|Chapter 12: Thermal properties of ma.notYet: Latent heat calculations (E = mL) are a separate chapter. Also not yet: kinetic theory equations, gas laws (pV = constant, p1V1/T1 = p2V2/T2), Kelvin-scale calculations, internal energy as a sum of kinetic and potential energy, Maxwell-Boltzmann ideas, heat-loss corrections, coefficients of expansion, and A Level thermal physics.
209|Chapter 12: Thermal properties of ma.example: A 0.50 kg block of aluminium is heated by an electric heater that supplies 9000 J of energy. Its temperature rises from 20 °C to 40 °C. Calculate the specific heat capacity of aluminium, stating its unit. Answer: ΔT = 20 °C; c = E/(mΔT) = 9000 / (0.50 × 20) = 900 J/(kg °C).

209|Chapter 13: Waves.teaches: Transverse and longitudinal waves; wavefronts; amplitude, wavelength, frequency (Hz), period, wave speed. Uses v = fλ and f = 1/T, with rearranging. Reading wave diagrams. Reflection, refraction and diffraction shown with ripple tank wavefronts. Sound waves, compression and rarefaction. Echo speed calculations. Simple SI units, with kHz and ms conversions.
209|Chapter 13: Waves.notYet: Snell's law and refractive index (n = sin i / sin r), critical angle and total internal reflection (a later chapter on light), the electromagnetic spectrum, Doppler effect, interference and path difference, superposition, standing waves, phase difference, intensity, and the derivation of v = fλ. Also avoid decibels and wave-particle ideas.
209|Chapter 13: Waves.example:
A wave in the sea has a distance of 12 m between two neighbouring crests. A floating cork rises and falls 5 times in 10 s as the waves pass. (a) State the wavelength. (b) Calculate the frequency. (c) Calculate the speed of the wave.

Answer: (a) 12 m. (b) f = 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5 Hz. (c) v = fλ = 0.5 × 12 = 6 m/s.

209|Chapter 14: Properties of waves.teaches: Wave terms: wavefront, amplitude, wavelength, frequency, period, crest, trough. Reading these from transverse wave diagrams. Using v = fλ and T = 1/f with simple numbers. Reflection, refraction (waves slow down in shallow water, wavelength shortens, frequency unchanged) and diffraction through gaps and around obstacles. Ripple tank. Sound as longitudinal. Light and sound speeds.
209|Chapter 14: Properties of waves.notYet: Not taught: refractive index n = sin i/sin r, critical angle, total internal reflection (Chapter 15). Also not taught: Huygens' principle, path difference, interference or superposition, Doppler effect, phase difference in radians, standing waves, wave-particle duality, and diffraction gratings. Avoid quantitative Snell's law calculations.
209|Chapter 14: Properties of waves.example: Water waves in a ripple tank have a frequency of 5.0 Hz and a wavelength of 3.0 cm. (a) Calculate the speed of the waves. (b) The waves move into shallower water, where they slow down. State what happens to the frequency and to the wavelength. Answer: (a) v = fλ = 5.0 × 3.0 = 15 cm/s (0.15 m/s). (b) The frequency stays the same at 5.0 Hz; the wavelength decreases.

209|Chapter 17: Refraction of light.teaches: Refraction as change of direction when light crosses a boundary because its speed changes. Normal, angle of incidence i, angle of refraction r (measured from the normal). Air to glass bends toward the normal. Refractive index n = sin i / sin r, and n = c/v. Critical angle, total internal reflection, sin c = 1/n. Prisms, optical fibres, thin lenses, ray diagrams, and apparent depth.
209|Chapter 17: Refraction of light.notYet: Not yet taught: Snell's law with different media written as n1 sin θ1 = n2 sin θ2, dispersion calculations, Fresnel equations, polarisation, wave-front (Huygens) derivations, the lens formula 1/u+1/v=1/f, magnification calculations, and the physics of the eye or of telescopes. Avoid A Level optics.
209|Chapter 17: Refraction of light.example: A ray of light travels from air into a glass block. The angle of incidence is 40° and the angle of refraction is 25°. (a) Calculate the refractive index of the glass. (b) State what happens to the speed of light as it enters the glass. Answer: (a) n = sin 40° / sin 25° = 0.643 / 0.423 = 1.5 (1.52). (b) The speed decreases, and the ray bends toward the normal.

209|Chapter 15: Light.teaches: Reflection: law (angle of incidence = angle of reflection), normal, plane mirror images (virtual, same size, same distance behind). Refraction: bending at boundaries, n = sin i / sin r, critical angle, total internal reflection, optical fibres, prisms. Converging and diverging lenses, focal length, principal axis, ray diagrams, real and virtual images, magnifying glass. Dispersion, the spectrum, monochromatic light, speed of light 3.0×10⁸ m/s.
209|Chapter 15: Light.notYet: Not taught: Snell's law derived from wave theory, lens equation 1/u+1/v=1/f, magnification calculations by formula, diffraction, interference, polarisation, photon energy, refractive index as c/v for A Level, lens aberrations, compound microscope or telescope, thin-film effects, wave-particle duality.
209|Chapter 15: Light.example:
A ray of light travels from air into glass. It hits the boundary with an angle of incidence of 45° and the angle of refraction is 28°. (a) Calculate the refractive index of the glass. (b) State what happens to the speed of light as it enters the glass.

Answer: (a) n = sin i / sin r = sin 45° / sin 28° = 0.707 / 0.469 = 1.5 (about 1.51). (b) The light slows down, and bends towards the normal.

209|Chapter 16: Reflection of light.teaches: Light reflection at plane mirrors: the law of reflection (angle of incidence = angle of reflection, both measured from the normal). Ray diagrams with ruler and protractor. Properties of the plane-mirror image (same size, upright, virtual, same distance behind the mirror, laterally inverted). Locating images by construction. Uses: periscopes, ambulance writing. Experiment: pin method.
209|Chapter 16: Reflection of light.notYet: Refraction, Snell's law, refractive index, critical angle and total internal reflection (later chapters). Curved mirrors, concave mirror focal length, mirror formula, magnification calculations. Wave-front or Huygens explanations, polarisation, diffraction, and optical fibres. Do not ask for calculations with v = fλ.
209|Chapter 16: Reflection of light.example: A ray of light hits a plane mirror. The angle between the incident ray and the mirror surface is 30°. (a) What is the angle of incidence? (b) What is the angle of reflection? Answer: (a) The angle of incidence is measured from the normal, so it is 90° − 30° = 60°. (b) The angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, so it is 60°.

209|Chapter 20: Sound.teaches: Sound as a longitudinal wave from vibrating sources, with compressions and rarefactions. It needs a medium and cannot travel through a vacuum. Speed is roughly 330 m/s in air, higher in liquids and higher still in solids. Learners use v = d/t, including echoes (distance doubled). They know frequency in Hz, amplitude as loudness, and pitch. Hearing range is 20 Hz to 20 kHz, and ultrasound lies above it. They read oscilloscope traces and use v = fλ.
209|Chapter 20: Sound.notYet: Not taught: decibel scale or intensity calculations, Doppler effect, standing waves and resonance in pipes, harmonics, beats, interference of sound, formal derivations of the speed of sound from elasticity and density, and Fourier analysis. Do not ask about the temperature dependence of sound speed in formulae, or about acoustic impedance.
209|Chapter 20: Sound.example:
A ship's sonar sends an ultrasound pulse down to the sea bed and detects the echo 0.40 s later. The speed of sound in sea water is 1500 m/s. Calculate the depth of the water.

Answer: The pulse travels to the sea bed and back, so total distance = speed × time = 1500 × 0.40 = 600 m. Depth = 600 ÷ 2 = 300 m.

209|Chapter 19: The human eye.teaches: Structure and function of the eye: cornea, iris, pupil, lens, retina, optic nerve, ciliary muscles, suspensory ligaments. Light is refracted to form a real, inverted image on the retina. Accommodation (changing lens shape) for near and distant objects. Short and long sight, their causes, and correction with diverging or converging lenses. Pupil reflex in bright and dim light.
209|Chapter 19: The human eye.notYet: No lens formula or power in dioptres. No calculating focal length or image distance. No rod and cone biochemistry, no neural pathways, and no A Level optics (diffraction, resolution limits). No astigmatism or cataract surgery. Ray-tracing is qualitative only. Do not require biology detail such as the fovea or blind spot.
209|Chapter 19: The human eye.example:
A person with short sight sees distant objects as blurred. (a) State where the image of a distant object is formed in this eye. (b) Name the type of lens in glasses that corrects this. 

Answer: (a) In front of the retina, because the eye's lens is too strong or the eyeball is too long, so the light rays are focused too soon. (b) A diverging (concave) lens, which spreads the rays slightly before they enter the eye so the image falls on the retina.

209|Chapter 18: Lenses.teaches: Converging and diverging lenses; refraction through lenses; principal axis, optical centre, principal focus (focal point) and focal length. Ray diagrams with three standard rays for real and virtual images. Image properties: real/virtual, upright/inverted, magnified/diminished. Magnifying glass use. Short-sight and long-sight correction with lenses. Simple scale drawing.
209|Chapter 18: Lenses.notYet: Lens formula 1/u + 1/v = 1/f, power in dioptres, and the magnification formula with calculations. Also not taught: the lensmaker's equation, refractive index calculations with Snell's law, aberrations, and compound microscope or telescope ray analysis. Diverging lens real images and sign conventions are also beyond this level.
209|Chapter 18: Lenses.example: An object is placed 6 cm from a converging lens of focal length 10 cm, so it is closer to the lens than the principal focus. (a) State the distance of 10 cm using the correct term. (b) Describe the image formed, using three words. (c) Name a device that uses a lens in this way. Answer: (a) focal length. (b) virtual, upright, magnified. (c) magnifying glass.

209|Chapter 21: Properties of sound.teaches: Sound is a longitudinal wave from vibrating sources and needs a medium. Compression and rarefaction. Frequency in Hz, pitch, amplitude and loudness. Audible range about 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz. Speed of sound in solids, liquids and gases (about 330 m/s in air). Echoes and v = d/t. Ultrasound. Reading oscilloscope traces. Measuring the speed of sound.
209|Chapter 21: Properties of sound.notYet: No decibel calculations or logarithmic scales, intensity in W/m², Doppler effect, standing waves, resonance in pipes, harmonics or overtones, Fourier analysis, or derivation of v = √(γP/ρ). No A Level wave equations. Don't ask for calculations of oscilloscope time-base settings beyond simple period = 1/f.
209|Chapter 21: Properties of sound.example: An oscilloscope shows two sounds, A and B. Trace B has the same height as trace A but twice as many waves across the screen. Describe how sound B differs from sound A. Answer: B has a higher frequency, so a higher pitch. It has the same amplitude, so the same loudness.

209|Chapter 23: Magnetism.teaches: Magnetic and non-magnetic materials (iron, steel, nickel, cobalt). Poles: like repel, unlike attract. Magnetic fields, field lines drawn N to S, closer together where stronger. Plotting with compasses. Induced magnetism. Magnetically hard (steel) and soft (iron) materials. Making magnets and demagnetising. Uses of electromagnets.
209|Chapter 23: Magnetism.notYet: Not yet: magnetic flux density in tesla, force on a current-carrying wire (F=BIL), Fleming's left-hand rule calculations, electromagnetic induction, transformers, domain theory in depth, Earth's core dynamo, hysteresis, magnetic permeability. Avoid quantitative field-strength calculations. Motor and induction topics belong to later chapters.
209|Chapter 23: Magnetism.example: A student brings the north pole of a bar magnet close to an unmagnetised iron nail. The nail is attracted to the magnet. (a) Explain why the nail is attracted. (b) State which type of pole is produced at the end of the nail nearest the magnet. Answer: (a) The magnet induces magnetism in the iron nail, so the nail becomes a temporary magnet, and unlike poles attract. (b) A south pole is produced at the nearest end.

209|Chapter 22: Hearing.teaches: Chapter 22 (Sound, Hearing): sound as a longitudinal wave from vibrations; needs a medium, no sound in a vacuum; compressions and rarefactions; speed in solids > liquids > gases (about 330–340 m/s in air); frequency in Hz, audible range 20–20 000 Hz; ultrasound; amplitude and loudness, frequency and pitch; echoes; v = d/t; v = fλ; oscilloscope traces; the ear.
209|Chapter 22: Hearing.notYet: Decibel scale and intensity calculations; the physics of resonance and standing waves in pipes; Doppler effect; superposition and interference of sound; speed of sound formulae from bulk modulus or temperature; detailed cochlea mechanics; Fourier analysis; and the ultrasound imaging calculations of A Level.
209|Chapter 22: Hearing.example: A student stands 85 m from a tall wall and claps once. She hears the echo 0.50 s later. Calculate the speed of sound in air. Answer: the sound travels there and back, so the distance is 2 × 85 = 170 m. Speed = distance ÷ time = 170 ÷ 0.50 = 340 m/s.

209|Chapter 24: Electromagnetism.teaches: Magnetic field of a current-carrying wire, circular field lines and the right-hand grip idea; solenoid field like a bar magnet; electromagnets (soft iron core, more turns or more current gives a stronger field); uses such as relays and electric bells; force on a current-carrying wire in a field and Fleming's left-hand rule; the simple d.c. motor with split-ring commutator; ways to increase motor speed.
209|Chapter 24: Electromagnetism.notYet: Not taught: F = BIL or magnetic flux density calculations, Faraday's and Lenz's laws and induced e.m.f. calculations (these come in the next chapter), force on a moving charge (qvB), flux linkage, hysteresis, back e.m.f., a.c. motor details, and transformer equations. Also avoid formulae for solenoid field strength.
209|Chapter 24: Electromagnetism.example: A student makes an electromagnet by winding insulated wire around an iron nail and connecting it to a battery. State two ways she could make the electromagnet stronger. Answer: Increase the number of turns of wire on the nail; increase the current (for example by adding another cell or using a higher voltage). Any two of these ideas, or using a larger soft-iron core, earn the marks.

209|Chapter 27: The motor effect.teaches: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (motor effect). Force direction is found with Fleming's left-hand rule (thumb = force/motion, first finger = field N to S, second finger = conventional current). Force is larger with a stronger field or larger current. Reversing current or field reverses the force. Simple d.c. motor: coil, split-ring commutator, brushes. Qualitative explanation only.
209|Chapter 27: The motor effect.notYet: No F = BIL calculations, magnetic flux density in tesla, or flux linkage. No Lenz's law, back-emf, or motor efficiency. No electromagnetic induction or generators (later chapters). No vector cross products, circular motion of charges (F = Bqv), Hall effect, or torque equations.
209|Chapter 27: The motor effect.example:
A straight wire carrying a current is placed between the north and south poles of a magnet, with the magnetic field pointing from left to right. The wire is pushed upwards. (a) Name this effect. (b) State two ways to increase the force on the wire. (c) The current is reversed. State what happens to the direction of the force.

Answer: (a) The motor effect. (b) Increase the current; use a stronger magnet (stronger magnetic field). (c) The force is reversed, so the wire is pushed downwards.

209|Chapter 26: Forces on currents in ma.topic: Chapter 26: Forces on currents in magnetic fields
209|Chapter 26: Forces on currents in ma.teaches: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force. The force reverses if the current or the field direction reverses. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction. The force is larger with a stronger field or a larger current. Applications are the simple d.c. motor (coil, split-ring commutator, brushes) and the moving-coil loudspeaker. Also covered are the ammeter/galvanometer, and the energy transfer electrical to kinetic.
209|Chapter 26: Forces on currents in ma.notYet: Not required: F = BIL calculations, magnetic flux density in tesla, flux linkage, Lenz's law, back e.m.f., the Hall effect, force between parallel wires, F = Bqv, or circular motion of charges. Also avoid generator and transformer calculations, which belong to the electromagnetic induction chapter. Avoid torque formulae.
209|Chapter 26: Forces on currents in ma.example:
A straight wire carrying a current lies at right angles to a magnetic field between two magnets, and the wire is pushed upwards. (a) State two changes that would each make the wire be pushed downwards. (b) State one change that would increase the size of the force. (c) Name the part of a d.c. motor that reverses the current in the coil every half turn.

Answer: (a) Reverse the direction of the current; reverse the direction of the magnetic field (swap the magnet poles). (b) Increase the current, or use stronger magnets. (c) The split-ring commutator.

209|Chapter 28: Generators.teaches: Electromagnetic induction: an e.m.f. is induced when a conductor cuts magnetic field lines or the flux linking a coil changes. Factors: speed of movement, field strength, number of turns, coil area. Simple a.c. generator (coil, magnet, slip rings, brushes), the shape of the output graph, and how rotation speed changes peak voltage and frequency. Also the direction of the induced current (Lenz's law, in words), and d.c. versus a.c.
209|Chapter 28: Generators.notYet: Faraday's law as an equation (e.m.f. = rate of change of flux), magnetic flux in webers, formulae for e.m.f. = BLv or NBAω, r.m.s. and peak value calculations, three-phase supply, back e.m.f., self-inductance, eddy current calculations, and Fleming's rules beyond their qualitative use.
209|Chapter 28: Generators.example:
An a.c. generator has a coil rotating between the poles of a magnet. (a) Explain why an e.m.f. is induced in the coil as it turns. (b) State two ways of increasing the peak e.m.f. produced. (c) What happens to the frequency of the output if the coil is rotated faster? 

Answer: (a) The coil's wires cut through the magnetic field lines (the magnetic field linking the coil changes), so an e.m.f. is induced. (b) Any two of: rotate the coil faster; use a stronger magnet; use more turns on the coil; use a coil with a larger area. (c) The frequency increases (and the peak e.m.f. also increases).

209|Chapter 25: The magnetic effect of c.topic: Chapter 25: The magnetic effect of current
209|Chapter 25: The magnetic effect of c.teaches: Current in a wire produces a magnetic field. Field lines around a straight wire are concentric circles, further apart as distance increases. Direction is found with the right-hand grip rule. A solenoid has a bar-magnet-like field, and its poles are found from the current direction. Field strength rises with more current, more turns and an iron core. Electromagnets are used in relays, circuit breakers and bells. The motor effect is introduced with Fleming's left-hand rule.
209|Chapter 25: The magnetic effect of c.notYet: Avoid A Level ideas: magnetic flux density B in tesla, F=BIL, F=Bqv, the formula B=μ₀I/2πr, Lenz's law, and flux linkage. Avoid electromagnetic induction calculations, transformer equations and detailed DC motor torque. Avoid Ampère's law and domain theory.
209|Chapter 25: The magnetic effect of c.example: A student wraps insulated wire around an iron nail and connects it to a battery to make an electromagnet. (a) State two ways to make the electromagnet stronger. (b) Conventional current flows around the coil clockwise when viewed from the left end. State how you can tell which end is the north pole. Answer: (a) Increase the current (e.g. add another cell) and increase the number of turns of wire (an iron core is already present). (b) Look at the end of the coil. If the current flows anticlockwise, that end is a north pole. If it flows clockwise, that end is a south pole. So the end viewed is a south pole, and the other end is a north pole.

209|Chapter 29: The transmission of elec.teaches: Power transmission by the National Grid: step-up transformer raises voltage so current falls and power loss (P = I²R) falls in cables. Transformer structure (primary, secondary, soft iron core, alternating current). Equations Vp/Vs = Np/Ns and VpIp = VsIs for 100% efficiency. P = IV. Advantages of high-voltage overhead lines, and step-down transformers for homes.
209|Chapter 29: The transmission of elec.notYet: Not taught: three-phase supply, reactance, impedance, RMS and peak values, mutual inductance, Faraday's law equations (EMF = −N dΦ/dt), eddy current calculations, real efficiency percentages beyond a simple ratio, power factor, capacitors, or DC transmission. Avoid transformers with variable load or phasor diagrams.
209|Chapter 29: The transmission of elec.example: A transformer has 200 turns on the primary coil and 2000 turns on the secondary coil. The primary is connected to a 230 V a.c. supply. The secondary is connected to a device that draws 0.50 A. Assume the transformer is 100% efficient. (a) Calculate the secondary voltage. (b) Calculate the current in the primary coil. Answer: (a) Vs = Vp × Ns/Np = 230 × 2000/200 = 2300 V. (b) Power out = 2300 × 0.50 = 1150 W; Ip = 1150/230 = 5.0 A (5.00 to two decimal places).

209|Chapter 31: Electric motors.teaches: A current-carrying wire in a magnetic field feels a force (motor effect). Fleming's left-hand rule gives the directions. A simple d.c. motor has a coil, permanent magnets, a split-ring commutator and carbon brushes. The commutator reverses the current every half turn, so the coil keeps turning. Speed and force increase with more turns, a stronger magnet or a larger current. Reversing the current or the field reverses the rotation. Everyday uses of motors.
209|Chapter 31: Electric motors.notYet: Not required: F = BIL calculations, magnetic flux, torque or moment calculations, back e.m.f., a.c. motors, induction or brushless motors, motor efficiency calculations, Lenz's law, and the mathematics of the field around a wire or between poles. Generators and transformers belong to other chapters.
209|Chapter 31: Electric motors.example:
The diagram shows a simple d.c. motor with a coil between two magnets. (a) State the job of the split-ring commutator. (b) State two ways to make the coil turn faster. (c) State what happens to the direction of rotation if both the current and the magnetic field are reversed.

Answer: (a) It reverses the direction of the current in the coil every half turn, so the force keeps the coil rotating in the same direction. (b) Any two of: increase the current, use a stronger magnet, add more turns to the coil. (c) It stays the same, because reversing both reverses the force twice.

209|Chapter 30: Electric circuits.teaches: Circuit symbols and diagrams (cell, battery, switch, lamp, resistor, variable resistor, ammeter, voltmeter, fuse, LDR, thermistor, diode). Current in series and parallel, p.d. sharing, V = IR, ohmic and non-ohmic I–V graphs, combined resistance (series R1+R2, parallel is lower), and potential divider basics. Units: A, V, Ω, C, J. Q = It, E = QV. Uses simple numbers.
209|Chapter 30: Electric circuits.notYet: Kirchhoff's laws by name, internal resistance or emf calculations, Thevenin methods, reactance, capacitors, time constants, RMS values, or the derivation of the parallel formula. Also no complex mixed networks, no potential divider derivations from first principles, and no power-loss analysis of cables.
209|Chapter 30: Electric circuits.example: Two resistors of 4.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω are connected in series to a 12 V battery. (a) Calculate the total resistance. (b) Calculate the current in the circuit. (c) Calculate the p.d. across the 6.0 Ω resistor. Answer: (a) 4.0 + 6.0 = 10 Ω. (b) I = V/R = 12/10 = 1.2 A. (c) V = IR = 1.2 × 6.0 = 7.2 V.

209|Chapter 32: Electronic devices.teaches: Analogue vs digital signals; electronic components and symbols (LDR, thermistor, variable resistor, diode, LED, relay, transistor as a switch); potential divider with two resistors in series, using V1 = V_in × R1/(R1+R2); sensing circuits (light/temperature); logic gates NOT, AND, OR, NAND, NOR with truth tables; relay uses.
209|Chapter 32: Electronic devices.notYet: No transistor gain or bipolar current equations (Ib, Ic, hFE), no op-amps or comparators, no Boolean algebra or XOR, no combining more than two gates, no Thevenin or loaded potential dividers, no capacitors/RC time constants, no diode I-V curve analysis, no rectification waveforms or ripple.
209|Chapter 32: Electronic devices.example:
A potential divider has a 6.0 V supply connected across a fixed 4.0 kΩ resistor in series with a thermistor. At a high temperature the thermistor resistance falls to 2.0 kΩ. (a) Calculate the potential difference across the fixed resistor. (b) State whether the p.d. across the thermistor rises or falls as the temperature rises, and explain briefly.

Answer: (a) Total resistance = 4.0 + 2.0 = 6.0 kΩ. V across fixed resistor = 6.0 × 4.0/6.0 = 4.0 V (the thermistor has 2.0 V). (b) It falls: as the thermistor's resistance decreases, it takes a smaller share of the supply voltage, so the p.d. across it drops and the p.d. across the fixed resistor rises.

209|Chapter 2: Describing motion.teaches: Speed = distance ÷ time, with average speed and units m/s and km/h. Distance–time graphs: flat line means stationary, straight slope means constant speed, steeper means faster, and gradient gives speed. Acceleration as change in speed per unit time, a = (v − u)/t, in m/s². Speed–time graphs show speeding up, slowing down and constant speed.
209|Chapter 2: Describing motion.notYet: Not yet taught in this chapter: the vector/scalar distinction, velocity and displacement. Also not covered: the equations of motion (v² = u² + 2as, s = ut + ½at²), areas under graphs for distance (this comes in later chapters), tangents on curved graphs, free fall with g, terminal velocity, Newton's laws and F = ma, and calculus.
209|Chapter 2: Describing motion.example: A cyclist accelerates from rest to 8.0 m/s in 4.0 s. Calculate her acceleration. Answer: a = (v − u) ÷ t = (8.0 − 0) ÷ 4.0 = 2.0 m/s².

209|Chapter 33: Radioactive materials.teaches: Atomic structure: protons, neutrons, electrons, their relative charges and masses. Proton (atomic) number Z, nucleon (mass) number A, nuclide notation, isotopes. Background radiation and its sources. Detecting radiation (Geiger-Müller counter). Properties of alpha, beta, gamma: ionising power, penetration, deflection in fields. Decay equations, half-life from graphs/tables, uses, safety.
209|Chapter 33: Radioactive materials.notYet: Not at IGCSE: binding energy, E=mc², mass defect, neutrinos/antineutrinos, quarks, exponential decay formula N=N0e^-λt, decay constant, activity in becquerels calculations, mass spectrometry, nuclear fission/fusion energy calculations, A Level ideas such as the inverse-square law for gamma, and random-decay statistics.
209|Chapter 33: Radioactive materials.example:
A nucleus of radium-226 (proton number 88) emits an alpha particle. (a) State the number of neutrons in a radium-226 nucleus. (b) State the proton number and nucleon number of the nucleus formed. [3 marks]

Answer: (a) 226 − 88 = 138 neutrons. (b) An alpha particle is a helium nucleus (4 nucleons, 2 protons), so the new nucleus has proton number 86 and nucleon number 222.

209|Chapter 34: Nuclear reactions.teaches: Nuclear fission (U-235 absorbs a neutron, splits into two smaller nuclei plus neutrons, releases energy, chain reaction) and nuclear fusion (light nuclei such as hydrogen isotopes join to form helium; the Sun's energy; very high temperature and pressure needed). Learners write balanced nuclear equations using nucleon and proton numbers, and know the isotopes 2H and 3H. They compare fission and fusion, and know about reactors, control rods and moderators at an outline level.
209|Chapter 34: Nuclear reactions.notYet: Not required: E = mc² or mass defect calculations, binding energy per nucleon curves, critical mass, reactor engineering detail, quantum tunnelling, Coulomb barrier calculations, neutrinos or positrons in the proton–proton chain, and half-life calculations (covered in radioactivity chapters).
209|Chapter 34: Nuclear reactions.example: Question: In a nuclear fusion reaction, two hydrogen nuclei (deuterium, 2H with proton number 1) join to form a helium nucleus (3He with proton number 2) and one other particle. (a) What is the other particle? (b) Explain why fusion needs a very high temperature. Answer: (a) A neutron (nucleon number 2+2 = 4 = 3+1; proton number 1+1 = 2 = 2+0). (b) Nuclei are positively charged and repel each other. At very high temperature they move fast enough to overcome this repulsion and get close enough to fuse.

209|Chapter 1: Making measurements.teaches: Measuring length and volume with rulers, vernier and micrometer scales, and measuring cylinders. Reading scales and finding zero errors. Measuring small quantities by taking many (e.g. 40 pins, 20 swings). Density = mass ÷ volume (g/cm³, kg/m³), including irregular solids by displacement. Timing with stopwatches. Pendulum period, T = total time ÷ number of oscillations.
209|Chapter 1: Making measurements.notYet: Not taught: uncertainty calculations or percentage error, significant-figure error propagation, vectors and scalars, speed and acceleration, pressure in liquids (p = ρgh), weight and gravitational field strength, moments, SHM equations, T = 2π√(l/g), logarithmic graphs, and relative density.
209|Chapter 1: Making measurements.example: A student wants an accurate period for a pendulum. She times 20 complete swings and gets 36.4 s. (a) Calculate the period. (b) Explain why timing 20 swings is better than timing 1 swing. Answer: (a) 36.4 ÷ 20 = 1.82 s. (b) Human reaction-time error in starting and stopping the stopwatch is about the same size in both cases, but it is a much smaller fraction of a long time. This makes the period more precise, and the error is shared across 20 swings.

209|Chapter 3: Forces and motion.teaches: Force as push/pull changing speed, direction or shape; resultant force; F = ma (N, kg, m/s²); W = mg with g = 10 N/kg; mass vs weight; gravitational field strength; free fall, air resistance, terminal velocity and speed–time graphs; scalars vs vectors; adding collinear forces and simple vector diagrams; momentum p = mv and conservation (simple collisions).
209|Chapter 3: Forces and motion.notYet: No calculus, SUVAT equations, resolving forces into components with trigonometry, impulse as FΔt (unless the syllabus extension is flagged), centripetal force formula mv²/r, Newton's law of gravitation, drag equations, relativistic mass, or inelastic/elastic energy-loss analysis in 2D.
209|Chapter 3: Forces and motion.example:
