A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 3000 N forwards and a resistive force of 600 N backwards. (a) Calculate the resultant force. (b) Calculate the car's acceleration.

Answer: (a) 3000 − 600 = 2400 N forwards. (b) a = F/m = 2400 ÷ 1200 = 2 m/s².

209|Chapter 5: Forces and matter.teaches: Forces change size, shape or motion of solids; compression, tension, bending, stretching, twisting. Load–extension graphs for springs and elastic cords; extension = length − original length. Hooke's law: extension proportional to load; limit of proportionality; elastic vs plastic behaviour. Pressure = force ÷ area (p = F/A), in Pa or N/m²; area in cm² and m²; effects of area on pressure.
209|Chapter 5: Forces and matter.notYet: Not taught: Young modulus, stress, strain, energy stored in a spring (area under graph, ½kx²), spring constant for springs in series/parallel, yield point, fluid pressure p = ρgh (comes in later chapters), atmospheric pressure calculations, gas laws, Pa-to-kPa derivations, calculus, vector resolution.
209|Chapter 5: Forces and matter.example: A spring has an original length of 10.0 cm. A load of 2.0 N stretches it to 14.0 cm. The spring obeys Hooke's law. (a) State the extension. (b) What is the length of the spring with a load of 3.0 N? Answer: (a) 14.0 − 10.0 = 4.0 cm. (b) Extension is proportional to load, so 3.0 N gives 4.0 × 3.0/2.0 = 6.0 cm extension, length = 10.0 + 6.0 = 16.0 cm.

209|Chapter 6: Energy transformations an.topic: Chapter 6: Energy transformations and energy transfers
209|Chapter 6: Energy transformations an.teaches: Energy stores (kinetic, gravitational potential, chemical, elastic, thermal, nuclear, electrical) and transfers (mechanical work, electrical, heating, waves). Sankey-style energy conversions, conservation of energy, efficiency. Calculations: Ek = ½mv², ΔEp = mgΔh (g = 10 N/kg), W = Fd, P = E/t. Units: J, kJ, W.
209|Chapter 6: Energy transformations an.notYet: Not yet taught: relativistic energy (E = mc²), work done with force at an angle, exponential decay, Gibbs/free energy, entropy, specific heat capacity calculations (Chapter 11), derivation of Ek from equations of motion, power as F×v, elastic energy ½kx² calculations, A Level terms (internal energy, efficiency in thermodynamic cycles).
209|Chapter 6: Energy transformations an.example: A skier of mass 60 kg stands at the top of a slope 50 m higher than the bottom. (a) Calculate the gravitational potential energy she loses going to the bottom (g = 10 N/kg). (b) Assuming no energy is lost to friction or air resistance, calculate her speed at the bottom. Answer: (a) ΔEp = mgΔh = 60 × 10 × 50 = 30 000 J (30 kJ). (b) Ek = ½mv² = 30 000, so v² = 2 × 30 000 ÷ 60 = 1000, v ≈ 32 m/s.

209|Chapter 7: Energy resources.teaches: Energy resources: fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas), nuclear fuel, biofuels, wood as non-renewable vs renewable; wind, waves, tides, hydroelectric, geothermal, solar. Electricity generation, advantages and disadvantages (cost, reliability, pollution, CO2). Sun's energy from nuclear fusion of hydrogen to helium. Energy comes from the Sun. Simple world energy use data and graphs.
209|Chapter 7: Energy resources.notYet: Not yet taught in this chapter: E=mc² calculations, binding energy, mass defect, fission chain reaction details, efficiency calculations, power = energy/time, kWh costs, stellar life cycles, Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams, proton-proton chain steps, quantum or photovoltaic physics.
209|Chapter 7: Energy resources.example:
Question: Name the nuclear process that releases energy in the Sun, and state one reason why wind power is described as renewable but coal is not.
Answer: Nuclear fusion (hydrogen nuclei join to form helium). Wind is renewable because it is continually replaced by the Sun's heating of the atmosphere and will not run out; coal takes millions of years to form, so it is used up faster than it is replaced.

209|Chapter 4: Turning effects of forces.teaches: Moment = force × perpendicular distance from the pivot (N m, or N cm). Turning effect and pivot. Principle of moments: for equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments = sum of anticlockwise moments. Simple balanced beams, metre rules and see-saws. Centre of mass, including finding it for a lamina by plumb line. Stable, unstable and neutral equilibrium. Low centre of mass and wide base increase stability. Tilt angle.
209|Chapter 4: Turning effects of forces.notYet: Not needed: torque and couples as defined terms, moment of inertia, angular momentum, resolving forces at angles, trigonometry (sin/cos) for moments, calculus for centres of mass, beams with several unknown support forces, and A Level rotational dynamics. Avoid moment questions where the force is not perpendicular to the distance.
209|Chapter 4: Turning effects of forces.example: A uniform metre rule is balanced at its 50 cm mark. A 4.0 N weight hangs at the 20 cm mark. At which mark must a 3.0 N weight hang on the other side to balance the rule? Answer: The 4.0 N weight is 30 cm from the pivot. Anticlockwise moment = 4.0 × 30 = 120 N cm. Clockwise moment must equal this: 3.0 × d = 120, so d = 40 cm. The mark is 50 + 40 = 90 cm.

209|Chapter 8: Work and power.teaches: Work done = force × distance moved in the direction of the force (W = Fd), in joules. Energy transfer: work done equals energy transferred, including g.p.e. (mgh) and k.e. (½mv²). Power = work ÷ time = energy transferred ÷ time, in watts (W, kW). Simple numerical problems, with g = 10 N/kg and rearranging equations. Cases with no work, e.g. a force with no movement.
209|Chapter 8: Work and power.notYet: Force at an angle to the motion (resolving components, W = Fd cosθ). Power = Fv. Efficiency calculations (they come later in the course). Variable forces, work as the area under a force–distance graph, calculus, or power in AC circuits (P = IV). Also avoid the A Level terms 'rate of change' and 'momentum'.
209|Chapter 8: Work and power.example:
A crane lifts a 200 kg load vertically through 15 m in 20 s. Take g = 10 N/kg. a) Calculate the work done by the crane. b) Calculate the power of the crane.

Answer: a) Weight = 200 × 10 = 2000 N. Work done = force × distance = 2000 × 15 = 30 000 J (30 kJ). b) Power = work ÷ time = 30 000 ÷ 20 = 1500 W (1.5 kW).
